mechanisms.category: Gear spinners / fidget gears (spur, helical, herringbone gear rings, gear bearings)
mechanisms.examples: Printables search counts as of 2026-10-15 (fuzzy search, so treat as upper bounds): 'gear fidget' 572 results, 'fidget spinner' 1,085, 'gear bearing' 137. Gear Fidget https://www.printables.com/model/550127-gear-fidget (5.7k likes); Gear Fidget Spinner https://www.printables.com/model/558900-gear-fidget-spinner; Perfect Gear Bearing https://www.printables.com/model/114535-perfect-gear-bearing (18.6k downloads); Emmett's original Gear Bearing, Thingiverse thing:53451 (mirror https://www.3dgo.app/models/thingiverse/53451); MakerWorld Kinetic Fidget Gear https://makerworld.com/models/3030090 (0.4 mm clearances); Gear Fidget Ring https://www.printables.com/model/551263-gear-fidget-ring-print-in-place; Spinning Gear Fidget Button https://printables.com/model/122042-spinning-gear-fidget-button-print-in-place; Cross-axis helical https://makerworld.com/models/2199646
mechanisms.how_it_works: Captive involute gears mesh inside a frame or ring. Helical or herringbone teeth hold the gears axially, so the parts cannot fall out. You get continuous spin, and the gear ratios give visual interest.
mechanisms.print_in_place: Yes. This is the archetypal print-in-place fidget: rotation axes run along Z, with a 0.3-0.4 mm mesh gap and herringbone teeth for retention.

mechanisms.category: Planetary / epicyclic spinners (including eccentric and multi-speed planetaries)
mechanisms.examples: Printables 'planetary gear fidget' 68 results. Planetary Gear Fidget Toy 100% PIP https://www.printables.com/model/744660-planetary-gear-fidget-toy-100-print-in-place (31k downloads); https://www.printables.com/model/1130329-print-in-place-planetary-gear-fidget-spinner; The Eccentric Gear Fidget (off-centre sun) https://www.printables.com/model/900241-the-eccentric-gear-fidget; Eccentric Planetary Gears 12 https://www.printables.com/model/1755291-eccentric-planetary-gears-12; PIP eccentric cycloid planetary https://www.printables.com/model/184669-print-in-place-eccentric-cycloid-planetary-gear; 'Planetario' split-ring 4-speed (x1, x1/2, x1/4, x1/16), whose author says it was collision-checked in code: https://www.printables.com/model/1862543; MakerWorld 2-tooth planet ring https://makerworld.com/models/1692091
mechanisms.how_it_works: A sun, planets and a ring gear. Holding one member and turning another gives a fixed ratio, so differential speeds are visible. Split-ring and compound versions add more speed stages.
mechanisms.print_in_place: Yes, routinely, as one flat print with a ~0.35 mm mesh gap. Eccentric versions can pop apart: the 900241 author reports some units disassembled by themselves.

mechanisms.examples: Nested Hypocycloid Spinner (print-in-place, may fuse) https://www.printables.com/model/143028-nested-hypocycloid-spinner-fidget-toy (93 likes); Hypocycloid teaching fidget https://www.printables.com/model/450158-hypocycloid; Tusi Couple illusion (motor, 64T in 128T ring, magnets dragging steel balls; not a hand fidget and not print-in-place) https://www.printables.com/model/1757607 (4 likes). Searches for 'cardan gear' found no fidgets. Theory: https://www.firgelliauto.com/blogs/mechanisms/cardan-straight-line-mechanism
mechanisms.how_it_works: A pinion rolls inside a ring of twice its pitch diameter, so every point on the pinion's pitch circle traces a straight diameter with sinusoidal speed. Several points together look like a rotating circle.
mechanisms.print_in_place: Possible: a planet in a ring with a carrier arm (143028 does it). No one has published a hand-held, print-in-place Tusi fidget that drives a character feature.

mechanisms.print_in_place: Yes. The flexures are in-plane and printed flat. PLA fatigue limits life.

Heart gear keychain https://www.printables.com/model/775478 (2.7k downloads); Elliptical gear with no centre pivot https://www.printables.com/model/1533767 (remix of PerryT; elliptical pair originally Thingiverse thing:205); Elliptical gear fidget (assembled) https://www.printables.com/model/1378760; Involute elliptical fidget (685 bearings, formulas in CAD) https://www.printables.com/model/1457206; Non-circular gear fidget spinner (triangle/oval/square sets, assembled, glue) https://www.printables.com/model/1815713; Educational non-circular gears (conjugate pitch curve computed for an eccentric ellipse; involute teeth generated by a virtual rack, undercut where curvature is tight) https://www.printables.com/model/1504479; Variable-speed gear https://www.printables.com/model/1466012; Nautilus print-in-place https://www.makerworld.com/en/models/2747133; Nautilus spinner https://www.printables.com/model/1386213; experimental software-made collection https://www.printables.com/model/1862237. Research: Xu, Fu, Song, Zhou, Fu, Mitra, 'Computational Design and Optimization of Non-Circular Gears', CGF 2020 https://diglib.eg.org/handle/10.1111/cgf13939
mechanisms.how_it_works: Conjugate pitch curves roll without slip, so the speed ratio varies through each turn (speed-up and slow-down).
mechanisms.print_in_place: Mostly assembled on pins or bearings. Few are print-in-place (nautilus on MakerWorld). None found drives a character expression, and none uses a pitch curve synthesized from a target motion profile in a fidget.

mechanisms.category: Cam toys / automata / cam-follower expressive figures
mechanisms.examples: Printables 'automaton' ~1,000 results, but most are crank-box sculptures. Inchworm automaton https://www.printables.com/model/892037; Cam & follower PIP demo (pear cam) https://www.printables.com/model/1617593; Click-Wink BUNNY (print-in-place: pressing an ear drives an internal lever-cam that rotates an eye disc to a wink, with a click) https://www.printables.com/model/1393629 (100 likes); MakerWorld Mechanical Waving Fidget Cat (print-in-place, gear-driven arms wave when the base moves; one small support) https://makerworld.com/models/2856164; Robives cam nodding sheep (paper) https://www.robives.com/project/agreeablesheep/; tube-man cam shaft https://makerworld.com/models/897639; All3DP automata roundup https://all3dp.com/2/3d-printed-automaton-automata-models/. Research: Coros et al., 'Computational Design of Mechanical Characters' (SIGGRAPH 2013) https://studios.disneyresearch.com/2013/07/21/computational-design-of-mechanical-characters/ ; Thomaszewski et al., 'Computational Design of Linkage-Based Characters' (2014) https://ri.cmu.edu/publications/computational-design-of-linkage-based-characters
mechanisms.how_it_works: A rotating cam or eccentric lifts a follower that moves a head, wing, eye or arm. In the Disney work, cam shapes and linkages are synthesized from user-sketched motion curves.
mechanisms.print_in_place: Crank automata are almost always multi-part. Only a handful of hand-held print-in-place cam-expression fidgets exist (Click-Wink Bunny, Waving Cat). None advertises a cam profile computed from a target motion.

mechanisms.examples: Printables 'rolamite' 0 real hits; 'rolling contact joint' 1, a German knee model that is assembled and printed in PETG, whose author warns that seams must not sit on the thin bands: https://www.printables.com/model/1039873; BYU D-CORE https://www.printables.com/model/598201 and https://techtransfer.byu.edu/deployable-compliant-rolling-contact-element-d-core; Halverson 2007 multistable CORE thesis https://scholarsarchive.byu.edu/etd/895; Rolamite background https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolamite
mechanisms.how_it_works: Cylinders or cams roll on each other, held by crossed flexible bands. That gives a moving instantaneous centre and near-zero friction, and band shaping can make it multistable.
mechanisms.print_in_place: Not demonstrated as a fidget. Thin printed bands fatigue, and FDM needs PETG/TPU-like bands or very thick-ratio flexures.

mechanisms.print_in_place: Yes (flat flexures). Life is limited in PLA; PETG is better.

gaps: Rolamite / rolling-band / CORE rolling-contact mechanisms: there are zero real Printables hits for 'rolamite'. The only rolling-contact joint found (1039873) is an assembled knee demo, plus the BYU D-CORE research model. No print-in-place fidget uses one.

Hand-held print-in-place Tusi couple / cardan straight-line drive: only a motorised magnet table (1757607) and two hypocycloid spinners exist. Nothing uses the straight-line output to animate a character feature, for example eyes sliding, a peeking head or a pupil oscillating.

Non-circular gears with a pitch curve synthesized from a desired motion profile (dwell, quick snap, ease-in/out) driving an expression: existing non-circular fidgets are decorative ellipse, heart or nautilus pairs, mostly assembled. The only computed-conjugate example (1504479) is an educational demo. Research exists (Xu et al. 2020) but not as a toy.

Cams synthesized from a target follower motion inside a print-in-place hand-held toy: there are cam demos and multi-part crank automata, but Click-Wink Bunny's lever-cam is the only print-in-place expression cam found, and nobody claims a computed profile.
Sarrus or other straight-line pop-up linkages as a print-in-place fidget: none found. Hoberman versions need supports or assembly.
Kresling / origami twist bistable fidgets in FDM: none; they appear only in research papers.

Constant-force, zero- or negative-stiffness compliant mechanisms tuned to a target force curve as a kids' fidget: 3 models in total and none child-oriented. Haptic force-curve design research exists (Aalto UIST 2018).
Multistable (more than 2 states) compliant mechanisms used as an expression selector, for example a face cycling through moods: one pentastable demo (94613), no character use.
Hand-held print-in-place escapements (tick-tock fidgets): none. Existing ones need nails, weights or assembly.
Heart-cam push-push latches as print-in-place character toys: one Aug 2026 model (1804883) and a few pen mechanisms. Printed springs creep, which is the known failure.

Spherical linkages, Peaucellier/Watt straight-line linkages, Klann linkages and Lissajous/harmonograph mechanisms as fidgets: essentially absent (Printables: Peaucellier 0, Klann 0, 'four bar linkage' 1, 'linkage fidget' 0).
Gravity ramp walkers and stick-slip descenders as character toys: rare (AT-AT 1146942, T-rex 1392661, woodpecker 1862612).

Novelty caveat for judges: these are already taken, so 'a character that does something' is not novel by itself. Click-Wink Bunny (lever-cam wink), the MakerWorld Waving Cat (gear arms), bistable eyes, iris-blink glasses and Capiflexi (nodding head). One Printables account (TonyHanma, Sep-Oct 2026) has published many 'collision-checked in code / physics checked' mechanical toys: Planetario 4-speed planetary, Capiflexi arc-dovetail flexi with nodding head, stick-slip woodpecker, 12-leg Strandbeest, Graham escapement clock, Geneva calendar, crank automata, rack-launched top, anti-gravity double cone, nested puzzle ball. A new design should not re-use those mechanisms and should claim novelty on a computed element not seen there.
printing_lessons: Lateral clearance values that work in published print-in-place fidgets: 0.3 mm (keychain spinner 1424794, Helix Screw 472552); 0.35 mm (MakerWorld gimbal, Capiflexi, autonomous.ai planetary mesh gap); 0.4 mm (MakerWorld Kinetic Gear 3030090, ROBOuroboros 1188339); 0.45 mm hinge with 0.3 mm stacking (infinity-cube customizer 475027); 0.5 mm spherical (Gyro-Cube 3030509). Use at least 0.35 mm for kids' toys, where reliability beats tightness.

Sovol design table (0.4 nozzle, 0.2 layers), per side: PLA tight 0.15-0.20, smooth 0.20-0.30, loose 0.30-0.40 mm. PETG needs about 0.05-0.10 mm more per side. Tune in 0.05 mm steps with clearance coupons (Printables 53276 parametric tolerance test; MakerWorld 137989 and 538503 vertical test; VERSO cube hinge coupons). Parts printed in place need more clearance than the same parts printed apart and assembled (MakerWorld 137989).

Vertical (Z) gaps need at least 1-2 layer heights (0.2-0.4 mm). Keep the designed 1-layer gap equal to the actual layer height (MyMiniFactory planetary clamp). Put rotation axes along Z so clearances are in XY, which is much more reliable than horizontal axes.

Horizontal pins: use 45-50 deg cones or bulged pins with conical roofs instead of cylinders. Teardrop holes avoid sagging bores. Capiflexi uses 50 deg neck cones (40 deg overhang) and pins with a 45 deg bulge. Bridges up to ~7.7 mm printed fine; give 0.5 mm extra room on the sag side.

Elephant foot is the #1 cause of first-layer fusing. Add 0.5-1.0 mm x 45 deg chamfers at the bottom edges of pin and socket, and/or use slicer elephant-foot compensation of 0.1-0.2 mm. Capiflexi pulls the first 0.3 mm of every part in by 0.2 mm.

Seams: keep the Z-seam off bearing surfaces and thin flexures. A large seam can weld a bearing to its body (keychain spinner 1424794), and a seam on a thin band kills it (rolling joint 1039873). Random seam helped the eccentric planetary. Enable Z-hop so the nozzle does not smear across gaps.

No supports or brims near moving gaps: supports fill joint clearances and weld them. Keep any brim 0.2-0.25 mm from the object, away from gaps. Let the plate cool fully before removal; removing hot can fuse the mechanism (Gyro-Cube).

Don't scale print-in-place models: hinges tuned at 100% fuse when scaled down (infinity cubes, Snap-Flex). Tune by scaling a part only ±1-2% (Mighty Makers' dragon head). Emmett's gear bearing, designed for ABS, fused in PLA unless scaled or re-toleranced (tol 0.4 worked, per Ed Nisley's knurled variant).

Gear meshes: zero CAD backlash binds because FDM extrusion bulges. One parametric planetary used 0.12 mm tooth backlash with 0.4 mm pin clearance; print-in-place sets more often use a 0.3-0.35 mm mesh gap. Herringbone or double-helical teeth give axial retention. Friction-only captive gears can pop out: the Eccentric Gear Fidget 900241 sometimes 'disassembled by itself', which is a choking risk for kids.

Expect break-in: many print-in-place joints are stiff off the bed. Flex each joint, starting at the extremities. Some designs crack joints loose deliberately (Easy Strandbeest), run water over gears (eccentric planetary 1755291), or use a little oil, wax or soap, especially for PETG, which has high self-friction (Wobble Toggle 943743).

Flexures and springs: PLA living hinges generally fail before ~1,000 cycles (Springer study s00170-019-04196-x). The BYU bistable clicker remix lasts 'many hundreds of cycles'. A Tough-PLA hinge showed fatigue by ~400 cycles. Printed springs creep and lose preload: one push-push designer switched to a rubber band, and a nodding-cat designer needed a steel spring. Design flexures for low strain (long, tapered, stress-relieved centre, as in the Wobble Toggle update), lay layers along the flexure length, and prefer PETG for repeated flexing. The harmonic drive 273061 is PETG-only.

Thin acoustic features need exact widths: the noisemaker reed should be exactly two extrusion widths. PLA clicks louder than PETG (clicky keychain 943654). Tougher PLA runs smoother but clicks quieter (push-to-open 2834862). Silk PLA is too weak for repeated snapping and shrinks more (Mimetics, ROBOuroboros).

Ship clearance variants or a test joint: designers publish 0.2, 0.25 and 0.3 mm versions (Thangs spinner 995119) or tight, easy and easiest snap versions (Clickit). ROBOuroboros includes a single test joint.

Child safety precedent: the UK OPSS recalled a 3D-printed articulated dragon fidget (PSD 2603-0143, 2026) because 'small parts can easily detach or break off during reasonably foreseeable use' and fit the small-parts cylinder, so it failed the Toys (Safety) Regulations 2011. A separate UK report covered an 18-piece printed animal set. EN 71-1 and ASTM F963 apply; the UF-SAFE maker framework (https://makerworld.com/models/1916868) warns that thin-walled printed parts can compress. Every moving part should be geometrically captive (no friction-only retention) and no feature should be breakable into a piece under the cylinder size.

concepts.name: Snooze Stack (Frog Totem)
concepts.tagline: Squish the stack and the frogs fall asleep one by one (tick, tick, tick). Pull it apart and they wake up in the same order.
concepts.character: Three chubby kawaii frogs stacked in a totem. The top frog wears a lily-pad hat. Each frog's big half-moon eyes sit on top of its head, and the chin of the frog above (or the hat brim) acts as its eyelid. The frogs' dangling legs are the sliding 'skirts' that hug the head of the frog below. As printed, every frog is awake with wide half-moon eyes and a smile. When squished, each frog's eyes close to sleepy '‿ ‿' slits in a top-to-bottom wave, and the belly arch lines flip. Skins share one mechanism core and change only the silhouette and face engraving; each skin is still one single print: (1) Frog family. (2) Cat-loaf tower: three loaf cats, eyes under the chin of the cat above, tails as the skirts. (3) Dango/snow-buddy trio with a beanie hat. Any intermediate state is stable (0, 1, 2 or 3 asleep), so it doubles as a 'sleepiness counter'.
concepts.mechanism_summary: A monolithic series chain of three bistable compliant cells (curved double beams) linking four rigid bodies: hat, frog 1, frog 2 and frog 3 (the base). Each snap-through moves the next body 2.8 mm and closes one frog's eye apertures. The snap ORDER is programmed purely by the beams' Z-depth, so it survives printer flow and line-width errors.
concepts.mechanism_detail:
Each cell sits in the 'belly window' of the upper body (hat, F1, F2). It has two parallel cosine arches: span L=46, rise h=1.5, in-plane width t=0.45 mm (exactly one extrusion line), arch pitch 2.5 mm. They are clamped into 4 mm side walls with r0.8 root fillets and joined at midspan by a 4 mm rigid stem that runs down into the next body's head between its eyes. As printed, the arches sag down (∪, stress-free). Squeezing pushes the stem up through snap-through to the mirror (∩) state.

Nonlinear corotational Euler-Bernoulli FE (E=3.0 GPa, 32 elements, displacement control through the force limit points), per mm of beam depth bz:
- Squish snap threshold 0.415 N/mm at d=0.58 mm.
- Pull-back threshold -0.155 N/mm at d=2.5 mm.
- Second stable state at d=2.79 mm.
- Peak bending+axial strain 1.00% (during the snap); 0.66% while resting in the squished state.
- Mesh-converged: 16 vs 64 elements differ by less than 1%. Matches the Qiu et al. 2004 asymptotes (740 and 370 EIh/L^3 per beam) within 4-8% at Q=8.

Depths bz = 5.0 / 7.0 / 9.8 mm (top to bottom, ratio 1.4):
- Squish snaps at 2.07 / 2.90 / 4.07 N.
- Pull snaps at 0.78 / 1.09 / 1.52 N.
The child's squeeze is force-controlled, so cells snap strictly in threshold order: hat->F1 first (F1 falls asleep), then F2, then F3. Pulling restores them in the same top-down order.

Motion: 3 DOF (one translation per cell). Motion is transmitted only by flexure bending, with no sliding contact under load. Total stroke is 3 x 2.79 = 8.4 mm (78 -> 69.6 mm tall).

Hard stops: each stem ends in a T-head inside a pocket. The compression stop at 3.2 mm caps strain at about 1.05%; the extension stop is at -0.4 mm. Hard overloads therefore go into the 4 mm frames, not the beams.

Guides: each upper body's leg-skirts overlap the next body's head shoulders with 45° V-tongue/groove interlocks (1.2 mm deep, at least 9 mm engagement). These carry Z loads, twist and bending.

Eyes: each eye is the void between the upper body's chin lid (∪-shaped lower edge) and the lower body's cup-shaped socket. The vertical gap is 3.7 mm as printed (awake), 0.9 mm when resting asleep, and 0.5 mm at the stop. A 1.2 mm black floor on the socket side slides under a 45° undercut on the chin, 0.4 mm above the floor.

Sound: a crisp PLA 'tick' on each squish snap and a softer 'tock' on each pull snap.
concepts.computational_design_element:
Python (numpy) in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Apps/023789a6-f9f1-563f-a565-9790ebbd0388/scratchpad/ideation/compliant/:

(1) corobeam.py is a 2D corotational beam FE (Crisfield) that traces the full snap-through force-displacement curve and the max fiber strain of a pre-curved double beam with midspan rotation constrained.

(2) A parameter search over span, rise and line width (sweep_bistable.py, lowstrain.py) picked the arch: bistable with |F_pull|/F_squish ≈ 0.37, stroke at least 2.75 mm, peak strain at most 1.0% (about 1/3 of PLA yield strain), and kid-range forces.

(3) Sequence programming (stack_mc_final.py): all three cells have identical in-plane geometry and differ ONLY in Z-depth. FDM layer count is exact, so common-mode errors in flow, line width and modulus scale every cell equally and cancel in the ordering. A 20,000-print Monte Carlo (σ_common=0.03 mm, σ_cell=0.015 mm, ±3% local stiffness) gives: squish order preserved 99.3%, pull order 100%, all cells bistable 100%. With σ_cell=0.025 it is 92.4% / 98.9%.

(4) Eye apertures are computed as the sweep of the target 'sleepy slit' curve along the FE stroke vector plus stop margin, with rounded corners, then collision-checked at every pose.

The honest story: 'the shape of the belly arches and the three beam depths were computed so the frogs fall asleep top-to-bottom at kid-sized forces without over-straining PLA, even on a badly calibrated printer.'
concepts.fidget_loop: Squeeze the stack between thumb and fingers or between palms. It goes tick... tick... tick: three distinct snaps at about 2, 3 and 4 N. Each snap drops the stack 2.8 mm and shuts one frog's eyes, top frog first. Pull the hat and the feet apart and it goes tock-tock-tock at about 0.8, 1.1 and 1.5 N; the frogs wake up in the same order. That is 6 snaps per cycle. Every partial state holds, so kids can 'count' sleepers, do one-at-a-time nudges, or squish-and-pull rapidly. Feedback is tactile (force drop at each snap), auditory (tick/tock) and visual (eyes closing in a wave, stack shrinking 11%).
concepts.closest_prior_art:
- BYU-style Bistable Compliant Fidget Clicker (printables.com/model/230835) and bistable fidget button (233611): one bistable element, two states, no character.
- Halloween bistable bookmark with eyes that click left or right (298442): a single bistable eye toggle.
- Pentastable compliant demo (94613).
- Click-Wink Bunny (1393629): a lever-cam wink.
- Capiflexi (1862625).
- Research: Restrepo et al. 2015 'Phase transforming cellular materials'; Shan et al. 2015 'Multistable architected materials for trapping elastic strain energy'; Zhang, Auzinger and Bickel, TOG 2021, 'Computational design of planar multistable compliant structures'.
concepts.novelty_argument:
No printable toy found chains bistable cells in series. Multistable 'metamaterial' columns with sequential snapping exist only in research, with the order left to chance or set by in-plane thickness grading, which FDM flow error scrambles.

Three things are new here:
(a) The snap order is programmed by Z-depth (layer count), a manufacturing-aware trick that is robust to extrusion error. Monte Carlo confirms the order is kept in 99% of prints.
(b) Each snap drives an expression, because a frog's eyelid is the chin of its neighbor. The face state is a readout of the chain's mechanical state: a 4-state mechanical counter rendered as sleepy frogs.
(c) The arches are strain-budgeted to 1.0% peak for PLA life, versus the 3-4%+ typical of printed clickers.

It is not a gear, infinity cube, flexi chain, slider, popper, Geneva or planetary, and it differs from 2-state clickers and from TonyHanma's mechanisms (planetary, arc-dovetail flexi, stick-slip, Strandbeest, escapement, Geneva).
concepts.print_strategy:
- Orientation: print flat, face up, 13 mm tall, one piece. No supports, no bridges.
- Overhangs: the only ones are the 45° V-interlock flanks and the 45° chin undercuts over the eye floors.
- Beams: all beams start on the bed. Slice with Arachne at 0.45 mm wall line width so each arch is exactly one line along its length. Layers then run along the bending direction, and single-line walls have no Z-seam. Check the preview so no beam is dropped or gap-filled.
- Settings: 0.2 mm layers; 0.4×45° first-layer chamfers on every moving-gap edge plus 0.15 mm elephant-foot compensation; 15% gyroid infill and 4 top/bottom layers in the bodies.
- Bed: no brim (glue stick); if needed, a brim only on F3's flat base edge. Let the plate cool before removal.
- Optional color: one filament swap at Z=1.2 mm (black for the first 6 layers, then body color) makes black eye floors.
- Material: PLA works. PETG is recommended for kids (ductile, better fatigue): use t=0.50 mm, which gives similar forces at E≈2.1 GPa and ε≈1.1%.
- After printing: no break-in needed; just squish and pull twice.
- Ship a single-cell force coupon (bz=5) so users can sanity-check their printer.
concepts.key_dimensions_mm:
- Overall: 54 W × 78 H as printed (awake) / 69.6 H fully asleep × 13 T; about 28 g PLA.
- Body heights: hat 14.5; F1 and F2 23 each; F3 (base with feet) 17.5.
- Belly windows: 46 wide × 8.5 tall.
- Arches: L 46, rise 1.5, width 0.45, double-arch pitch 2.5, depth bz 5.0 / 7.0 / 9.8 (hat / F1 / F2).
- Stems 4 wide; side walls 4; leg skirts 3 thick with 1.2 deep 45° V-tongues.
- Stroke per cell 2.79 (stop at 3.2, extension stop 0.4).
- Eyes 7 wide × 3.7 tall half-moon voids (0.9 asleep at rest, 0.5 at the stop) with 1.2 floors.
- Outer edge fillets r 1.5-2.
concepts.clearances_mm:
- Sliding/shear gaps between bodies: 0.45 in-plane.
- V-interlock faces: 0.45 normal (0.64 horizontal).
- Arches to window walls: at least 1.5 in-plane.
- Stem T-head stops: 3.2 compression gap, 0.4 extension gap.
- Eye voids: 3.7 as printed.
- Eye-floor Z gap: 0.4 under a 45° chin undercut. No flat horizontal gaps over moving parts.
- First-layer chamfers: 0.4×45° on both sides of every moving gap.
- All gaps are vertical slots through the part, the most reliable print-in-place geometry.
concepts.child_safety:
- Single monolithic print: no pins, axles or captive loose parts, and nothing is designed to separate.
- Strain and overload: peak beam strain 1.0% (about 1/3 of PLA yield, 1/4 of PETG). Hard stops cap travel both ways, so a hard squeeze or yank loads the 4 mm frames, not the beams. V-interlocks keep twisting and bending off the beams.
- Edges: all outer edges r ≥ 1.5 mm, no points or thin protrusions. Feet, hat and skirts are at least 3 mm thick.
- Gaps: the outer silhouette only has 0.45 mm shear slots.
- DEVIATION from the 2 mm guideline: the eye apertures close from 3.7 mm. They are blind pockets with a 1.2 mm floor, below the 5 mm finger-probe size, have rounded lips, and never close below 0.5 mm. Closing is driven only by the child's own squeeze through 2-4 N snaps.
- Residual small-parts risk: if a 0.45 mm arch cracked in two places, a 23 × 0.45 × 5-10 mm sliver could fit the small-parts cylinder. Mitigations: low strain; beams recessed inside windows; optional 2 mm bridge straps over each window top; PETG recommended for under-8s; inspect before giving.
- Target 6+. 3D-printed toys are uncertified, and the documentation will say so.
risks: Force scatter: FDM line-width error of ±0.03 mm changes the snap forces by about ±30% (the order is robust, the absolute feel is not). Ship a force coupon and a 0.50 mm-line variant.

PLA creep/set if left squished for weeks (0.66% resting strain). Pull-back force may weaken. Mitigations: store 'awake' (the as-printed, stress-free state); PETG option; FE shows a large bistability margin (|F_pull| ≥ 0.78 N).
Fatigue: 1.0% peak strain is about 30 MPa in PLA. Expect on the order of 10^4-10^5 snaps per cell in PLA, more in PETG. Needs physical cycling tests.
Slicers may drop or merge 0.45 mm single-line arches or add gap fill. Requires Arachne, the correct min wall width, and a preview check.
Frame compliance at the arch roots softens the clamp and lowers the forces relative to the clamped FE. Include frame springs in the FE or tune bz after a coupon test.
Beam-fracture sliver could be a small part (see child_safety).
Eye apertures (3.7 mm) exceed the brief's 2 mm pinch guideline. They are blind and under the probe size, but the judges should weigh this.
The visual change is modest (eyes 3.7 -> 0.9 mm, stack -11%). It relies on the black-floor color swap for contrast; single-color prints read through shadow only.
Over 78 mm tall with a high centre of gravity: it may tip over when standing on a desk (display only).
concepts.modeling_plan:
Python generator snooze_stack.py with one params dict (L, h, t, pitch, bz list, stroke, stop gaps, clearances, skin). Toolchain: manifold3d (CrossSection 2D booleans/offsets -> extrude per Z band), numpy, optional build123d for top-edge fillets.

Structure:
(1) Core: four body cross-sections: outer frames, belly windows, stems with T-head stop pockets, and leg skirts.
(2) Arches: built from the same cosine centerline used in the FE, offset ±t/2, extruded to each cell's bz, unioned with r0.8 root fillets.
(3) V-interlocks: triangle-prism solids (Manifold.hull of offset cross-sections at two Z levels, giving exact 45°) added to tongues and subtracted, with the 0.45 offset, from grooves.
(4) Eye module: swept void polygon (target slit ⊕ stroke vector), a 1.2 mm floor footprint on the socket body, and a 45° chin undercut built by hull.
(5) Skin module: silhouette splines plus engraved faces (frog / loaf-cat / dango), keeping core interfaces fixed.
(6) First-layer chamfers: built by subtracting hulled edge prisms.

Exports: one STL, plus a 3MF/notes with the Z=1.2 color change. OpenSCAD is only for quick previews.
concepts.verification_plan:
(1) FE: re-run corobeam.py on the CAD-exported arch centerlines, with convergence (16/32/64 elements) and a Qiu-formula cross-check (already done in ideation: <1% and 4-8%). Add a frame-compliance spring at the roots, using the frame stiffness from a beam model.
(2) Kinematic pose sweep: for s ∈ {-0.4, 0, 0.25 … 3.2} in each cell and for all 4^3 state combinations, translate the bodies cumulatively and replace each arch by its FE-deformed polyline at that s. Then check that manifold3d pairwise intersection volume is 0 (except at the designated stop faces at the end poses) and that the minimum clearance from trimesh proximity sampling is at least 0.35 mm.
(3) Topology: the mesh is ONE connected component (nothing can detach), and each beam's cross-section is 0.45 ± 0.01 at several Z slices.
(4) Overhang analysis: no downward faces steeper than 45° from vertical except Z=0, and no bridges.
(5) First-layer slice at Z=0.2: all moving gaps at least 0.45 after a simulated +0.15 elephant foot.
(6) Eye-aperture metrics per pose (open/closed areas, slit widths) and renders of the 4 states (0-3 asleep) as an expression storyboard, using xvfb-run openscad or trimesh/matplotlib.
(7) Re-run the Monte Carlo ordering with the as-modeled bz.
(8) Fragment check: for each beam, the two highest-stress sections give the fragment bounding box versus the small-parts cylinder, and whether the window retains it.
(9) Physical: print the single-cell coupon and measure snap forces with a kitchen scale against the FE prediction (2.07 N for bz=5).

concepts.name: GiggleMochi (the PLA squishy)
concepts.tagline: A squishy made of hard plastic: press its head and it melts at a constant ~3 N while its face scrunches into a laugh.
concepts.character: A round mochi-cat, 62 × 64 mm, with tiny ears, bean eyes, an 'ω' cat mouth, puffy blush cheeks and a little head tuft between the ears, which is the button. Pressing the tuft squeezes the eyes into happy '^ ^' arcs and opens the ω mouth into a laugh. The expression is ANALOG: it follows the thumb, so half a press is a giggle and a full press is a belly laugh. A belly arch line flips smile-ward as it is squished. Skins share the same core (TOP/BOTTOM interfaces, springs, belly beam): (1) Mochi-cat. (2) Hamster with round ears and a buck-tooth jaw lobe. (3) Puffy chick: the head-feather tuft is the button, and the beak halves open as the ω lobes. Each skin is one single print.
concepts.mechanism_summary: A monolithic quasi-zero-stiffness (constant-force) compliant suspension. A central TOP body (tuft + face bar + philtrum column + jaw) translates 3.55 mm down inside the BOTTOM body ring. It is held by a negative-stiffness double curved beam in the belly, in parallel with positive-stiffness folded-leaf springs under the ears. Their stiffnesses were computed to cancel into a flat force plateau. The TOP/BOTTOM interfaces are shaped so that the only closing voids are the eyes and the only opening voids are the mouth.
concepts.mechanism_detail:
1 DOF (vertical translation of TOP). It is guided at two levels 40 mm apart, which makes it tilt-stiff: the belly double beam (midspan rotation constrained) and two folded-leaf springs at the head. 45° V-interlocks on the philtrum/cheek and tuft/ear shear faces provide Z retention.

Negative-stiffness element: two parallel cosine arches (L=48, rise h=1.9, t=0.45 one line, pitch 2.8, depth 5.0 mm), bowed up (∩) as printed. The jaw stem pushes midspan down through the snap-through region but never into the second well. FE, NS beam alone: +2.6 N peak at 0.55 mm, then a nearly linear -1.1 N/mm slope down to -1.1 N at 3.4 mm.

Positive element: two folded leaf springs (each 2 stages × 2 parallel leaves of 16 × 0.45 × 9.9 mm, 3 mm trusses) from the tuft to the ear walls, giving k = 1.32 N/mm. Leaf strain is 0.94% at the stop.

Sum (FE, E=3.0 GPa): force rises 0 -> 3.31 N in the first 0.6 mm (about 6 N/mm, a firm 'skin'), then stays at 3.31-3.35 N from 0.6 to 3.4 mm (±0.6% nominal: the 'melt'). A hard stop at 3.55 mm makes the force rise steeply with a soft 'tok'; an up-stop sits at -0.45 mm.

Peak strain 1.22% (NS arch, only at the stop), about 1.1% mid-plateau. Total force stays above 0 everywhere, so it is MONOSTABLE and returns by itself. It is stress-free at rest, so there is no creep set, unlike bistable clickers.

Face: TOP's face bar lower edge and BOTTOM's cheek shelves bound two 5 W × 4.0 H arched-bean eye voids, which close to 0.45-0.6 mm '^' arcs. The jaw (TOP) and upper lips (BOTTOM) bound the ω mouth, two 4 mm-wide lobes either side of the 5 mm philtrum, opening 0.45 -> 4.0 mm. Black 1.2 mm floors (eye floors on TOP, mouth floor on the jaw) slide under 45° undercuts.
concepts.computational_design_element:
Python in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Apps/023789a6-f9f1-563f-a565-9790ebbd0388/scratchpad/ideation/compliant/ (corobeam.py, squish_design*.py, squish_low2.py, squish_final.py).

(1) Nonlinear corotational FE of the NS double arch, which traces the full snap-through curve and strain.

(2) Co-optimization of arch rise h, beam depth bz and folded-leaf stiffness k (leaf length and depth) to maximize the width of a MONOTONE plateau within ±6-8% at 3-4 N, subject to: strain ≤ 1.25% up to the stop, total F > 0 (monostable), and leaf strain from 3tδ/(nL²). Result: a 2.8-2.95 mm plateau. Rejected alternatives: a single Q-tuned arch gives only about 0.55 mm of plateau; arch + stretching beam gives about 1.15 mm; arch + linear bending spring gives about 2.9 mm.

(3) 'One line width everywhere' robustness: every compliant member is a single 0.45 mm line, so flow errors mostly scale the force rather than tilt the plateau. A 4,000-print Monte Carlo (σ_common 0.03, σ_member 0.015 mm) gives: springs back 100%, plateau force 2.3-4.6 N (5-95%), median plateau half-band 9%. 4.7% of prints get a slight soft snap; fix by biasing k +5% or shipping two leaf-length presets. One parameter also gives an optional 'giggle-snap' preset (k -15%).

(4) Aperture synthesis: the eye and mouth outlines are sweeps of the target closed '^' and open 'D' shapes along the 3.55 mm stroke, collision-checked per pose.

The story: 'this belly arch and these ear springs were computed so their forces cancel into a 3.3 N marshmallow plateau'.
concepts.fidget_loop: Hold the body in the palm and press the head tuft with the thumb. It is firm for half a millimetre, then 'gives' at an eerily constant ~3.3 N for about 3 mm, like squishing a marshmallow, while the eyes squeeze into ^ ^ and the ω mouth opens into a laugh. It bottoms out with a soft 'tok'. Release and it rises smoothly back to its calm face. Kids can do slow squishes, fast pumping, or hold half-way for a 'giggle'. Feedback is mainly haptic (the unusual zero-stiffness give that rigid plastic normally never has), plus visual (an analog face morph) and the soft end tok. It is silent in the middle of the stroke, which suits classrooms.
concepts.closest_prior_art:
- Constant-force crank-slider with a cantilever riding a computed cam path (printables.com/model/583491).
- Spiral spring fidget (231346); ortho-planar spring (596315); BYU ortho-planar / constant-force compliant mechanisms.
- Bobble Bot (1188378, spring-loaded, 3 parts); Wobble Toggle (943743).
- Commercial foam/TPU squishies and stress balls (soft materials, not mechanisms).
- Research: quasi-zero-stiffness isolators combining negative and positive stiffness (Carrella, Brennan and Waters, J. Sound Vib. 2007); Aalto 'One Button to Rule Them All' force-curve rendering (UIST 2018); Qiu, Lang and Slocum 2004 curved-beam snap-through.
concepts.novelty_argument:
The prior-art map lists only 3 constant-force printed models, none child-oriented and none tuned by nonlinear FE. No printed toy renders a quasi-zero-stiffness 'squish' from rigid PLA, and none couples such a force curve to a facial expression.

The new mechanism pairs a negative-stiffness snap-through arch (operated inside its unstable region, but held monostable by computed positive springs) with a fold-spring guide. The result is a toy that feels soft while being hard plastic.

Two design principles are also new for printables:
- Stiffnesses are co-optimized for a flat plateau, with every flexure kept to one extrusion width so printer error mostly scales the force rather than the feel.
- 'Aperture topology': with a single translation, every TOP-over-BOTTOM interface is arranged so the eyes are the only closing voids and the mouth the only opening void, giving an analog expression dial.

It is not a clicker (no snap), slider, gear, flexi chain, popper or Geneva drive.
concepts.print_strategy:
- Orientation: print flat, face up, 13 mm tall, one piece. No supports, no bridges.
- Overhangs: only the 45° V-interlock flanks and the 45° undercuts above the eye and mouth floors.
- Thin members: the NS arches and all eight leaves are single 0.45 mm Arachne lines along their length (layers parallel to the bending, no seams).
- Settings: 0.2 mm layers; 0.4×45° first-layer chamfers on all moving-gap edges; elephant-foot compensation 0.15; 15% gyroid infill. No brim near gaps; a brim on the outer base edge only if needed.
- Optional color: one filament swap at Z=1.2 mm (black, then body color) for dark eyes and mouth.
- Material: PETG recommended for kids (ε stays 1.2% while forces drop about 30% at E≈2.1 GPa; compensate with t=0.50 lines or bz ×1.4). PLA works.
- After printing: cool the plate before removal. No break-in; press 3 times.
concepts.key_dimensions_mm:
- Overall: 62 W × 64 H × 13 T; about 25 g.
- TOP: tuft button 16 wide (rises 3 above the ear shoulders, dimpled); face bar 16 wide; philtrum column 5 wide; jaw 14 wide.
- BOTTOM: ring with 7 wide cheek-puff walls, ears, cheek shelves and base.
- NS belly arches: L 48, rise 1.9, width 0.45, pitch 2.8, depth 5.0.
- Folded springs: 2 per side position, 8 leaves of 16 × 0.45 × 9.9, trusses 3 wide.
- Travel: 3.55 to the stop (plateau 0.6-3.4).
- Eyes: 5 × 4.0 open -> about 0.5 arcs.
- ω mouth: 2 lobes 4 wide, 0.45 -> 4.0 open.
- Edge fillets r 1.5-2.
concepts.clearances_mm:
- Shear/sliding gaps between TOP and BOTTOM: 0.45 in-plane.
- V-interlocks: 0.45 normal.
- Folded-leaf stage-to-stage gaps: ≥ 2.3 (each stage moves 1.78).
- NS arch window: ≥ 4.0 below the jaw and around the arch travel.
- Stops: 3.55 down, 0.45 up.
- Eye voids: 4.0 at rest. Mouth: 0.45 at rest.
- Floor Z gap: 0.4 under 45° undercuts.
- First-layer chamfers: 0.4×45°.
- All gaps are vertical slots; there are no flat Z gaps over moving parts.
concepts.child_safety:
- Single monolithic print: nothing designed to detach, no pins, no loose captive parts.
- Strain and overload: peak strain 1.22%, reached only at the hard stop, which takes any harder squeeze. The up-stop prevents over-extension if the tuft is pulled. Two-level guidance plus V-interlocks protect the flexures from twisting and drops.
- Edges: all exterior edges r ≥ 1.5, ears and tuft at least 6 mm thick, no points.
- Gaps: only 0.45 mm shear slots reach the silhouette.
- Pinch DEVIATION from the 2 mm guideline: the eye voids close from 4.0 mm. They are blind pockets with floors, under the 5 mm finger probe, closing only under the child's own thumb against a 3.3 N plateau, and never below 0.45 mm.
- The mouth lobes open to 4.0 mm and close on release with at most about 3.3 N.
- Residual small-parts risk is the same as concept A (a fractured 0.45 mm leaf or arch sliver). Mitigations: enclosed windows, low strain, PETG for young kids, inspection.
- Target 6+. Uncertified 3D-printed toy, and the documentation will say so.
risks: Plateau flatness is sensitive to line width and frame compliance (MC median ±9%, plateau force 2.3-4.6 N across prints, 4.7% show a slight soft snap). Mitigate with k bias, two leaf-length presets, or a calibration coupon.

Off-centre thumb presses tilt TOP and make the shear faces rub, adding friction and hysteresis that blur the 'zero-stiffness' feel. Mitigated by guidance 40 mm apart, V-interlocks and a wide dimpled tuft.
There is no click. Some kids may find the silent squish less satisfying than a clicker; the optional 'giggle-snap' preset or an end-stop tok helps.
Fatigue at 1.1-1.22% strain in PLA (about 35 MPa): roughly 10^4-10^5 presses. PETG recommended. Needs physical cycling tests.
The FE assumes ideally clamped arches and linear folded leaves. Real root and frame compliance and large-deflection leaf effects shift the curve, so re-run the FE on CAD geometry with root springs.
The interleaved TOP/BOTTOM face topology (cross-shaped TOP inside the ring, with the ω mouth split by the philtrum) is the most intricate CAD and limits skin freedom.
The eyes are small (5 × 4 mm). Expression contrast relies on the black-floor color swap.
0.45 mm single-line flexures depend on correct slicer settings (Arachne min wall width, no gap fill).
concepts.modeling_plan:
Python generator giggle_mochi.py with a params dict (arch L/h/t/pitch/bz, leaf L/t/b/stages, travel, stops, clearances, eye/mouth targets, skin). Toolchain: manifold3d (CrossSection 2D booleans/offsets -> extrude) + numpy; build123d optional for filleted outer edges.

Structure:
(1) TOP and BOTTOM as 2D cross-sections built from primitives (tuft, face bar, philtrum, jaw; ring, ears, cheek shelves, base). Every TOP-BOTTOM boundary is generated as either a vertical shear line (0.45 offset) or a computed aperture (eye: closed '^' arc swept by the 3.55 stroke vector; mouth: closed line swept the opposite way).
(2) NS arches from the FE centerline, offset ±t/2, extruded to bz 5.0, with r0.8 root fillets into the ring and stem.
(3) Folded leaves generated parametrically (stage count, leaf length, truss) in pockets between tuft and ears.
(4) Stops as T-head pockets.
(5) V-interlocks and 45° floor undercuts as hulled prisms.
(6) Black floors as 1.2 mm footprints.
(7) Skin module: silhouette, ear and blush relief, and the jaw-lobe shape.

Export: single STL, plus a 3MF/notes for the Z=1.2 color change.
concepts.verification_plan:
(1) Re-run the FE (corobeam.py) on CAD-exported centerlines, adding frame/root compliance. Add a large-deflection beam FE of the folded leaves (also with corobeam) to replace the linear-k assumption. Recompute the total F(d): the plateau should be within ±8% over at least 2.5 mm, with F > 0 everywhere.
(2) Pose sweep from s = -0.45 to 3.55 in 0.1 steps: translate TOP, insert the FE-deformed arch and leaf polylines (with the truss at s/2). Check that manifold3d intersection volume is 0 except at the stop faces at the end poses, and that the minimum clearance is at least 0.35 mm via trimesh sampling.
(3) Topology: one connected component; flexure widths 0.45 ± 0.01 by slicing.
(4) Overhang scan: nothing beyond 45° except bed faces.
(5) First-layer gap check with a +0.15 elephant-foot offset.
(6) Tilt check: apply an off-centre 4 N load 8 mm from the axis in a small linearized model (arch rotation stiffness + leaf axial stiffness). Lateral drift at the shear faces must stay below the 0.45 gap.
(7) Aperture metrics and renders at s = 0, 1.2, 2.4, 3.4 for the expression storyboard (calm -> giggle -> laugh).
(8) Re-run the Monte Carlo with the as-modeled geometry.
(9) Physical: a coupon of the arch + leaf module; push it on a kitchen scale with a 0.5 mm-step jig to measure F(d) against the FE plateau of 3.3 N.

concepts.name: Peek-a-Boo Pod (twin-cam peeker)
concepts.tagline: Turn the belly dial and a chick peeks out, ducks, then pops out of its egg. The order of moves comes from a storyboard, and a computer turned that storyboard into two spring-free cams.
concepts.character: Default skin: a chick in a cracked egg. The yellow chick head (rocker part) sits behind a white front shell whose crack is a rounded zig-zag. The eyes are engraved pockets 1.2 mm deep. With a filament swap at z=7.2 and z=7.8 they show as dark eyes. The beak and cheek blush are raised details that sit only on areas never covered by the shell. The dial is a Ø34 'flower sticker' on the egg belly. When hidden, only the fluff tuft or ears show above the crack. One storyboard plays per dial turn: the eyes peek out to 45% and hold, as if looking around; the chick ducks; it pops up 12 mm, leaning 16° like a curious head-tilt; it holds; then it hides. The cams make a soft 'tok' at each reversal. Other skins use the same mechanism core and change only the front shell and head outline: a bunny in a magician's top hat (ears always visible), a ghost in a pumpkin, and a kitten in a sock.
concepts.mechanism_summary: The thumb dial is a rotor on a fixed post. It carries two stacked plate cams, A and B, each 3 mm thick. A single rocker part (head, neck and two follower arms) pivots on a second post 16 mm to the left. Arm A rides cam A above the rotor centre, and arm B rides cam B below it, on a different layer. Each cam pushes the rocker in one direction, so the pair holds the rocker captive both ways (desmodromic) and no spring is needed. A 3.8:1 lever turns 3.2 mm of cam lift into 12 mm of head travel. The dial can turn either way; reversing plays the storyboard backwards.
concepts.mechanism_detail: Geometry, relative to the rotor centre O: pivot P = (-16, 0). Follower nose centres sit at O + (-8, +8) and O + (-8, -8). These points lie on the circle whose diameter is PO, so each nose moves radially to the cam and the geometric pressure angle is zero at mid-stroke. Arm length P to nose is 11.3 mm; nose radius is 2.0 mm. Head centre is 43 mm from P. Rocker swing is 16°, which gives 3.16 mm of nose lift and 12.0 mm of head travel along the arc, with the head leaning 16° as it rises. Layer stack (face-up): back plate z 0-2.0; cam B and arm B z 2.4-5.4; cam A and arm A z 5.4-8.4; front shell z 8.8-11.2; dial z 8.8-12.2 (Ø34, 1 mm proud). Degrees of freedom: rotor revolute about post 1, rocker revolute about post 2. The cams couple them, so the system has 1 DOF. Below the front shell, the rocker's hidden portion is a sector of an annulus centred on P. Its edges therefore stay a constant 0.45 mm from the body walls. Loads: a thumb force of about 3 N on the Ø34 dial gives about 50 N·mm of torque. That is roughly 5.5 N normal force at the cam contact, at r ≈ 9 mm. With PLA-on-PLA μ ≈ 0.3 (friction angle 17°) and a maximum pressure angle of 30°, the drive is about 70% efficient or better and cannot self-lock. There are no flexures, so there is no fatigue or creep; the only wear is sliding on 3 mm-wide cam faces. Retention: both posts are Ø8 with a 45° V-ridge 1.0 mm high running in V-grooved bores. The rocker post connects the back plate to the front shell, so it is supported at both ends. The rotor post is cantilevered from the back plate. The dial rim has a 45° chamfer that runs under the matching chamfered edge of the front-shell hole, so the rotor is captive both ways along Z. Desmodromic play is 0.30 mm per cam contact, 0.6 mm in total at the nose, which gives ±1.1 mm of head jiggle (cute, and it produces the reversal 'tok'). The head weighs about 5 g.
concepts.computational_design_element: The cams are computed from a storyboard; nobody drew them. Keyframes give normalised head lift u against dial angle: (0°,0) (10°,0) (85°,0.45) (115°,0.45) (170°,0.12) (185°,0.12) (280°,1.0) (305°,1.0) (360°,0). The steps are: (1) blend the keyframes with cycloidal segments, so acceleration is continuous; (2) solve rocker angle β(θ) = Δβ·(u - 0.5); (3) find the follower nose-centre path in the rotating cam frame, which is the pitch curve; (4) offset it inward by the nose radius to get the cam profile; (5) compute cam B independently for arm B from the same β(θ), so the pair is conjugate and leaves zero free play other than the clearance. Constraints checked numerically: pressure angle (pitch-curve normal against nose velocity) ≤ 30°; convex radius of curvature of the pitch curve > nose radius + 1 mm, so no undercut; profile radius ≤ 11 mm; head travel = 12 mm. scipy.optimize tunes the pivot location, nose positions and keyframe timings (±10°) to minimise the peak pressure angle. A prototype run is in computed-profiles/cam2.py. Results: peak pressure angle 30.3°, 95th percentile 24.2°, profile radius 7.7-10.9 mm, minimum convex pitch radius 5.1 mm (3.1 mm on the profile), lift 3.16 mm to 12.0 mm at the head. The first geometry (pivot at -14) peaked at 34.9°, and the optimiser moved it. Two further shapes are also computed: the rocker's clearance cavity, as the swept envelope plus 0.45 mm, and the dial torque ripple, which is reported so the 'heavier' feel lands on the POP. The honest story: 'You tell it when to peek and when to hide, and the computer shapes the cams so the chick does exactly that, with no spring.'
concepts.fidget_loop: Roll the scalloped Ø34 dial continuously with the thumb while the other fingers hold the egg back. Each turn plays the four-beat choreography: peek, duck, POP, hide. You feel four soft 'tok's as the nose crosses its clearance from cam A to cam B at each reversal, plus a light torque rise in the 90° before the POP. Turning the dial backwards plays the sequence in reverse. A fast flick spins the dial through 1-2 cycles.
concepts.closest_prior_art: Click-Wink BUNNY (printables 1393629): a print-in-place lever-cam wink with a click, but a single hand-drawn lever-cam and a press input. MakerWorld Waving Cat (2856164): gear-driven arms. Push puppets (1268170) and the peek-a-boo alligator (1283455) use string, springs, or are decor only. Heart-cam push-push latches (1804883) depend on springs that creep. Coros et al., 'Computational Design of Mechanical Characters' (SIGGRAPH 2013), synthesises cams from motion curves, but its results are assembled, crank-driven research automata. TonyHanma's 'code-checked' toys contain no cam synthesis. No conjugate (dual-cam, spring-free) mechanism was found in the fidget space.
concepts.novelty_argument: 1. It is the first hand-held, print-in-place, spring-free desmodromic (conjugate twin-cam) mechanism in a fidget. Two cams on separate layers trap one rocker, removing the printed-spring creep that defeats push-push and bobble toys. 2. The cam shapes are synthesised from a multi-beat character storyboard with optimised pressure angles. Existing cam toys show one hand-drawn lobe that makes one motion. 3. A continuous rotary fidget input produces a timed narrative (peek, duck, pop, hide), not a repeated single motion. 4. The rocker layout (noses on the Thales circle of PO, 3.8:1 lever) is computed to keep the pressure angle at 30° or below inside a Ø22 cam envelope. The prior-art map lists 'cams synthesized from a target follower motion inside a print-in-place toy' as an open gap.
concepts.print_strategy: Print face-up as one print with three bodies: body, rotor and rocker-head. The back plate (z 0-2.0) sits on the bed. The rocker is printed in the hidden pose (β = -8°), and the rotor angle is chosen so both noses sit at mid-clearance. All moving interfaces are vertical walls (cam faces, post bores, arc-shaped rocker edges) with lateral clearance. Every Z interface is a 2-layer (0.4 mm) air gap: rotor and rocker over the back plate, and front shell over the rotor and rocker tops. These print like a support interface. To reduce fusing, the tops of the moving parts carry 0.3 mm-high 'skate' ribs, so the front shell's first layer touches only narrow lines. Pillars and the rocker post keep front-shell bridge spans at 10 mm or less. The V-ridges and chamfers are 45°; there are no other overhangs and no supports. A 0.6 × 45° chamfer on the first layers of every moving edge counters elephant foot, and no brim is used. Use 0.2 mm layers, 3 perimeters, 15% gyroid infill, seam on the rear outer edge, and Z-hop on. Optional filament swaps: z 2.4 yellow, z 7.2 black, z 7.8 yellow (pupils), z 8.8 white (shell). Let the plate cool before removal. Break in by turning the dial 20 times both ways. PLA works; PETG is quieter and wears better.
concepts.key_dimensions_mm: Egg body 58 W × 70 H × 12.2 T; 82 H with the chick fully popped. Dial Ø34 with 8 rounded scallops of r = 3 mm, 1.0 mm proud. Rotor cam layers 3.0 + 3.0 thick, profile radius 7.7-10.9. Posts Ø8 with 1.0 mm 45° V-ridge. Rocker: arms 11.3 mm to nose centre, nose r = 2.0, arm section ≥ 4 × 3 mm; head lever 43 mm; visible head about Ø36; swing 16°; travel 12. Back plate 2.0, front shell 2.4, perimeter wall 2.4. Outer edge fillets r ≥ 1.5 (crack zig-zag r = 2). Mass about 22 g.
concepts.clearances_mm: Cam face to follower nose: 0.30 per side, 0.6 total (designed conjugate). Post bores: 0.40 radial, with V-ridge 0.40 normal. Dial to front-shell hole: 0.40. Rocker arc edges to body walls: 0.45 constant (concentric with P). Rocker frame to rotor at non-contact zones: ≥ 0.6. All Z gaps: 0.40 (two 0.2 mm layers). First-layer chamfers: 0.6 × 45°.
concepts.child_safety: Only three bodies, all large. The smallest is the rotor, whose Ø34 dial exceeds the 31.7 mm small-parts cylinder, so it fails the cylinder test even if forced out. The rocker-head is longer than 50 mm and the body is 58 × 70. Every moving part is captive by geometry, not friction: V-ridged posts plus the sandwich between back plate and front shell. There are no flexures, pawls or thin tabs to snap off, and the posts are Ø8. The cam nip points are inside a sealed cavity whose only openings are 0.4 mm gaps. Moving-to-fixed boundaries are either overlaps in Z with 0.4 mm gaps or arcs concentric with the pivot (constant 0.45 mm), so no in-plane gap opens and closes within finger reach. The head pops outward into free air, away from the body. Drive torque is limited to thumb torque, about 60 N·mm or less. All outer edges have r ≥ 1.5 and there are no points. Plates are 2.0-2.4 mm thick with pillars ≤ 10 mm apart, which tolerates squeezing. Label: 6+, a 3D-printed toy that is not certified to EN 71 / ASTM F963, adult to inspect for cracks.
risks: The front shell's first layer may lightly fuse to the rotor and rocker tops across the 0.4 mm gap. Mitigations: skate ribs, a cooled plate, and a deliberate break-in twist. A 0.5 mm-gap variant is the fallback.
A 30° peak pressure angle in PLA with μ ≈ 0.3 may feel notchy before the 280° POP. Mitigation: re-optimise for 26° by stretching the POP to 100° or adding 1 mm of pitch radius.
Desmodromic clearance gives ±1.1 mm head jiggle. If it reads as sloppy, provide 0.25 mm and 0.35 mm variants plus a single-cam test coupon.
Sliding wear on the PLA cam faces over thousands of turns. Recommend PETG and orient the seam away from the cams.
The cantilevered rotor post can tilt under cam load. The dial chamfer under the front shell carries the moment; the sweep must still confirm nose contact at worst-case tilt.
The diagonal 'lean-out' path (33° from vertical) may need skin-specific crack and shell outlines to read well.
Engraved eyes are visible only with filament swaps or good lighting. Single-colour prints need deeper (2 mm) eye pockets.
concepts.modeling_plan: Use Python throughout. (1) numpy/scipy synthesis module (extending scratchpad cam2.py) outputs the pitch curves, cam profiles, β(θ) and the optimisation report. (2) manifold3d builds the core: CrossSection polygons for the cams, offset by clearance and nose radius; extrude per layer; revolve the V-ridged posts; build the rocker from the arc-sector neck plus arms plus a head-plate placeholder; cut the body cavity as the Minkowski-free swept envelope (union of rocker poses every 1°, offset +0.45). (3) build123d builds the skins (egg, top hat, pumpkin) as filleted lofts and extrusions with r ≥ 1.5 edges, the crack polyline with r = 2 rounds, and head outlines and relief. These are exported to mesh and merged with the core in manifold3d. A parameter dict holds skin choice, clearances, storyboard keyframes and layer heights. Export one 3MF/STL with three disjoint bodies, plus STEP of the skins and a clearance-coupon STL (one cam-nose pair at 0.25, 0.30 and 0.35).
concepts.verification_plan: 1. Kinematic sweep at 0.5° steps from 0 to 360°: pose the rotor by θ and the rocker by β(θ), then check manifold3d intersection volume between every pair of bodies (must be 0). Sample nose-to-cam distances to confirm each contact gap stays between 0.25 and 0.35. Use trimesh proximity to confirm all other gaps are ≥ 0.40, and repeat at ±0.3° rotor tilt. 2. Recheck pressure angle and curvature on the meshed profiles, not just the analytic curves. 3. Overhang analysis: no downward face with normal angle > 45° except the designated 0.4 mm Z-gap interfaces. Measure bridge spans of the front-shell underside (≤ 10 mm) by distance transform to supports. 4. Wall-thickness check: ray-cast thickness ≥ 1.2 everywhere and ≥ 2.0 on the plates. 5. Child-safety checks: compute the in-plane distance between every moving and fixed edge in the same Z band over the sweep, and flag any gap that varies across 2 mm; bounding-cylinder test that every body exceeds Ø31.7 × 25.4. 6. Retention test: try a 1 mm displacement of each moving body along ±Z and in-plane at sample poses and confirm interference, so the parts are captive. 7. Renders: headless OpenSCAD or matplotlib PNG frames at keyframes plus an animated GIF of the storyboard, and plots of u(θ), pressure angle and torque ripple. The prototype numbers above come from scratchpad /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Apps/023789a6-f9f1-563f-a565-9790ebbd0388/scratchpad/ideation/computed-profiles/cam2.py.

concepts.name: Head-Tilt Pup (centrode-rolling neck)
concepts.tagline: Nudge its cheek and the pup does a curious 'huh?' head-tilt: its head lifts 3 mm and tilts up to 28°. A computer derived the gear curves it rolls on from that gesture alone.
concepts.character: Default skin: a puppy in a hoodie. The hood is the back plate, a rounded hood silhouette behind the head. The collar and scarf form the front plate, covering the neck. The head has floppy ears, big raised dome eyes with highlight dots, a button nose and blush cheeks. At rest the head is centred and slightly sunk into the collar, looking content. Nudge it sideways and it perks up 3 mm while tilting up to 28° toward that side, with the tilt easing in slowly and speeding up near the end. The pose stays where you leave it. Other skins use the same rolling core and pin: an owl in a nest (the nest is the collar), a robot whose headphones form the collar, and a kitten in a knitted scarf.
concepts.mechanism_summary: This is a two-part print-in-place 'geared rolling neck' with no hinge and no spring. The head plate rolls without slipping on a toothed cradle in the body. The cradle and the head's runner are the fixed and moving centrodes of the target gesture, so rolling one on the other reproduces exactly that pose curve: slide, lift and eased tilt together. A pin rising from the back plate runs in a computed slot in the back of the head, which keeps the teeth meshed. Everything sits in a sealed sandwich between the hood back plate and the collar front plate. The motion has 1 DOF and is driven directly by the thumb.
concepts.mechanism_detail: Target pose curve over t ∈ [-1, 1]: head centre x = 10t mm, y = -3(1 - t²) mm (dips 3 mm at centre, so the head rises as it moves aside), tilt φ = -28°·t·(0.8 + 0.2t²). The instantaneous centre is IC = H + (-ẏ, ẋ)/φ̇. Fixed centrode (cradle pitch curve): a U-shaped curve spanning x ±18.8, 14.6-28.6 mm below the rest head centre, arc length 48.9 mm, minimum radius of curvature 14.5 mm. Moving centrode (head runner, head frame): x ±14.6, y -25.6 to -8.8, arc length 48.9 mm (equal arc lengths confirm pure rolling), minimum radius 11.8 mm. Teeth: module 1.25, pressure angle 25°, about 12.5 teeth across the travel, plus 2 run-out teeth at each end; working depth 2.5 mm. Guide: a Ø5 pin fixed on the back plate at (0, -6) relative to the rest head centre runs in a slot in the head that is 20.7 mm long (head frame x ±6, y -10 to -3). The pin is functionally redundant with the rolling constraint. With 0.35 mm normal slot clearance the mesh can separate by at most 0.35 mm, far less than the 2.5 mm working depth, so the teeth cannot skip. Layers: hood back plate z 0-2.0; head plate and body cradle z 2.4-7.4 (5 mm); collar front z 7.8-10.2. Above the collar line the head's visible face is thickened to z 10.2, plus up to 1.2 mm of eye relief. Every point of that raised region stays at least 6 mm from the collar edge at all poses (computed). Driving: a thumb push on the cheek acts 17-26 mm above the IC, which gives a strong rolling moment. Rolling teeth have little friction; most resistance comes from sandwich sliding on skate ribs. End stops: the rounded slot ends meet the pin, a soft 'boop'. Gravity: the 3 mm centre valley gives a weak centring force of about 0.05 N for an 8 g head. It is not relied on; the pose simply holds. No flexures.
concepts.computational_design_element: Centrode synthesis from a gesture. A designer specifies the expressive pose curve (x, y, φ)(t). The code computes the instantaneous-centre locus numerically, which becomes the cradle pitch curve. It maps that locus into head coordinates to get the runner pitch curve, then checks that the arc lengths match, which proves rolling without slip. scipy then optimises the gesture parameters (travel X, tilt φmax, easing e, dip h) to maximise expressiveness (tilt ≥ 25°, lift ≥ 2.5 mm) subject to manufacturability: centrode radius of curvature ≥ 8 mm (about 6× module), IC depth within the neck band of 15-28 mm, and an integer tooth count. The scan in scratchpad scan.py shows why the computer matters. With easing 0.2 and no dip, the centrodes form a 2.6 mm cusp, which cannot be printed. Adding a 3 mm dip raises the minimum radii to 14.5 and 11.8 mm. That computed dip is what produces the 'perks up' part of the expression. Teeth are made by rack generation along the runner. The cradle teeth are then generated as the Boolean complement of the head teeth swept through 400 poses (manifold3d union), offset by the backlash, so the pair is conjugate by construction. The slot is the fixed pin swept in head coordinates plus clearance. The honest story: 'We described the head-tilt we wanted; the computer worked out the only two curves that roll into exactly that motion.'
concepts.fidget_loop: Rock the head left and right with a thumb on its cheek or ear, like a worry stone that answers back. Rolling teeth give a fine, soft 'tik-tik-tik' texture. Each change of direction gives a 'tok' as the backlash flips, and each end of travel gives a rounded 'boop'. The motion is smooth and continuous, a slide, lift and tilt combined, with no hinge feel. The head stays in whatever pose you leave it, so kids can 'pose' it (sad, curious, sleepy). Quick alternating nudges make a 'no-no' waggle, and a two-thumb push-pull rhythm gives a steady fidget.
concepts.closest_prior_art: Capiflexi (printables 1862625): a nodding head on 50° cone pivots, which is a pure rotation about a hinge. Bobble Bot (1188378) and the MakerWorld nodding cat (2562076) need springs. Rolling-contact joints such as the rolling knee (1039873) and BYU CORE/D-CORE use bands, are assembled, and are not fidgets. Non-circular rack-and-pinion and educational conjugate gears (1504479) are decorative or educational. Classic centrode theory (Reuleaux) underlies the method, and geared rolling knees exist in robotics. No print-in-place character fidget was found whose joint is synthesised from a gesture.
concepts.novelty_argument: The joint is computed from the target motion (inverse kinematics to centrodes to teeth), not chosen from the catalogue of hinge, slider and gear. The resulting coupled slide, lift and eased tilt is impossible for a pin hinge, a cone pivot or a flexi chain. It replaces springs and flexures (the known failure mode of bobbleheads and printed springs) with pure rolling contact, so it does not fatigue. It needs only two printed parts, a single fixed pin, and no assembly. The method generalises: the same code can turn any 1-DOF gesture a designer animates (a shy duck, a sleepy droop, a proud chin-up) into a printable joint. That is a direct, honest 'AI-designed mechanism' story. The prior-art map lists rolling-contact mechanisms as a near-empty gap (0 rolamite hits, 1 assembled rolling joint) and has no gesture-synthesised joints.
concepts.print_strategy: Print face-up as one print with two bodies. The hood back plate (z 0-2.0) sits on the bed, and the head is printed in the centre pose, which is the most symmetric and gives the largest uniform clearances. The cradle teeth, runner teeth and pin-in-slot are all vertical walls, so their clearances are lateral in XY, the most reliable PIP direction. The pin is part of the body and rises from the back plate, so it prints well supported. The head's slot is a blind pocket from the back, and its ceiling is a 5.8 mm bridge. The head plate prints over the back plate across a 0.4 mm gap, on 0.3 mm skate ribs. The collar prints over the head's runner region across a 0.4 mm gap. Body pillars beside the cradle keep collar bridge spans at 10 mm or less. There are no supports; the only overhangs are 45° chamfers and the eye domes. Moving bottom edges get a 0.6 × 45° chamfer. Use 0.2 mm layers, 3 perimeters, 15% gyroid infill, seam hidden at the hood's rear edge, and no brim. Optional filament swaps: z 2.4 head colour, z 10.2 black for the eye domes and nose. Cool the plate before removal, then break in by rocking end to end 20 times. PLA or PETG both work.
concepts.key_dimensions_mm: Overall 62 W × 78 H × 10.2 T (11.4 at the eye relief). Head about Ø40, 50 wide across the ears, head plate 5.0 thick. Travel ±10, lift 3, tilt ±28°. Cradle pitch curve 37.6 wide, 14 deep, arc 48.9; runner arc 48.9; teeth m1.25, 25° pressure angle, about 12.5 in mesh plus 2 run-out each end. Pin Ø5; slot 20.7 long × 5.8 wide. Hood back plate 2.0; collar 2.4. Ears at least 6 mm thick in-plane with r ≥ 2 rounds. Outer fillets r ≥ 1.5. Mass about 20 g.
concepts.clearances_mm: Tooth backlash 0.35 normal; tip-to-root radial 0.45. Pin-slot 0.35 radial, normal to the slot. Head to body middle-layer walls ≥ 0.6 at all poses (from the computed swept envelope). Z gaps 0.40 (two layers). Skate ribs 0.3 high. First-layer chamfers 0.6 × 45°. Variants for tuning: backlash 0.30 and 0.40.
concepts.child_safety: Two bodies, both far larger than the small-parts cylinder: the head is about 40 × 50 and the body 62 × 78. The head is captive in three ways: the sandwich between hood and collar holds it in Z, the pin-in-slot holds it in-plane, and the mesh holds it in-plane. It cannot be pried out without breaking 2 mm plates. There are no flexures, tabs or thin protrusions; the ears are at least 6 mm thick. Teeth and pin are inside a sealed cavity whose openings are 0.4 mm gaps. Every visible moving-to-fixed boundary is a Z overlap with a 0.4 mm gap. The raised face never comes within 6 mm of the collar edge in-plane at any pose, so no gap opens and closes within finger reach. The child's own push is the only driving force. All edges are rounded with r ≥ 1.5. Label: 6+, a 3D-printed toy that is not certified to EN 71 / ASTM F963, adult to inspect for cracks.
risks: Travel is bounded (±10 mm), so the fidget is a rocking or posing loop rather than continuous spinning, and it may hold attention less than a dial. The tick texture and posing mitigate this.
The large-area 0.4 mm Z gaps (head over hood, collar over runner) could fuse on poorly tuned printers. Mitigations: skate ribs and a 0.5 mm-gap variant.
Module 1.25 teeth with 0.35 backlash in PLA may feel gritty or wear. Mitigations: PETG and a backlash-variant coupon.
Gravity centring is negligible, so the head will not 'bobble back'. Copy and expectations must say it 'holds a pose'.
The eased tilt with 0.35 mm slop may show slight wobble at the extremes (about 1° of tilt play).
Tooth tips near the ends of travel, where the cradle's curvature is lowest, need contact-ratio verification (≥ 1.2). Run-out teeth are added for this.
concepts.modeling_plan: Use Python. (1) centrode.py (scratchpad prototype centrode3.py) takes the gesture parameters, computes the fixed and moving pitch curves and the pin slot, and runs the scipy optimiser with curvature and IC-depth constraints and integer-tooth rescaling of X. (2) manifold3d builds the teeth. Head runner teeth come from discrete rack-generation along the moving centrode, as a CrossSection. Cradle teeth are the cradle blank minus the union of the head-teeth CrossSection transformed to 400 poses, then offset by the backlash. The slot is the union of the pin circle in head frame over the poses, offset by 0.35. These are extruded to the middle layer, and the body cavity is the swept head envelope plus 0.6. (3) build123d builds the character skins (hood, collar or scarf, head outline, ears, eye domes, blush) with fillets r ≥ 1.5, merged in manifold3d. A parameter dict holds skin, gesture, module and clearances. Export one 3MF/STL with two disjoint bodies, plus a mini test coupon (a 3-tooth cradle segment with pin) at 0.30, 0.35 and 0.40.
concepts.verification_plan: 1. Pose sweep at 400 steps of t: head pose (x, y, φ)(t) against the fixed body. Check manifold3d intersection volume = 0 and minimum clearance ≥ 0.30 at the teeth, ≥ 0.33 at the slot and ≥ 0.40 elsewhere (trimesh proximity sampling). 2. Conjugacy check: at each pose, find the tooth pair in contact and confirm the gap ≈ backlash and a contact ratio ≥ 1.2. Re-solve the free motion with clearances (minimise the gap function), and confirm the realised tilt deviates by at most 1.5° from the target and the mesh separation by at most 0.35, so no skip is possible. 3. Retention: test 1 mm probes in ±Z and in-plane for interference at 20 poses. 4. Pinch check: compute in-plane distances between the head's exposed region and the fixed parts in the same Z band over the sweep (every gap must be ≥ 6 mm or Z-overlapped). 5. Overhang analysis (> 45° faces only at the designated gaps), bridge spans ≤ 10 mm, ray-cast wall thickness ≥ 1.2 (plates ≥ 2.0). 6. Small-parts bounding check for each body. 7. Renders: OpenSCAD or matplotlib frames at t = -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5 and 1, an animated GIF, and plots of the centrodes and IC depth. Prototype numbers come from /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Apps/023789a6-f9f1-563f-a565-9790ebbd0388/scratchpad/ideation/computed-profiles/centrode3.py and scan.py.

concepts.name: Peek-Up Pals (computed-coupler peeking critter)
concepts.tagline: Scroll the thumb wheel or roll the toy along a table. A friend rises over its wall, tilts its head to look around, then ducks back down. One hidden four-bar loop does all of it, and a computer search found its shape.
concepts.character: A plaque-style kawaii critter hiding behind a wall. It has a round 36 mm head, big engraved eyes with a highlight pillar, blush cheeks and a small smile. Shared core with 3 skins (each skin swaps only the head outline and the wall outline; pivot coordinates stay the same): (1) Chick in a cracked egg, where the wall is a rounded zig-zag eggshell (r>=2 mm); (2) Bunny in a magic hat, with short rounded ears that stay inside the head envelope and a hat-brim wall; (3) Kitten in a cardboard box, with box flaps as the wall. What the motion makes it do: it rises from hiding with its head tilted about 24 deg ('who's there?'), sweeps its head across to about -15 deg while peeking with just its eyes over the wall, then ducks back down. Each wheel turn is one peek. Pushing the head down by hand spins the wheel backwards.
concepts.mechanism_summary: A Grashof crank-rocker four-bar. The thumb/roller wheel is the crank, and the head is rigidly fixed to the coupler, so the head moves on the synthesized coupler motion. That motion is a near-vertical 20.7 mm rise with only ±4.6 mm side drift and a 30 deg curious head-tilt sweep. There are no slides, cams or tracks; all joints are vertical (Z) pins. A low-strain flexure pawl gives 12 detent clicks per turn, with a deeper detent at the peak pose so the peek can be held.
concepts.mechanism_detail: Coordinates in mm, origin at the wall-top centre line, y up (saved in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Apps/023789a6-f9f1-563f-a565-9790ebbd0388/scratchpad/ideation/linkages/linkage_params.json). Crank/wheel centre A=(-1.5,-40.9), crank a=10.0. Rocker pivot D=(12.5,-5.4), rocker c=28.3. Coupler B-C b=29.0. Ground |AD|=38.2. Grashof check: s+l=48.2 < p+q=57.3 with the crank shortest, so the crank turns fully and the mechanism has 1 DOF. Head centre P sits in the coupler frame at u=29.7 along BC from B and v=-15.0 normal to it; head 'up' axis offset -112.1 deg from BC. Over one crank turn: P.y goes from -18.4 (hidden) to +2.4 (peeking), a 20.7 mm rise; P.x stays within ±4.6 mm. Tilt starts at about +24 deg while rising, passes through 0 near the top and reaches about -15 deg while descending. About 26% of the cycle is spent in the top 20% of travel. Minimum transmission angle is 58.9 deg, so motion is smooth and backdrivable in both directions. Max |dy/dθ| is 11.1 mm/rad (mean 6.6). A 10 N thumb force on the R21 rim (210 N·mm) gives at most about 19 N on the head in its fast zone; the drive is the child's own thumb, so force is self-limited. With a Ø36 head (R18) the wall top sits at y=+1. Hidden: the head top is at -0.4, fully hidden. Peeking: 19.4 mm of head shows, with eyes (centre +4, r4.5) from y≈2 to 11 above the wall. Rigid bodies: frame, wheel+crank pin, rocker, coupler+head (4 bodies, 1 print). Layer stack: wheel L1, rocker L2, coupler+head L3, front wall L4. B never comes closer than 18.8 mm (surface gap) to the rocker in L2. The D pin is 38.2 mm from A, outside the R21 wheel. Joints: A and D are captive 45 deg V-ridge pins ending inside their own layers, so nothing protrudes into the coupler/head layer. B (on the wheel) and C (on the rocker) are Ø4 pins in blind Ø4.8 bores in the coupler. The front wall always covers B and C (they stay below y=-4.6; the wall covers y<+1), so the coupler cannot lift off. Wheel R=21 with a knurled rim (24 rounded ridges, r1). The rim protrudes 3 mm through a ~100 deg window at the bottom/bottom-right. Because the coupler boss reaches r=15 from A, the frame can keep a lip annulus r15.5-18 over the wheel in L2-L3, which closes the slit between wheel face and front wall. Detent: 12 bumps on the wheel inner rim. The pawl is an in-plane cantilever, 14 mm long, 1.2 mm thick, 4 mm tall, with 0.5 mm engagement: about 1.1 N, 0.46% strain, about 21 N·mm detent torque. One bump is 0.2 mm deeper at the peak pose for a haptic 'hold'. Rolling on a table: one peek per 132 mm of travel.
concepts.computational_design_element: Four-bar motion generation with timing, solved by global optimization. Ten parameters: A(x,y), D(x,y), a, b, c, the head point (u,v) on the coupler and the head-axis offset. Search: scipy differential_evolution, 8 seeds, popsize 30, using closed-form circle-intersection kinematics at 180 crank angles. Penalties: rise <22 mm; head side drift >4 mm; transmission angle <40 deg; fraction of the cycle in the top 20% of travel <0.45; head-tilt sweep while peeking outside 26-40 deg or off-centre; tilt >12 deg while hidden; joints outside the body keep-in zone; total height (head top to wheel bottom, wheel R=a+11) >80 mm. The crank is forced near the centre line (|Ax|<=1.5) so the wheel is centred and the toy can be rolled. Result: rise 20.7 mm, drift ±4.6 mm, tilt sweep 30 deg, transmission ≥58.9 deg, 80 mm tall. The pure four-bar's top-dwell limit (~26%) is the honest trade-off; the deeper detent gives a haptic pause at the peak. Scripts: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Apps/023789a6-f9f1-563f-a565-9790ebbd0388/scratchpad/ideation/linkages/peek4bar5.py and peek_report5.py. Story: 'a computer searched thousands of link shapes to find one loop of four bars that lifts the head nearly straight up out of hiding while tipping it curiously side to side, without any track or cam.'
concepts.fidget_loop: Ways to play: (a) scroll the knurled rim with a thumb while holding the toy upright; (b) stand it on a table and roll it along like a push-toy, one peek per 13 cm; (c) push the head down by hand and watch the wheel spin backwards (the mechanism is backdrivable). Feedback: 12 soft detent clicks per turn; the deeper 'peak' click pauses the head at its best peek; a continuous rise, tilt and duck plays on every turn. Endless one-way or back-and-forth rotation, with no end stops to fatigue.
concepts.closest_prior_art: MakerWorld 'Mechanical Waving Fidget Cat' 2856164 (gear-driven arms); Click-Wink BUNNY, Printables 1393629 (lever-cam wink); peek-a-boo alligator pop-up (decor), Printables 1283455; traditional wooden push-along toys with crank-driven figures, and stick 'bunny-in-a-cone' puppets; Coros et al., 'Computational Design of Mechanical Characters' (SIGGRAPH 2013), for motion-synthesized linkages, done there as multi-part crank automata; TonyHanma's Capiflexi nodding head (flexi chain, not a synthesized coupler).
concepts.novelty_argument: No print-in-place hand-held toy found carries a character's head on a four-bar coupler that was synthesized for motion. Here a single pin-jointed loop with no slider, slot or cam both lifts the head out of hiding nearly straight and performs an expressive head-tilt sweep, because position and orientation were optimized together. The head is guided only by revolute joints, which free up more reliably than PIP sliders. The same 1-DOF core gives three play modes: thumb scroll, roll-along on a table, and push-back backdrive. The prior-art gaps list linkage path synthesis for characters as essentially absent in fidgets (Printables: 'four bar linkage' 1, 'linkage fidget' 0).
concepts.print_strategy: One print, face up, no supports, 0.2 mm layers. Stack (z, mm): L0 back plate 0-1.8 (on the bed); L1 wheel 2.2-5.4; L2 rocker 5.8-8.8; L3 coupler+head 9.2-13.2; L4 front wall 13.6-15.4, fused to the back plate through the perimeter walls. All pins are vertical, so clearances are in XY. V-pins use 45 deg flanks. Blind-bore roofs are ≤Ø5 bridges. Large stacked overlaps (wheel on back plate; coupler/head under the front wall) have 1 mm 'skid ribs' at ≤6 mm pitch on the lower surface: 0.4 mm gap at the ribs and 1.0 mm in the field.
