The upper part's first layer then bridges rib-to-rib (≤6 mm), which cuts tack area by about 80%, and the ribs become low-friction runners. Print pose is crank ≈80 deg (head at peak) to minimise head/wall overlap. 0.5 mm x 45 deg chamfer at the bottom edge of every moving part and bore (elephant foot). Seam set to rear/aligned away from bores. Let the plate cool before removal, then break in with about 20 wheel turns. Estimated 25-30 g PLA, about 2-2.5 h.
concepts.key_dimensions_mm: Body 64 W x 62 H (head hidden) / 82 H (head peeking) x 15.4 T. Wheel Ø42, 3 mm rim exposure over a ~100 deg arc, 24 knurl ridges. Head Ø36 x 4.0 thick (bunny ears inside the envelope). Crank 10.0, coupler 29.0, rocker 28.3, ground 38.2. Link widths: coupler bar 8, rocker 7, bosses Ø8-9. Pins Ø4 (B, C); V-pins Ø6 (A), Ø5 (D). Front wall and back plate 1.8, perimeter walls ≥2.0. Detent pawl 14 x 1.2 x 4.
concepts.clearances_mm: Pin radial 0.40 (Ø4 in Ø4.8). V-pin normal gap 0.40 on 45 deg flanks. Z gaps 0.4 at skid ribs, 1.0 in the field. Moving parts to perimeter wall ≥0.6. Head to pocket sides 0.6; head to wall plate (Z) 0.4. Wheel rim to window edges 0.5. Detent engagement 0.5 radial. Design rule: ≥0.35 lateral everywhere, verified by sweep.
concepts.child_safety: Every exposed moving part is bigger than the small-parts cylinder in two axes: head Ø36, wheel Ø42. The small internal bodies (rocker ~36x9, pins) are fully enclosed between 1.8 mm plates with ≤0.6 mm gaps, so they cannot exit even if a pin breaks. No exposed scissoring links. Pinch points: the head/wall shear line has a 0.4-0.6 mm gap and no closing wedge, because nothing surrounds the head above the wall. The rim window gap is 0.5 mm. All drive force comes from the child's own thumb, about 20 N max at the head. Edges r ≥1.5 mm, eggshell zig-zag r ≥2. Head neck section ≥10 x 4 mm. Compact 15 mm thick slab for drop tolerance. Target 6+. Note: home 3D prints are not EN71/ASTM F963 certified; inspect for cracks.
risks: Large stacked overlaps can tack after printing. Mitigated by skid ribs, 0.4/1.0 mm gaps and printing in the peak pose, but this needs a test coupon on the target printer.
Pin play is amplified at the head: 0.4 mm play at B/C over a ~30 mm lever gives about ±1 mm and ±1.5 deg head wobble (acceptable, but it reads as looseness).
A pure four-bar gives only ~26% top-dwell; the motion reads as a continuous bob unless the deeper peak detent works well.
The rim exposure window and wall-top shear line need careful rounding to avoid catching skin; verify the gap function over the full sweep.
Rolling on a table relies on rim friction; PLA on a smooth table may slip. Option: add a TPU-free tread pattern with sharper knurl spacing.
Head-to-wheel stack is 15.4 mm thick; thinner layers risk V-pin strength.
concepts.modeling_plan: build123d for B-rep bodies with fillets, plus manifold3d for booleans and sweeps. Single source of truth: linkage_params.json (optimizer output) plus a clearance/layer table. Modules: core.py (frame: back plate, perimeter, lip annulus, A/D V-pins with revolved 45 deg ridge profiles, rim window, skid-rib generator, detent pawl), links.py (wheel with knurl, crank pin B and detent bumps; rocker with C pin; coupler as the hull of bosses at B and C plus a neck to the head mount), skins/*.py (head outline, face engraving 1.0 mm, highlight pillars, wall outline; chick/bunny/kitten), assemble.py (place bodies at the print pose, crank 80 deg, and export one multi-body STL/3MF plus per-body STLs). All edges filleted ≥1 mm (1.5 on exterior). OpenSCAD only for quick headless preview renders.
concepts.verification_plan: 1) Kinematics: re-solve the loop at 720 crank angles and assert closure error <1e-6, transmission angle ≥55 deg and Grashof margin. 2) Collision sweep: transform the body meshes with manifold3d at each angle, require pairwise intersection volume = 0 for bodies sharing a layer, and min lateral clearance ≥0.35 mm via cKDTree on surface samples. Include the B-pin-through-L2 and coupler-vs-lip checks. 3) Pinch/gap function: track gaps between moving exterior surfaces and fixed edges over the cycle; flag any closing gap in the 2-12 mm band. 4) Printability: face-normal overhang map (>45 deg from vertical only where resting on ribs); bridge-span check on downward horizontal faces (≤6 mm, or ≤10 mm at bores); Z-gap audit at the print pose. 5) Wall thickness by inward ray casting (≥1.6 mm shells, ≥1.2 mm flexure). 6) Small parts: bounding-cylinder fit test per body, plus an enclosure/escape test for any body that fits. 7) Detent: beam formula and a small FE check of strain and force. 8) Renders: PNG at hidden, rising and peak poses, plus an animated GIF of the cycle for each skin.

concepts.name: Boo Buddy (squeeze-to-peek-a-boo)
concepts.tagline: A shy friend covers its eyes with its paws. Squeeze its cheeks halfway and it peeks through its paws; squeeze all the way and the paws fly open: BOO! Let go and it hides again. A computer synthesized the paw path.
concepts.character: A round 'mochi' bear with toe-bean paws, a little nose that stays visible between the paws (12 mm gap), and big eyes. The eyes are Ø8 holes that show a dark back plate (one M600 colour swap), each with a Ø2 highlight pillar. At rest it is shy, with its eyes covered. A half squeeze makes it peek through its paws (paws lift and tilt about 22 deg). A full squeeze makes it 'BOO!': jazz-hands paws swing out to the cheeks, turned about 43 deg palms-out. Squeezing only one side opens one paw, a one-eyed peek or wink. Skins on the same core, swapping face outline, ears and paw outline: bear, lop bunny, robot (block hands, round 'lens' eyes), little monster (horn nubs, three-toe paws).
concepts.mechanism_summary: Two independent, mirrored four-bars. Each cheek is a squeeze pad (the input rocker) on a compliant butterfly pivot, which is also the return spring. A forearm-and-paw coupler, steered by a short internal output rocker, carries the paw through three synthesized keyframes: covering the eye, peeking, then BOO. A 16 deg cheek rotation (5.2 mm at the joint) becomes a 12.8 mm paw sweep plus 43 deg of paw rotation. Hard stops on the pads keep overload out of the flexures and linkage.
concepts.mechanism_detail: Coordinates in mm, origin at the face centre; right side shown, left mirrored. Saved in linkage_params.json. Pad virtual pivot O1=(26,-30). Pad joint Q1 at r1=18.8 (arm 2.4 deg off vertical), rest (26.8,-11.2). Coupler/forearm Q1-Q2 L=10.0, Q2 rest ≈(14.1,-11.6). Output rocker O2=(28.3,-2.9), r2=14.4. Paw reference point in the Q1→Q2 frame: u=13.3, v=-20.1. Input: pad rotation 0→16 deg; the outer grip surface at r≈20 moves about 5.5 mm per side. Achieved paw poses vs targets: rest (12.8,8.4), 0 deg (eye centre (12,7)); half-squeeze (18.7,12.2), -22 deg; full (25.0,12.1), -43.5 deg. Max pose error 3.0 mm, rotation error <2 deg. Minimum transmission angle 34.8 deg. |Q1-O2| ≥8.4 mm keeps the bosses printable. The linkage stays in x>8 so the mirrored pair never collide. Each side is 1 DOF; the sides are independent, giving 2 DOF total. Bodies: frame, 2 pads, 2 output rockers, 2 forearm-paws (7 rigid bodies, 1 print). Layers: pad L1, rocker L2, forearm-paw L3 riding on top of the face. The Q1 pin (on the pad) passes through L2 clear of the rocker (≥5 mm surface gap, to be confirmed by sweep). The O2 pin rises from the back plate through L1, ≥8.4 mm from the pad joint. Return spring and pivot: a butterfly flexure, two in-plane leaves converging on O1, each L=30, h=7 (Z). Thickness is tapered t(s)=t_tip·sqrt(M(s)/M_tip), 0.9 mm at the tip to 1.8 mm at the root, which gives uniform bending strain of about 0.6-0.7% (PLA) at 16 deg. The pair gives roughly 4-6 N squeeze per side at full travel; the PLA estimate at 12 deg/L24 was 7.6 N at 0.65%. The pad has an inner hard stop at 16 deg, which coincides with the BOO pose, and an outer stop at 0 deg. A child squeezing or pulling harder only loads rigid stop ribs. The pad is Z-sandwiched (no out-of-plane twist on the leaves) and carries a dovetail keeper wider than its exit opening. Pad edges are arcs about O1 (0.6 mm gap, including a 0.3 mm budget for virtual-centre drift).
concepts.computational_design_element: (1) Numerical three-position motion generation (Burmester-type) with prescribed timing. Nine parameters (r1, pad-arm angle, O2 x/y, r2, coupler L, paw point u/v, paw orientation offset). Search: differential_evolution with closed-form kinematics over 49 pad angles. The keyframes cover → peek → boo are pinned to pad angles 0/8/16 deg. Penalties: transmission <35 deg, joints outside |x|≤28/|y|≤30, encroaching on the mirrored half (x<8), pin spacing <8.5 mm. Scripts: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Apps/023789a6-f9f1-563f-a565-9790ebbd0388/scratchpad/ideation/linkages/boo3.py and boo.py. Earlier runs showed the trade-off honestly: a cramped 8 mm cluster reached ±2 mm accuracy but was unprintable; enforcing printable spacing needed 16 deg of input. (2) Flexure leaf taper computed for uniform strain under the actual moment distribution, integrated with Euler-Bernoulli in numpy. To do: verify with a large-deflection elastica (scipy solve_bvp) that virtual-centre drift stays <0.3 mm against the rigid kinematic model, and compute the force-squeeze curve. Story: 'the computer found where to put four hidden joints so that squeezing the cheeks moves the paws through three hand-drawn poses: covering, peeking and BOO, and it shaped the springy cheek hinges so they bend evenly and don't wear out.'
concepts.fidget_loop: Squeeze and release, like a stress ball with a show. The amount of squeeze controls the expression continuously: half a squeeze peeks, a full squeeze is BOO. Squeezing one side gives a one-eyed peek; alternating sides makes it 'wave'. Tactile: springy, progressive resistance, ending in a soft 'tock' as the pad meets its inner stop exactly at the BOO pose. On release the paws snap back over the eyes with a light 'tick' on the outer stop. Kids can also push the paws open by hand (backdrivable). Sound is quiet: PLA-on-PLA taps only.

The paw motion is not a simple rocker swing: the coupler motion was synthesized numerically through three expressive keyframes (pose and orientation), so the paws lift, slide and turn palms-out. That gives analog, graded expression (half squeeze peeks) and independent left/right expressions from two 1-DOF loops. The pads are compliant-pivot rockers whose leaves are tapered by computation for uniform strain. This combines the rigid-link precision of a synthesized four-bar with a spring-return squeeze, with no hardware. The prior-art map lists both character-oriented force-shaped compliant mechanisms and linkage-synthesized character motion as gaps.
concepts.print_strategy: One print, face up, no supports, 0.2 mm layers. Printed at the rest pose so the flexures are unstressed. Stack (z, mm): L0 back plate 0-2.0, with the first 1.2 mm in a dark colour (M600 swap) so the eye holes show dark pupils; L1 pads 2.4-5.6 inside core pockets; L2 output rockers 6.0-8.6; core face surface at 8.6; L3 forearm+paw 9.0-12.5 plus a 1.0 mm toe-bean relief (about 13.5 mm total). All pins vertical. The Q1/Q2 pins end in 45 deg mushroom heads (Ø6 on Ø4) on the forearm top. A 'collar/bib' bridge of ≤8 mm span arches over each forearm near the cheek with a 0.4 mm gap for pry resistance. The paw's first layer bridges the Ø8 eye holes. Under the paws and forearms the face has skid ribs (0.4 gap) at ≤6 mm pitch with a 1.0 mm field gap. Flexure leaves are printed in-plane, so bending stresses run along the perimeters rather than across layers. Use ≥3 perimeters (whole leaf = perimeters, no infill seams) and keep seams away from the leaves. 0.5 mm elephant-foot chamfers on moving parts. Break-in: 20 squeezes per side. PETG recommended for long flexure life (add +0.05 mm to the clearances); PLA works with a shorter life. About 20 g, about 1.5-2 h.
concepts.key_dimensions_mm: Body 66 W (77 with pads proud at rest; pads stand 5.5 mm proud each side) x 70 H x 13.5 T. Eyes Ø8 holes at (±12,7). Paw mitten about 14 x 16, forearm 7 wide x 3.5 thick, forearm+paw ≈34 long. Pad grip face about 22 long x 12 thick, r≥3 edges. Linkage: r1 18.8, coupler 10.0, rocker 14.4, O1→O2 ≈27. Pins Ø4 (Q1, Q2), Ø5 V-pin (O2). Flexure leaves 30 x 7 (Z), t 0.9→1.8. Paw gap at rest 11.6-12.
concepts.clearances_mm: Pin radial 0.40. Mushroom head and collar Z gap 0.4. Paw/forearm over face: 0.4 at ribs, 1.0 field. Pad pocket arcs 0.6 (incl. 0.3 flexure-centre drift). Pad dovetail keeper 0.5. Flexure leaves to any wall ≥1.0. Rocker to pad layer 0.4 Z. Mirrored linkages ≥2 mm apart by synthesis constraint. PETG: +0.05 mm on all.
concepts.child_safety: Forearm-paws (≈34 x 16) and rockers would fit the small-parts cylinder if freed, so they are made geometrically captive with redundancy. Each paw is held by two mushroom-headed Ø4 pins (layer-tension area ≈25 mm², roughly 300 N pull-off) plus a fixed collar bridge over the forearm, so prying loads the collar, not the pins. Rockers and flexures are fully enclosed in the sandwich, behind gaps ≤0.6 mm. Pads are captive by a dovetail keeper even if a leaf cracks. The failure mode is loss of spring return only, with no loose pieces. Pinch: paws only move apart from rest, so the minimum paw-to-paw gap is 11.6-12 mm (outside the 5-9.5 mm trap band). Paw-over-face and pad-edge interfaces are shear lines with ≤0.6 mm constant gaps (arcs about the pivot), with no closing wedges. Paws overhang only free air at BOO. Return force at the paw is low (a few N). Edges r≥1.5, pads r≥3. Hard stops protect against crushing or overpulling. Target 6+. Not certified; inspect the flexures periodically.
risks: Flexure fatigue: about 0.65% strain is fine for PETG but limits PLA to perhaps 10^4-10^5 squeezes. Failure is safe (captive) but ends the auto-return.
Transmission angle bottoms at 34.8 deg, so the end of the squeeze may feel slightly sticky. Can trade about 1 mm of pose accuracy for 40 deg.
Butterfly flexure virtual-centre drift and leaf compliance shift the paw path by about ±0.5 mm against the rigid model; needs an elastica check.
Low return force (4-6 N) against fresh print-in-place friction may leave paws short of fully covering the eyes until broken in; tune leaf thickness with a coupon.
Paw/forearm stacked over the face can tack; mitigated with ribs and the 0.4/1.0 mm gap scheme.
Prying the paws is the main abuse case. The collar bridge and two mushroom pins need a pull test on the printed part.
Seven bodies in one print means more joints that must all free up; any fused joint locks that side.
concepts.modeling_plan: build123d plus manifold3d, driven by linkage_params.json (right side; the left is generated by mirroring about x=0). Modules: frame.py (back plate with colour-split height, core with pockets, eye holes with highlight pillars, O2 V-pins, collar bridges, skid ribs, hard-stop ribs), pad.py (grip face with arcs about O1, dovetail keeper, butterfly flexure leaves with numerically tapered thickness swept from the t(s) table, Q1 pin), rocker.py, forearm_paw.py (hull of Q1/Q2 bosses plus forearm to the paw mitten at (u,v,offset), toe-bean relief, mushroom pin heads), skins/ (face outline, ears, paw outline). Exterior fillets 1.5 mm, internal 0.8. Export a multi-body STL/3MF at the rest pose plus per-body STLs; OpenSCAD only for previews.
concepts.verification_plan: 1) Kinematics: closure, transmission and pose-error report at 0/8/16 deg; sweep 0-16 deg in 0.25 deg steps for each side independently and for all 4 combinations (both, left only, right only, neither). 2) Collision: manifold3d pairwise intersection = 0 and cKDTree min lateral clearance ≥0.35 mm, including Q1 pin through the rocker layer and paw-paw distance. 3) Flexure: scipy elastica (solve_bvp) for leaf strain, force-squeeze curve and virtual-centre drift; feed the drift back into the sweep. 4) Pinch: gap-function tracking of all moving exterior edges; assert no closing gap in 2-12 mm. 5) Printability: overhang map (≤45 deg except mushroom/V cones at 45), bridge spans (collar ≤8, ribs ≤6, eye holes ≤8), Z-gap audit at the rest pose, min wall/leaf thickness by ray casting. 6) Safety: bounding-cylinder test per body; escape test (attempt ±Z and in-plane extraction against fixed geometry) for each body that fits; pull-off estimate for the pin heads. 7) Renders: three keyframe PNGs (shy / peek / BOO) per skin plus a GIF; plot paw path against target keyframes.

concepts.name: Side-Eye Sid: Tusi-Glance Cyclops
concepts.tagline: Scroll the tail-wheel and one big pupil slides dead-straight left and right with no slider. A planet gear rolling inside a ring twice its size carries it, and the egg-shaped gear pair was computed to make each glance hold and then dart.
concepts.character: Sid is a round one-eyed monster, 72 W x 82 H x ~20 D mm. He has two stubby rounded horns, a big recessed oval eye-white (36 x 22 mm) with a flush 10 mm dome pupil, blush cheeks, a small rounded fang smile and stubby feet. A knurled 'tail-wheel' pokes 5 mm out of his right side and back. Motion: classic cartoon shifty side-eye. He looks left and holds, darts right and holds. Skins share one core (eye centre (0,8), wheel axis (22,-12)) and are alternate front-shell/outline modules in the same parametric file; each prints as a complete one-piece toy. (a) Sid the monster. (b) Scanbot, a robot whose visor is the eye-white and whose pupil is the sweeping 'scanner light'. (c) Cap'n Pip, a pirate parrot with a printed eye-patch on one side and the moving eye on the other.
concepts.mechanism_summary: Thumb wheel, then a computed non-circular gear pair (16T driver : 32T follower, 2:1 average), then a carrier crank, then a Tusi couple: a 12T planet rolls inside a fixed 24T internal ring that forms the eye socket. A peg on the planet's pitch circle traces an exact straight 24 mm diameter. It pokes through a straight cosmetic slot in the eye-white cover and carries the pupil dome. One DOF, all axes along Z, all clearances in XY.
concepts.mechanism_detail:
TUSI STAGE: ring pitch R=12 (24T internal, m=1.0); planet r=6 (12T, +0.25 profile shift); carrier crank radius 6 from the eye centre. The planet's absolute rotation is -psi, so the planet pitch point is at x = r cos psi + r cos(-psi) = 12 cos psi, y = 0. That is an exact straight line, 24 mm of travel. The peg is 4 mm diameter on the planet top at r=6, and the dome pupil (10 mm diameter, 3 mm tall) sits above the cover. The slot is 5.0 x 29 mm in a 1.6 mm cover. The peg is never meant to touch the slot: 0.5 mm per side, against a predicted gear-slop deviation of <=0.35 mm. The planet spins under the dome, so the pupil is a plain dome and the sparkle highlight is printed on the fixed eye-white. Only a straight path allows this: any other planet point traces an ellipse, and an elliptical window would cut the centre of the cover free.

TIMING STAGE: centre distance a=30 mm (eye (0,8) to wheel (22,-12)). Two driver turns per carrier turn, so one thumb-wheel turn = one glance from one side to the other. Time-warp g=dphi/dpsi = 1.3 + c*|cos psi|^4, mean 2, giving an instantaneous ratio of 1.3 to ~3.6 (slow carrier near psi=0 and pi, i.e. the extremes). Pitch radii: driver N1 r1=a/(1+g) from 7.2 to 13.0 mm (16T); carrier N2 r2=a*g/(1+g) from 17.0 to 22.8 mm (32T); m=1.25; equal pitch perimeters of 125.8 mm (N1 counted over 2 turns). Both pitch curves are convex, with max tangent deviation 21 deg and min radius of curvature 7.9 / 14.2 mm. Use a 25 deg rack cutter to limit undercut on the small lobe (r=7.2 is equivalent to an 11.5T circle). Computed effect: the pupil is within 10% of an extreme 42% of the time (29% with circular 2:1 gears), and it spends 35% of the time crossing the middle 70% of travel (49% circular). So it holds each glance ~45% longer and darts ~1.4x faster.

DRIVE: thumb wheel 38 mm diameter x 4 mm, on the same part as N1. Its rim has a 45 deg V-ridge running in a V-groove in the back-plate opening; this is the bearing and the Z capture, so no axle is needed. The carrier N2 turns on a 6 mm stub axle from a body pedestal that ends below the planet layer, because the planet sweeps over the eye centre. Loads are thumb-only, friction torque ~1e-3 N*m. Bending stress in the 4 mm crank pin and peg is <1 MPa.
concepts.computational_design_element: (1) Inverse synthesis of the non-circular pitch curves from a target gaze timeline. The pupil law x = R cos psi(phi) is warped with g(psi), then phi = integral of g, r1 = a/(1+g), r2 = a*g/(1+g). Constraints: closure with 2:1 average and integer teeth (16/32 at m=1.25); convexity r^2 + 2r'^2 - r*r'' > 0; tangent deviation <= 21 deg; min curvature radius >= 7 mm. An optimizer over (gmin, p) maximizes hold fraction against those limits. Prototype scripts in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Apps/023789a6-f9f1-563f-a565-9790ebbd0388/scratchpad/ideation/rolling/c1c.py and c1b.py chose gmin=1.3, p=4. (2) Teeth by virtual hobbing: a 25 deg rack cutter is rolled without slip along each pitch curve, and ~720 poses are subtracted in a manifold3d CrossSection, so the pair is conjugate by construction. The same code cuts the Tusi ring and planet. (3) The slot and dome recess are computed as the swept envelope of peg and dome plus clearance, including Monte-Carlo slop. Honest story: the Tusi straight line is 13th-century geometry (Nasir al-Din al-Tusi). What was computed is the egg-shaped gear pair, solved backwards from 'hold the look, then dart', and the clearance-checked slot.
concepts.fidget_loop: Scroll the side/back tail-wheel with the thumb, or roll Sid along a table on the wheel. Each wheel turn: the pupil holds left, darts straight across, holds right. Continuous scrolling gives rhythmic shifty-eyes, and it works in both directions. Feedback: a soft gear rumble (16 driver teeth per turn, plus the Tusi mesh), the visible dart-and-hold rhythm, and smooth low-effort rotation. Quiet enough for a classroom.

Tusi illusion table 1757607: motorised, magnets, not hand-held. Character expression via ring or lever: Blinking Cat Glasses (MakerWorld 95121), Click-Wink Bunny (Printables 1393629). concepts.novelty_argument: The prior-art map lists no hand-held print-in-place Tusi couple that animates a character feature, and it explicitly names 'pupil oscillating' as an open gap. This design uses the theorem functionally: because the pupil peg's path is a perfect straight line, the face can be one continuous cover with a straight slot. A non-circular gear pair inverse-synthesized from a desired motion profile and driving an expression is a second listed gap (pitch curve computed from target timing, not a stock ellipse or nautilus). It is not a gear spinner re-skin: all gears are hidden, and the visible behaviour is the expression.
concepts.print_strategy: One print, face-up, back on the bed, no supports. Z stack: thumb wheel 0-4.0 printed directly on the bed inside a back-plate opening, captured by a 45 deg V-ridge/V-groove (no gap printing). Body pedestal 0-4.0 under the carrier. N1 4.0-8.6 (same part as the wheel). N2 4.4-8.6, printed over the pedestal and wheel top with a 0.4 mm (2-layer) gap. Eye ring (body) and planet 9.0-13.6 over N2. Cover 14.0-15.6 with the slot. Dome 16.0-19.0 in a recessed eye-white channel, flush with the face. Over-gap surfaces carry 0.5 mm-tall rails to cut contact area; bridges are <=6 mm. Every outer edge has a 1.5 mm fillet. Overhangs are only 45 deg chamfers on the V-ridge and on the conical tops of the axle stubs. Add elephant-foot compensation of 0.15 mm, or a 0.6 mm chamfer at the wheel's bed edge. Ship a 0.35/0.45 mm clearance coupon.
concepts.key_dimensions_mm: Body 72 x 82 x 20 (horns to 86 tall max optional). Eye-white recess 36 x 22. Pupil dome 10 dia, travel +/-12. Tusi: ring R12 (24T m1.0), planet r6 (12T), gear face width 4.6. Non-circular pair: m1.25, a=30, N1 16T r7.2-13.0, N2 32T r17.0-22.8, face width 4.2-4.6. Thumb wheel 38 dia x 4, exposed 5 mm at right side and visible at back. Stub axle 6 dia; crank pin 4 dia; peg 4 dia; slot 5.0 x 29; cover 1.6 thick.
concepts.clearances_mm: XY moving fits 0.40-0.45 (axle holes +0.4 radial, wheel V-groove 0.45 normal). Gear meshes: 0.15 per flank tooth thinning (~0.3 backlash) plus 0.4 tip-root. Z gaps 0.4 (2 layers at 0.2) at every stacked interface. Peg to slot 0.5 per side. Dome to cover 0.4. Wheel rim to body window 0.5. All accessible gaps <=0.6 except the 5 mm slot.
concepts.child_safety: The thumb wheel/N1 (38 mm) and the carrier N2 (~46 mm) are larger than the 31.7 mm small-parts cylinder even if freed. The planet+peg+dome (~15 mm) is the only sub-cylinder part, and it is triple-captive: ring around it, carrier below, cover above. The dome is flush in a recessed channel, so it cannot be gripped, twisted or pried. The peg is 4-5 mm PLA and short (2.4 mm), so it carries no lever arm. Openings: a 5 mm slot whose floor is a smooth moving disc 2 mm down (no teeth exposed under the slot), and a 0.5 mm wheel gap. The mechanism is driven only by thumb torque. Radii >=1.5 mm everywhere, no protrusions thinner than 5 mm (horns are 10 mm stubs), walls >=2 mm. Note: 3D-printed toys are uncertified; age 6+.
risks: Four stacked print-over-gap interfaces (N2, planet, cover, dome) may tack together. Mitigations: 0.4 mm gaps, rails, a break-in instruction, and a clearance coupon. This is the main failure mode.
The 1-lobe 16T driver's small lobe (r=7.2) undercuts and may have weak or pointed tips. Mitigate with the 25 deg cutter and verify min tooth thickness >=1.1 mm, or fall back to gmin=1.4 (dev 18 deg).
The 12T m1.0 planet is fine-pitched for FDM with 0.35-0.45 clearances. It may need m1.1 (R=13.2) if test prints bind.
The large V-groove plain bearing of the thumb wheel adds friction, so the wheel scrolls rather than coasting like a flywheel.
Effective pressure angle up to ~41-46 deg at the steepest part of the non-circular pair. Thumb-driven, so tolerable, but it feels slightly lumpy.
A ~20 mm thick body is chunky; a slimmer variant needs smaller gear face widths.
concepts.modeling_plan: Python + manifold3d for all gears and booleans. ncgear.py synthesizes g(psi), produces pitch polylines, and generates teeth by virtual hobbing via CrossSection boolean of rolled rack-cutter poses, then extrudes. tusi.py builds the involute 24T ring and 12T planet with the same hobbing code. build123d builds the filleted outer shells, eye recess, horns and feet for each skin, exported as meshes and unioned and differenced in manifold3d. A single params dict holds m, a, R, clearances, layer height and Z-stack levels. Each skin is a function returning a front-shell solid. The keep-out volume is generated automatically as the swept volume of every moving part over 720 deg of input, offset by +0.4 mm, and subtracted from the body, so skins can't collide by construction. Export a print-pose 3MF/STL. OpenSCAD is used only to import STLs for headless renders.
concepts.verification_plan: (a) Kinematic sweep of thumb angle 0-720 deg in 1 deg steps. Pose N1, N2 and the planet. manifold3d intersection volume must be 0 for every part pair and against the body. trimesh proximity min clearance >=0.3 mm, except designed meshes. (b) Per-pose 2D mesh check: zero tooth overlap area, backlash band 0.2-0.4 mm, contact ratio >1.1 around the whole non-circular pair, closure and tooth-count integrity. (c) Pupil path: peg-centre deviation from the line (0 nominal), plus Monte-Carlo +/-0.2 mm part slop, giving slot-wall clearance >=0.15 mm. (d) Plot pupil x against thumb angle and report hold/dart metrics against the circular baseline. (e) Printability on the print-pose mesh: down-facing faces >45 deg must be on the bed or over a <=0.4 mm gap; bridges <=10 mm; ray-cast wall thickness >=1.2 mm; every moving part a separate shell with >=0.35 mm gaps. (f) Small-parts: minimal enclosing-cylinder diameter of each part. (g) Headless OpenSCAD renders at several poses, plus a matplotlib GIF of one glance cycle.

concepts.name: Hammy's Petal Wheel: gravity-indexed rolling track
concepts.tagline: Turn the flower slowly and Hammy's wheel waits in a petal, then whooshes over to the next one and lands with a soft thunk, every 120 deg. Hammy stays upright the whole time. The petal shapes were computed so it happens right on cue.
concepts.character: Hammy the hamster rides inside a 32.5 mm geared hamster wheel. Hammy is a 22 mm disc with a 19 mm visible face: big eyes, cheek pouches, tiny paws and cut-out ears. He hangs as a pendulum on the wheel hub, so he stays upright while the wheel spins under him. He leans back about 20 deg on each zoom ('wheee') and bobs forward on landing, with a ~12 deg 'running lean' while rolling. The frame is a smiling 3-petal flower, 82 x 78 x 14 mm, with an open centre window onto the track. Skins share the identical track core; only the outer outline (>=3.5 mm wall) and the rider art change. (a) Hammy in a blossom. (b) Puff, a chick, in a 3-puff cloud. (c) Kit, an astronaut kitten, in a 3-lobed space station. The rider disc art is a parameterized relief.
concepts.mechanism_summary: There is one geared wheel (24T). It is captured on a computed closed non-circular internal ring gear (57T): three internal 'pockets' joined by three convex inward 'humps'. A hub peg rides a groove along the computed centre path, so the wheel can never leave the teeth. Gravity alone rolls it. Turning the frame in the vertical plane makes a gravity-powered intermittent indexer built purely from rolling contact: the wheel dwells in a pocket until that pocket's potential well vanishes (a saddle-node) at a computed tilt, then rolls over the hump and drops into the next pocket. A free pendulum rider on the wheel hub stays upright.
concepts.mechanism_detail:
GEOMETRY: pitch curve = morphological closing (radius rho_h=12) of the union of three circles of rho_c=22, centred 16 mm from the toy centre at 120 deg spacing. Pitch perimeter 223.9 mm gives 57 teeth at m=1.25 (19 per lobe, 3-fold symmetric). Pitch bounding box 71.7 x 68 mm. Wheel r_p=15 (24T), OD 32.5, face width 9. Pocket internal mesh is equivalent to a 35.2T ring against the 24T wheel (difference 11, above the ~10 needed to avoid internal interference). Humps are external meshes with radius 12. The centre path is the inward offset by 15: 7 mm arcs in the pockets, 27 mm arcs over the humps, ~130 mm total.

BEHAVIOUR (computed): wheel-centre height is y(s,alpha) = x(s) sin(alpha) + y(s) cos(alpha). Equilibria are its local minima in s. The ideal quasi-static spill is ~84 deg past pocket-bottom. With rolling resistance c_rr 0.03-0.08 the 1-DOF dynamics (inertia factor 1.6) spill at 92-98 deg and run ~28 mm in ~0.2 s, peak speed 0.44 m/s, drop ~11 mm. Impact energy is ~1.2 mJ for the ~10 g moving mass: an audible soft thunk. It then sloshes 2-3 decaying rocks (~0.4 s) and settles. There is no runaway at 120 deg/s frame rotation for c_rr >=0.05. Fast swirls (>~300 deg/s) let it loop continuously, an intended second mode. Wheel absolute rotation = -s/r_p (s = rolled pitch arc), so it spins ~1.6-2 rad under Hammy per index.

RIDER: pendulum on a 4 mm pin. COM offset e~3 mm from a thick lower body and thin upper body with ear cut-outs. Steady lean from pin friction = asin(mu*r_pin/e) ~12 deg; inertial lean ~20 deg at the ~0.4 g zoom acceleration. Loads are gravity only (~0.1 N), so stresses are negligible. DOF: wheel 1 (constrained to the path), rider 1.
concepts.computational_design_element: (1) The track is synthesized from target behaviour, not drawn. Targets: 3 indexes per turn; spill tilt in an 80-100 deg window; drop >=10 mm; run >=25 mm; no runaway at <=180 deg/s for c_rr >=0.05; outer frame <=85 mm. Constraints: internal-mesh curvature rho >= r_p + 5m, external hump rho >=10, integer 3-fold tooth count. Design variables D, rho_c, rho_h (optionally pocket asymmetry for direction-dependent feel). Evaluation uses a quasi-static potential-landscape solver with saddle-node (well-vanishing) detection plus a 1-DOF rolling-dynamics simulation. A grid then Nelder-Mead search chose D=16, rho_c=22, rho_h=12. Prototypes are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Apps/023789a6-f9f1-563f-a565-9790ebbd0388/scratchpad/ideation/rolling/c2_track.py, c2_dyn2.py and c2_teeth.py. (2) The 57T non-circular internal ring's teeth come from virtual hobbing: the 24T involute wheel is rolled without slip along the pitch curve (rotation = s/r_p) and the union of its poses is subtracted in manifold3d, so pocket and hump teeth are conjugate by construction. (3) The hub groove is the computed centre path buffered by the peg radius + 0.45. Honest story: 'the petal shapes were computed so gravity makes Hammy zoom exactly once per petal and land with a thunk'.
concepts.fidget_loop: Turn the toy hand over hand like a little steering wheel, or roll it on its edge along a table. Every 120 deg: wait... whoosh... THUNK. Hammy leans back on the zoom and bobs forward on landing. Reversing the turn reverses the run. A fast swirl gives continuous loop-the-loop with a rattling purr; slow down and it settles back into petal-by-petal stepping. Feedback: tooth rumble during the run, the landing thunk you feel in the hand, the visible dwell-zoom rhythm, and the pendulum bob.
concepts.closest_prior_art: Loose marble-in-ring and hamster-wheel gravity toys. Circular hypocycloid/planetary spinners (Planetario 1862543, Nested Hypocycloid 143028), which are hand-driven. Non-circular gear fidgets (MakerWorld nautilus 2747133, 1815713), which are driven decorative pairs. Geneva intermittent fidgets (MakerWorld 2898056, 510930), which use pin-and-slot. Gravity/inertia character toys: Waving Cat (MakerWorld 2856164), stick-slip woodpecker 1862612, roly-poly 132273. Gomboc/self-righting bodies use the same 'shape from potential landscape' idea, but on a single solid.
concepts.novelty_argument: This is an intermittent indexer with no pins, slots, pawls, springs or detents. Both the dwell and the release come from the gravitational potential landscape of a closed non-circular internal ring gear, inverse-designed for spill angle, run, drop and no-runaway. The map shows non-circular gears only as driven decorative pairs, and gravity rollers only as loose marbles. A captive, geared, print-in-place rolling element, plus a computed spill track, plus an upright pendulum rider, is absent. Safety comes from size: the only rolling element is 32.5 mm, so it is not a small part even if freed. Repeatable, rhythmic and quiet, and it rewards slow or fast play differently.
concepts.print_strategy: One print, flat, back on the bed, no supports. Frame floor 0-2.4 with the hub groove cut 1.6 deep (0.8 mm floor under it). 0.5 mm-tall rails along the track lower contact area and sliding friction. Wheel 2.8-11.8, printed over the rails with a 0.4 mm (2-layer) gap; its 5.6 mm hub peg sits in the groove, 0.4 mm above the groove floor. The rider disc (3.2 thick) sits in the wheel's front recess on a 4 mm pin with a 45 deg conical cap. The wheel's front lip (inner radius 9.5) is 0.4 mm above the rider edge. The frame's front lip (12.2-13.8) overhangs the outer 2 mm of the wheel teeth and rack, giving Z capture and covering the mesh nip. With floor plus lips capturing Z, spur teeth suffice, which keeps non-circular tooth generation simple. Over-gap areas are lip annuli <=4 mm wide and the wheel bottom, bridging <=3 mm between rails. All outer edges R1.5. Print pose: wheel in the bottom pocket. Use slicer elephant-foot compensation; let the bed cool before removal.
concepts.key_dimensions_mm: Frame 82 x 78 x 14 (flower skin; all skins <=85). Pitch curve bbox 71.7 x 68; D=16, rho_c=22, rho_h=12. Ring 57T m1.25. Wheel 24T, r_p 15, OD 32.5, face width 9. Hub peg 5.6 dia; groove 6.5 wide x 1.6 deep along the ~130 mm centre path. Rider disc 22 dia x 3.2 (19 mm visible face); pin 4 dia in a 4.8 hole. Moving mass ~10 g. Frame wall >=3.5. Front lips 1.6 thick.
concepts.clearances_mm: Gear mesh: 0.15 per flank thinning (~0.3 backlash) plus 0.4 tip-root; centre path offset +0.1. Hub peg to groove 0.45 per side. Z gaps 0.4 (wheel to rails, peg to groove floor, both lips). Rider pin 0.4 radial; rider rim to wheel recess 0.6. Lip overlaps 1.5-2.0 in XY.
concepts.child_safety: The wheel (OD 32.5 mm) cannot fit the 31.7 mm small-parts cylinder even if released, and it is captive anyway (groove plus lips). The 22 mm rider is double-captive: wheel lip plus pinned. It is fully recessed and not graspable, but we flag it as the one sub-cylinder part. The gear-mesh nip is covered by the front lip. The open track window shows only a gravity-driven 10 g wheel (pinch force ~0.1 N). Other gaps are <=0.6 mm. No protrusions or thin features (thinnest structural element is a 1.6 mm lip backed by a 3.5 mm wall). Rounded R>=1.5 everywhere. Drop and squeeze robust. Note: 3D-printed toys are uncertified; age 6+.
risks: The wheel's bottom is printed over the floor with a 0.4 mm gap and may tack. Mitigations: rails, 2-layer gap, and a 'shake to free' break-in.
Real rolling resistance (tooth rattle, Z rub) may exceed the modelled 0.03-0.08 and delay spills. Keep margin; optionally D=18 (frame 84 mm) for an ~15 mm drop.
Fast swirl causes runaway looping. Intended as a feature, but it could make slow indexing feel less crisp for some children.
If pin friction is high or the rider's COM offset is too low, the rider gets dragged around. Ensure e >=3 mm; a conical pivot is the fallback.
Non-circular internal mesh at pocket/hump curvature transitions needs a 2D sweep check; may need rho_c=23.
It only works held vertically; flat on a table it does nothing. The landing thunk in PLA is gentle, not loud.
The 22 mm rider is a small part if both of its captures fail.
concepts.modeling_plan: Python. A track-synthesis module (shapely for the 2D design and optimisation loop) outputs a high-resolution pitch polyline. manifold3d CrossSection then builds: frame ring = skin outline minus (pitch region minus tooth spaces from virtual hobbing of the 24T wheel rolled along s), plus floor, groove (centre path buffered) and front lip; wheel = involute 24T spur, recess, lip, hub peg and pin; rider = disc with relief face and ear cut-outs. Skins are outline functions (flower, cloud, station) in build123d with fillets, converted to meshes and combined in manifold3d. One params dict (m, r_p, D, rho_c, rho_h, clearances, Z stack). Export the print-pose 3MF/STL with the wheel in the bottom pocket.
concepts.verification_plan: (a) Behaviour: quasi-static saddle-node analysis and 1-DOF dynamics over c_rr 0.03-0.10 and frame speeds 60-400 deg/s. Report spill angle, run, drop, impact energy and runaway threshold, with plots of the y(s,alpha) potential landscapes. (b) Kinematic sweep: wheel posed at 1440 positions along s with rotation s/r_p, rider at its gravity-down angle for each frame angle. manifold3d intersection with the frame = 0. Min clearance >=0.3 except the designed mesh. Per-pose 2D tooth overlap = 0 and backlash 0.2-0.4. (c) Hub peg to groove-wall clearance in every pose under +/-0.2 mm mesh slop. (d) Printability on the print-pose mesh: overhang map (down-facing >45 deg only on the bed or over a <=0.4 mm gap), bridge length, ray-cast wall thickness >=1.2, separate shells with >=0.35 gaps. (e) Small-parts cylinder test computed per part. (f) Headless OpenSCAD renders plus a matplotlib GIF of one full frame turn showing dwell, zoom and landing with the rider upright.

concepts.name: Purr-Bobble Kitty: a hand-powered, spring-free foliot escapement
concepts.tagline: Turn Kitty's yarn ball and her head shivers with giggles while she purrs. Inside is a 13th-century clock escapement with no springs, re-computed so a child's push can never jam it, and printed in one piece.
concepts.character: A kawaii kitty sits with a big yarn ball in her lap. The fixed frame is her body: round tummy, paws wrapped around the ball, tail curled around the base. Her HEAD is the escapement's foliot. It has huge round eyes, blush cheeks, a small 'w' mouth and two chunky rounded ears, and it pivots at the neck between the shoulders, shaking ±10° in a happy giggle-shiver. Gentle turning sounds like a purr: 30–60 clicks/s, close to a real cat's 25–50 Hz purr. Harder pushing rises to a buzz of about 175 clicks/s. Skins share the same core (ball/escape wheel, pallet pins, hub, bearings) and change only the frame outline and head shape. Each head's inertia is retuned so all skins feel the same. (1) Kitty with a yarn ball. (2) Bumble the bee: the ball is a flower, the head carries antennae and two round wings, and a hard push lands in the real bumblebee buzz band. (3) Pip the robot: the ball is a gear, the head has an antenna, and it makes a beep-boop rattle. Option: a floppy-eared puppy with a tennis ball, whose heavier ears give a slower, bigger wobble.
concepts.mechanism_summary: A planar, spring-free runaway (pin-pallet) escapement driven by the child. A crank knob on the yarn ball (optionally also a thumb-rolled rim) turns an 8-tooth symmetric star wheel. Its teeth alternately kick two pallet pins on the underside of the character's head. The head has inertia and no restoring spring, so it acts like the foliot of the earliest mechanical clocks: one tooth flank flings it, the next tooth on the other side catches it, reverses it and kicks it back. That makes one head oscillation per tooth. There is no hairspring and no mainspring: the thumb is the power source and the head's inertia is the regulator. The escapement also works as a speed governor, so the ball can never free-spin. It feels like turning through honey with a purring vibration, and it works identically in both directions.
concepts.mechanism_detail: BODIES and degrees of freedom: 3 print-in-place bodies. FRAME is the body. WHEEL (the yarn ball) rotates about Z, 1 DOF (φ). HEAD/FOLIOT rocks about a parallel Z axis 24.7 mm above the wheel centre, 1 DOF (ψ), with ±12.4° banking on the frame shoulders. The two are coupled only through intermittent pin-tooth contact. ESCAPE WHEEL: N=8 symmetric teeth, tip R 14.30, root R 8.90 (5.40 tall), tip land ≈1.0 mm, root land ≈0.9 mm, 0.7 mm fillets, tooth layer z 0–5. HEAD: two Ø4.29 pallet pins on an inverted-Y under-arm, at wheel coordinates (±12.98, 8.67). They sit 2.5 tooth pitches apart (112.5°) and 20.6 mm from the head pivot. The pivot is pulled 12% inside the tangent-intersection point, which adds a recoil component so the head is always driven and never locked. PHYSICS: the beat rate follows f ∝ √(T/I), set by thumb torque T and head inertia I, not by any spring. Simulated with a 2-DOF penalty-contact model, Coulomb μ 0.35, I_head 4e-6 kg·m² and wheel+thumb 4e-6 kg·m²: T=1 N·mm → 6 Hz head shake, 19.7° p-p, wheel 0.77 rev/s, 30 impacts/s. T=5 → 18 Hz, 20°, 1.6 rev/s, 60/s. T=10 → 26 Hz, 20°, 2.3 rev/s, 88/s. T=40 → 51 Hz, 22°, 5 rev/s, 175/s. Results are identical in reverse. Wheel speed scales ≈√T, which feels like a quadratic, honey-like damper with superimposed vibration. Peak pin-tooth forces are 5–36 N, i.e. Hertz line-contact pressure ≈20–45 MPa on 5 mm-long pins and ≈2.5 MPa interlayer shear in the pins. Ear tips at about 30 mm from the pivot travel ±5 mm. The head's kinetic energy is under 1 mJ. Very slow, displacement-driven turning (below about 0.3 rev/s) gives soft individual ticks with small nods, because the static forced swing is only 4.2° p-p. Above that, the head flies between the pins at the full ±10°. Gravity torque on the head (centre of mass about 9 mm above the pivot) is under 0.2 N·mm, negligible against 1–40 N·mm. Shaking the toy just jiggles the head like a bobblehead. DRIVE: a Ø10×6 crank knob at r 11 on the ball face, music-box style, which loads the wheel tangentially instead of pressing it into its bearing. Optionally a 60° frame window exposes the knurled rim for thumb-rolling. BEARINGS: the wheel's top is an 'umbrella'. Its 45° conical underside starts just outside the tooth tips (r 14.8, z 5.5) and flares to an R 21 V-ridge rim that runs in a frame V-groove wrapping about 240° (bottom and sides). This roofs over the pins, so the escapement is hidden and needs no supports. The head pivots on a Ø14 V-ridged hub cupped by two ≈100° frame 'shoulder' arcs. The neck (≥7.5 wide) rises through the gap between them, and the shoulders double as the ±12.4° banking stops.
concepts.computational_design_element: The whole escapement is synthesized by computation, not copied from a textbook anchor. (1) Parameterization: tooth count N, tip radius, tooth height, tip and root land fractions, pin radius, pin radial offset, pin span ((m+½) pitches), pivot tilt and banking angle. (2) Static screen: a signed-distance field of the wheel built with shapely and numpy. A configuration-space sweep (φ over 2 pitches × ψ over ±banking) runs for both pins, and a 'lazy' head is pushed through the free channel in BOTH rotation directions. A design is rejected if the channel has any dead end (a jam), if the print-pose clearance is under 0.5 mm, or if any contact pressure angle exceeds 90° − atan(μ) − 8° = 62.7°, the friction-lock margin. (3) A random search over 1,000+ samples gave about 40 statically feasible designs. (4) Dynamic check: a wheel+head penalty-contact simulation with Coulomb friction and banking, for T = 1–40 N·mm, both directions. (5) Tolerance-in-the-loop: the first dynamic optimum jammed if the pins printed 0.2 mm fat or the pivot shifted 0.4 mm (bearing play). Each design's working window of pin depth was therefore measured (≥2.2 mm wide), the design was re-centred in that window and scaled 0.8× to fit an 85 mm toy, then re-verified on all 8 corners of {pivot ±0.4} × {pin Ø ±0.2}, in both directions, at 3 and 20 N·mm. All corners run. It also runs for μ 0.2–0.6 (swing 11–24°) and head inertia 2e-6 to 1.6e-5 kg·m². (6) Per-skin tuning: each head's inertia is taken from its mesh (trimesh mass properties) and trimmed with internal pockets to hit the same f(T) curve. The head's lower outline is computed as the swept envelope of the umbrella rim over ψ=±12.4° plus 0.6 mm. The honest story: 'this tooth-and-pallet shape was computed so that a hand-pushed wheel can never jam the head, whichever way and however hard a child pushes, even if the printer is 0.2 mm off.' The working prototype scripts are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Apps/023789a6-f9f1-563f-a565-9790ebbd0388/scratchpad/ideation/haptic/: esc_opt.py (static screen), esc_dyn2.py (dynamics), esc_window.py (tolerance centring), esc_final_check.py (final checks). The final parameters are {N:8, Rt:14.2992, tooth_h:5.3968, tip_frac:0.0765, root_frac:0.1333, rp:2.1448, drho:1.8686, m:2, tilt:0.8792, psi_b:12.42}.
concepts.fidget_loop: Circle the crank knob with a fingertip, or roll the ball's rim with a thumb. The ball refuses to spin freely: it moves through 'honey' and purrs in your fingertip. Kitty's head shivers ±10° and her ears flick. A gentle push gives a soft purr of 30–60 clicks/s and a visible giggle-shake at 6–15 Hz. Push harder and the purr rises smoothly to a buzz of about 175 clicks/s as her head blurs. Let go and she stops instantly, because nothing coasts. Turning backwards works the same. Turning very slowly gives tick… tick… with tiny nods. Shaking the toy makes her bobble. Every skin feels the same but has its own 'voice', set by its different head inertia.
concepts.closest_prior_art: Swiss Escapement Desktop Fidget, Printables 710195: wind-up, needs 4 steel nails, a desk object that ticks for about 90 s. Watch-escapement desk toy, Printables 56648. 'Code-checked' Graham escapement clock, Printables 1862746 (pendulum). Assembled verge-and-foliot clock models. Pin-pallet runaway escapements inside kitchen timers and fuzes: metal, spring-driven, hidden. The Kit-Cat Klock, whose eyes and tail are motor-driven. Spring bobbleheads, e.g. Bobble Bot, Printables 1188378 (3 parts plus a spring). Character-motion fidgets: MakerWorld Waving Cat 2856164 (gear-driven arms) and Click-Wink Bunny, Printables 1393629 (lever-cam wink).
concepts.novelty_argument: The prior-art map lists no hand-held print-in-place escapement. Every escapement toy found is wind-up or weight-driven, assembled, and uses metal. The enabling insight is to go back before the balance spring, to the foliot. An inertia-only regulator needs no hairspring and no mainspring, which are exactly the parts FDM PLA cannot make reliably (creep, fatigue). The child's thumb becomes the mainspring and the character's head becomes the foliot, so the expression literally IS the regulator. The 'governor feel' is also new in fidgets: speed-limited, purring resistance that works in both directions. The geometry is not a textbook anchor, which would be one-directional and jam in reverse. It is a symmetric, bidirectional pin-pallet geometry found by computation, centred in its tolerance window and verified by contact dynamics. It also reuses none of TonyHanma's mechanisms: his Graham clock is a pendulum clock, not a hand-driven foliot.
concepts.print_strategy: One print, flat on its back, in PLA. PETG also works: friction up to μ 0.6 was simulated. 0.2 mm layers, no supports. All rotation axes are along Z, so every working clearance lies in XY. Layer stack: z 0–5 holds the escape teeth, pallet pins and the head's under-arm, all on the bed. The wheel umbrella's 45° underside rises from r 14.8 at z 5.5. The V-ridge rims of the wheel and the head hub run in 45° V-grooves, and the frame's upper lips overhang at 45°. The top surface is at z 14, and the crank knob goes to z 20. The only bridges are the umbrella between tooth flanks (≤5 mm). Wherever the head's under-arm passes under the umbrella, its top is clipped to the cone with a ≥0.5 mm gap (computed). The print pose is the computed maximum-clearance pose: 1.41 mm minimum pin-to-tooth clearance. Elephant foot: 0.6 mm × 45° chamfers on every moving part's bottom edge, plus 0.15 mm slicer compensation. Seams go at the frame rear, away from the bearings, with Z-hop on. Cool before removal, then break in with 5–10 turns each way. Edge fillets (≥1 mm) are applied on the B-rep before export. The face is a 0.6 mm emboss/deboss on the top surface, with an optional colour change at z 13.
concepts.key_dimensions_mm: Overall ≈62 W × 86 H × 14 T (20 at the crank knob). Escape wheel: 8 teeth, tip R 14.30, root R 8.90, teeth z 0–5; umbrella rim R 21 with 1.5 mm V-ridge; crank knob Ø10 × 6 at r 11. Head pivot 24.7 above the wheel centre. Pallet pins Ø4.29 × 5 at (±12.98, 8.67) from the wheel centre, 20.6 from the pivot, spanning 112.5° of the wheel. Banking ±12.4°. Head hub Ø14 with V-ridge. Neck ≥7.5 wide × 14 thick. Head ≈Ø34 plus ears; ears/antennae ≥8 wide at the root and ≥10 thick in Z. Head mass ≈8–12 g, I ≈ 4–8×10⁻⁶ kg·m². Total mass ≈25–30 g.
concepts.clearances_mm: V-ridge bearings (wheel rim and head hub): 0.45 normal gap. Escapement pin-to-tooth at the print pose: ≥1.41 (computed); the design tolerates pin Ø ±0.2 and pivot offset ±0.4. Z gap from the pins and under-arm (top z 5.0) to the umbrella underside: ≥0.5. Head lower edge to umbrella rim: swept-envelope gap 0.5–1.2. Head to shoulder arcs: concentric 0.5. Ear and wing tips to any frame edge: ≥3 (free air). Bottom-edge chamfers: 0.6.
concepts.child_safety: All three bodies are geometrically captive (V-ridge in V-groove, >180° wrap), and each is far larger than the small-parts cylinder: ball Ø42+, head ≈34×40, frame. There are no flexures, so nothing can fatigue and snap off. The pallet pins (Ø4.3) are internal, roofed by the umbrella, and loaded at only ≈2.5 MPa interlayer shear at peak. The only power source is the thumb, and the escapement limits it: head kinetic energy is under 1 mJ, and any pinch force at an ear tip is under 1 N. Every reachable relative-motion gap is a constant-width shear gap of 0.45–0.6 mm (<2 mm), and the escapement nip is hidden. All edges are filleted ≥1 mm. Ears, wings and antennae are chunky; as cantilevers loaded with 30 N they see ≈6 MPa in-plane and ≈4 MPa across layers. The crank knob is solid with a 2 mm root fillet. Note the buzz at hard push can be loud. Marked 6+; 3D-printed toys are not standards-certified.
risks: The simulation is a 2-D rigid model with penalty contact. Real PLA impact damping and stick-slip in the V-bearings could reduce the swing at slow speeds. Print a 25-minute escapement-only coupon first and film the swing.
Friction in the R 21 rim bearing adds drag (≈5–20 N·mm if the knob is pushed down hard). This eats into the 1–40 N·mm drive band; the knob placement favours tangential pull.
Wear: at 40 N·mm the peak pin contact (≈45 MPa) nears PLA yield, so hours of hard buzzing may flatten flanks. Typical child torques of 2–15 N·mm give 20–33 MPa. PETG or tough PLA helps.
Noise: 150+ impacts/s at hard push is a loud rattle-buzz. The kitty skin is tuned for the low-torque purr; softer banking pads could be added.
The visible 'giggle' (6–15 Hz) only happens at gentle pushes. Above ≈20 Hz the head is a blur, and below ≈0.3 rev/s the swing is small (4° static).
First-layer fusing under the pins, because the teeth and pins are both on the bed: needs good elephant-foot control.
The roofed topology (umbrella, two shoulder arcs, neck through the gap) needs careful CAD. The shoulder arcs are limited to about 100° each, so hub captivity relies on the V-ridge.
concepts.modeling_plan: A Python pipeline driven by one JSON of parameters. (1) Escapement 2-D profiles from the optimizer (shapely): star wheel, pin circles, and ψ-swept envelopes with offsets for the head outline and the frame cut-outs. (2) build123d: extrude the profiles into z-bands; revolve the 45° umbrella cone and the V-ridges/V-grooves; fillet (1 mm) and chamfer (0.6 mm bottom); add the crank knob; clip the under-arm to the cone. (3) Skins: 2-D character sketches (filleted unions of circles and ellipses) for the frame outline, head, ears and paws, plus a 0.6 mm face emboss. Each head is unioned onto the fixed core (hub, under-arm, pins) and its inertia trimmed with internal pockets. (4) Export STEP plus one multi-body STL/3MF. manifold3d handles fast boolean assembly and the clearance sweeps, and an optional OpenSCAD wrapper imports the STLs for headless renders.
concepts.verification_plan: (a) Configuration-space sweep on the real meshes: manifold3d poses the wheel at 720 φ steps × 100 ψ steps and checks zero intersection volume along the lazy-head channel in both directions. trimesh measures minimum distances at the print pose (≥1.4 pin-to-tooth, ≥0.45 bearings). (b) Pressure-angle audit along the contact path (<62.7°). (c) Re-run the contact-dynamics sim (esc_dyn2.py / esc_window.py) on the as-modelled profiles: T 1–40 N·mm, both directions, 8 tolerance corners, μ 0.2–0.6, and per-skin inertia from trimesh. Pass if it never jams, the swing is ≥12° p-p and there are few banking hits. (d) Swept-envelope gap checks: head vs umbrella, head vs shoulders, ears vs frame. (e) Overhang analysis: down-facing triangles steeper than 45° allowed only on bridges ≤5 mm. (f) Wall-thickness sampling (≥1.2 mm; pins ≥4 mm; neck ≥7.5 mm) and cantilever stress estimates for the ears and knob. (g) Small-parts check: no body or breakable feature fits the 31.7 mm cylinder. (h) Renders, via headless OpenSCAD on the STLs or matplotlib, plus an animated GIF of the simulated head swing. (i) Physical: print the escapement core coupon (wheel, pins, hub) before the full skin.

concepts.name: Drumroll Bunny: the endless-accelerando drum
concepts.tagline: Crank the drum at a steady pace and Bunny's drumroll seems to speed up forever. The tooth spacing and heights were computed to produce a Risset rhythm, an auditory illusion, that you hear and feel in your fingertips.
concepts.character: A kawaii bunny with big eyes, a pink nose and tall rounded ears sits with a round drum in its lap. The drum face is the top of the rotating drum, with a drum-skin texture, lug bumps and a Ø10 crank knob. Its two paws hold chunky mallets. The paws are the outer ends of two computed drumstick levers. They jump 0–4.7 mm on every beat: big alternating left-right strokes on the main beats and tiny twitches on the ghost notes, while the drumroll keeps accelerating. Skins share the same drum and lever core: (1) Drummer Bunny. (2) Two woodpeckers pecking a log disc in turn. (3) A tap-dancing hamster whose feet tap on its wheel.
concepts.mechanism_summary: One rotating drum carries two ratchet tracks stacked in Z. Their tooth angles follow a logarithmic time-warp and their drop heights follow a cross-fading loudness envelope. Two drumstick levers ride the tracks. Each lever is hinged to the body by a low-strain flexure leaf and also has a fail-safe captive hub. Each sawtooth lifts a stick, then drops it off a near-radial face so it snaps back and strikes the drum root: a real tap you hear and feel through the crank. Turned steadily, the 16 beats per revolution form a Risset rhythm. The main pulse accelerates continuously, new off-beats fade in and old ones fade out, and after one revolution the pattern hands over seamlessly to itself. The drumroll therefore seems to speed up forever. The drum is one-way, like a ratchet.
concepts.mechanism_detail: BODIES: 2 print-in-place bodies. FRAME+LEVERS is one body, with the levers joined by flexure leaves. DRUM has 1 DOF about Z; each lever has 1 compliant DOF. BEAT SCHEDULE (Risset, n=4, L=3 layers): θ_k = 360°·log2(1+k/16) for k=0…15, giving 0, 31.5, 61.2, 89.3, 115.9, 141.2, 165.4, 188.5, 210.6, 231.8, 252.2, 271.8, 290.6, 308.9, 326.5 and 343.5°. The intervals shrink smoothly from 31.5° to 16.5°, exactly a 2× tempo rise per revolution. Layer-sum loudness with sin² envelopes is 1.50, .67, 1.47, .50, 1.50, .35, 1.29, .23, 1.50, .13, 1.05, .06, 1.50, .02, .84, 0. LEVER PHYSICS: the flexure leaf is 1.2 × 6 × 22 mm (k_rot 137 N·mm/rad). The stick nose is 9 mm from the hinge and the paw is 30 mm from it. The nose rests at its unloaded neutral, c = 0.40 mm above the track root; this is also the print gap. A tooth of crest height h above the root lifts the nose by (h − c) and then releases it off a near-radial drop face. The lever snaps back at f_n ≈ 100 Hz, overshoots neutral and strikes the root at v = ω·√((h−c)² − c²). Inverting this law for the envelope gives crest heights of 1.80, 1.12, 1.77, 1.00, 1.80, 0.91, 1.62, 0.85, 1.80, 0.82, 1.42, –, 1.80, –, 1.25 and – mm. The three faded beats get no tooth. Tap speeds therefore range from 0.86 m/s down to 0.08 m/s, a range of 0 to −21 dB, plus silent beats. TWO VOICES: beats with k mod 4 ∈ {0,1} go to the left paw (track z 0–4.5, 7 teeth) and {2,3} to the right paw (track z 4.9–9.9, 6 teeth), so the main beats alternate L-R-L-R. The minimum same-track pitch is 21.2° (a 7.0 mm arc at R 19). Lever rotation is ≤8.9° and leaf strain ≤0.42%. The strain is one-directional (R≈0), so σ_a ≈ σ_m ≈ 7.4 MPa and the Goodman ratio is ≈0.64, which is high-cycle safe. The paw stroke is ≤4.7 mm. TURNING EFFORT: peak 26 N·mm, mean 5.4 N·mm, 12.3 mJ per revolution, which feels like a light music-box crank. FREE FALL: at 1 rev/s the drum surface moves at ≈120 mm/s, and the stick's snap-back quarter-period is ≈2.5 ms. Drop faces are therefore ≥80° (near-radial), so the stick falls clear and the tap sound does not depend on crank speed. REVERSE: the sticks are trailing pawls, so turning backwards meets a gentle ratchet stop. The stop load at the nose is ≈1.6 N, against ≈15 N Euler buckling of the leaf, and the captive hub also takes the load. BEARINGS: the top of the drum is a 45° umbrella covering the stick noses, with a V-ridge rim (R ≈23.5) running in a 240° frame V-groove. Cranking is tangential and drives a light, level load, which keeps the crank rate steady.
concepts.computational_design_element: (1) Risset synthesis. A nested multi-layer beat grid is folded into one revolution with a log2 time-warp. Every layer's tempo doubles exactly per revolution, so at the 360° seam layer j maps onto layer j+1. Loudness is computed per beat from cross-fading envelopes, and the seam is continuous to within ≈2%. (2) Inverse acoustic model. Each crest height is solved from the stick's snap-and-overshoot law, v = ω√((h−c)²−c²). The inputs are the flexure stiffness (beam theory) and the lever inertia. A 1-DOF contact simulation with PLA damping later refines the heights so each tap's speed matches the target envelope. (3) Two-voice assignment. A small combinatorial search splits the beats between the left and right sticks. It maximizes L/R alternation of the strong beats, subject to a same-track spacing of ≥7 mm and no more than 4 consecutive beats on one hand. (4) Ramp synthesis. Each ramp is a variable-pitch spiral segment shaped for level torque within its inter-beat window, with the pressure angle capped below 35° before friction. Each drop face is checked against the stick's free-return arc so the stick never brushes it. (5) A WAV preview of the computed click train lets you hear the illusion before printing. It is already generated at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Apps/023789a6-f9f1-563f-a565-9790ebbd0388/scratchpad/ideation/haptic/risset_drum_preview.wav by risset2.py. The honest story: 'the spacing of these teeth was computed from a logarithm, and their heights from the physics of the drumstick, so that a steady crank makes a drumroll that seems to accelerate forever.'
concepts.fidget_loop: Circle the crank knob with a finger or thumb, like a music box. Each tap comes through the drum as a small notch, and the paws visibly hammer, alternating left and right. Within one revolution the beat audibly speeds up. Ghost notes creep in between and grow while others fade. On the next turn it is still speeding up, and the next, forever: an endless drumroll. Turn slowly and you can count individual taps and watch them grow and shrink. Turn faster and the whole illusion runs faster. The crank's light, level torque (mean ≈5 N·mm) makes a steady pace come naturally. The result is a calming, repeatable loop with a 'how is it STILL getting faster?!' payoff.
concepts.closest_prior_art: Uniform-tooth ratchets and clickers: Clicking wheel (Printables 231691), clicking ratchet fidget ring (Printables 859158), MakerWorld Clicky Ratchet with two flexure pawls (3015240). Noisemaker/gragger (Printables 491686). Parametric 3D-printed music boxes, such as wizard23's Thingiverse generator, which computes pin positions and tine lengths: assembled, plucked-comb melodies. The 'physics-checked' stick-slip pecking woodpecker (Printables 1862612). Battery-powered drumming-bunny toys. Risset rhythms and Shepard–Risset illusions, which exist only in audio and music software.
concepts.novelty_argument: No fidget or printable toy found encodes an auditory illusion. Ratchets have uniform teeth, and music boxes play a fixed melody on plucked tines. Here the irregular tooth pattern is the product itself: computed from a log-time warp and an inverse physical loudness model so that a purely mechanical part produces endless acceleration. The claim 'computed to make X happen' is concrete and testable: preview the audio, then measure the print. Mechanically, it adds two-voice tracks stacked in Z and flexure-hinged drumstick levers whose overshoot-strike law serves as the loudness actuator. The character's motion IS the rhythm: paws alternate on the main beats and twitch on the ghost notes. It is distinct from the TonyHanma woodpecker, which is gravity stick-slip and not cam-scheduled.
concepts.print_strategy: One print, flat on its back, in PLA (crisper taps than PETG). 0.2 mm layers, no supports. The left track occupies z 0–4.5 and the right track z 4.9–9.9. Right-track teeth and the right stick's nose get 45° under-chamfers, since their overhang is ≤2.2 mm. There is a 0.4 mm Z gap between the track and nose layers. The 45° umbrella underside starts at the crest radius at z 10.4, the V-ridge rim sits at R ≈23.5, and the top surface is at z 15, with the crank knob to z 21. Flexure leaves are printed in-plane as exactly 3 perimeters (1.2 mm) with no infill, so the extrusion lines run along the leaf. In the print pose both noses are parked over a root dwell, 0.4 mm above the root and ≥0.6 mm from any tooth face. Use 0.6 mm bottom chamfers on the drum and levers, 0.15 mm elephant-foot compensation, seams at the frame rear, and Z-hop. Let it cool before removal, then break in with 3 slow turns.
concepts.key_dimensions_mm: Overall ≈64 W × 84 H × 15 T (21 at the knob). Drum: track root R 19.0, crest R up to 20.8; left track z 0–4.5, right track z 4.9–9.9; umbrella rim R ≈23.5; crank knob Ø10 × 6 at r 13. Teeth: crests 0.82–1.80 above the root, drop face ≥80°, ramps ≤28°, minimum same-track pitch 7.0 mm of arc. Levers: flexure leaf 1.2 × 6 × 22; nose 9 from the hinge; paw and mallet at 30; maximum nose lift 1.4 beyond neutral; paw stroke ≤4.7; fail-safe captive hub Ø7. Mallets and paws ≥6 thick; ears ≥9 wide.
concepts.clearances_mm: Drum V-bearing: 0.45 normal gap. Stick nose to root at print: 0.40. This is also the design's neutral offset c, so it enters the loudness law. Nose to tooth faces at the print pose: ≥0.6. Lever-to-frame slots: 0.6 constant shear gap. Fail-safe hub: 0.6 radial, never touching in normal use. Z gaps: 0.4 between track and nose layers, 0.5 under the umbrella. Bottom chamfers: 0.6.
concepts.child_safety: 2 bodies, both much larger than the small-parts cylinder. Each stick lever is attached by its flexure AND captured by a V-ridged hub, so even a fatigue crack cannot release it. Leaf strain is low anyway (0.42%, one direction). Teeth and noses are hidden under the drum umbrella, and the only exposed gaps are 0.45–0.6 mm shear gaps. The only power is a finger on a crank, and turning backwards meets a soft, low-load ratchet stop. Mallets and paws are thick (≥6 mm), rounded, and their travel is bounded by the frame. Single taps are moderate (≤0.9 m/s stick speed). Edges have ≥1 mm fillets. Marked 6+; not standards-certified.
risks: The strength of the illusion is perceptual. It needs a steady crank, and PLA taps give only ≈20 dB of dynamic range, so it may be weaker than in audio software. Check with the WAV preview and adjust the envelope exponent and layer count before printing.
If the drum stops with a stick resting on a crest, the leaf holds 0.42% strain and creeps, shifting the neutral by ≈0.1 mm over days. Mitigation: short crests and wide root 'parking' dwells.
The right track and nose are stacked in Z with a 45° under-chamfer, which leaves only ≈3 mm of contact height and makes them sensitive to Z-seam blobs.
It is one-way: children may try to force it backwards. The stop load is computed to be safe, but repeated forcing could mark the drop faces.
Tap loudness depends on clean, near-radial drop faces. Stringing or bulging could make the sticks brush the face and dull the taps.
PETG's higher damping and lower stiffness would make the taps quieter. PLA is preferred.
Flexure fatigue over 10^5–10^6 taps is predicted to be safe at this strain, but it is not yet tested.
concepts.modeling_plan: Python. risset2.py produces the tooth table. numpy then builds polar profiles for each track (dwell, spiral ramp, crest, near-radial drop) with tooth-face fillets, unioned with the drum core in shapely. build123d extrudes the two track bands, revolves the umbrella and V-ridge, applies the under-chamfers on the right-track teeth and nose, adds the fillets and the crank knob. Frame and levers come from 2-D sketches, with each flexure leaf an exact 1.2 mm strip; slot offsets and the hub V-ridge pockets are cut from these. The bunny outline, ears, paws, mallets and a 0.6 mm face emboss are added on top. One parameter JSON drives everything. Export STEP and STL/3MF, with manifold3d for the booleans and sweeps.
concepts.verification_plan: (a) Kinematic sweep: step the drum φ in 0.1° increments. Compute each stick's forced lift and contact point from the actual meshed profile (configuration-space contact), and check that the pressure angle stays below 35° before friction. (b) Free-return check: simulate each lever's snap (1-DOF with contact and damping) at 0.3, 0.6 and 1.2 rev/s. Confirm the nose strikes the root, not the drop face, and record impact speed per tooth to confirm the loudness table. (c) Leaf strain and buckling via an elastica solve with scipy. (d) Render a WAV from the simulated impacts, plus a spectrogram and onset-strength plot showing continuous acceleration and a seamless 360° wrap; let a human listen. (e) Mesh checks: zero intersection at the print pose (manifold3d), minimum clearances (trimesh), overhang analysis (down-facing normals steeper than 45° only on ≤2.2 mm chamfered overhangs), wall thickness, and small-parts fit. (f) Renders. (g) Physical: print a 2-tooth coupon with one lever to calibrate c and loudness before the full toy.

fixable_issues: The R21 wheel rim bearing is not in the dynamics model. During each impact, V-groove friction is about sqrt2*mu*Fn*21 mm, roughly 10 mm of effective moment arm. That is comparable to the 7-10 mm arm of the tooth contact itself, so close to half of each wheel impulse could go into the bearing. Expect more drive torque for the same beat rate and faster bearing wear. Add an Fn-proportional bearing friction term to esc_dyn2 before trusting the f(T) table.

Topology conflict. The head hub (pivot 24.7 mm above wheel centre, R7 plus ridge, so its bottom sits about 16.5 mm from wheel centre) overlaps the umbrella/rim zone (R14.8 to 22.5) in XY. It can only fit as a short hub of about 7 mm or less under the 45° cone (cone z = 5.5 + (r - 14.8)), with the shoulders also under the cone. This is solvable, but the CAD has to prove it.

Wear: Hertz pressure of 20-45 MPa at 30-175 impacts/s, plus sliding on the large-radius rim bearing. Once the 0.45 mm play wears past the verified ±0.4 mm pivot corner, the jam-free guarantee no longer covers it. Recommend PETG or tough PLA and a wear coupon.
The 175 Hz buzz at hard push is loud. The visible 'giggle' only happens in a narrow torque band.
Teeth and pins both start on the bed. Elephant-foot control matters, but the 1.41 mm print-pose clearance is generous.
best_ideas_to_keep: Every moving body is printed ON THE BED with XY-only gaps. The only print-over features are a self-supporting 45° umbrella cone and V-ridges, so there are no large-area Z-gap sandwiches anywhere.
No flexures and no springs: the foliot uses the head's inertia as the regulator, so there is nothing to creep or fatigue.

Tolerance-in-the-loop design: the geometry is re-centred in its working window and verified on 8 corners (pin Ø ±0.2, pivot ±0.4), both directions, μ 0.2-0.6 and an 8x inertia range. This is the best robustness engineering of the ten concepts.
Configuration-space jam screen plus a penalty-contact dynamics sim already exist and can be re-run on the as-modelled profiles.
scores.comment: The most printable rigid mechanism in the set. Its topology looks like a gear bearing: parts sit side by side on the bed with V-ridge capture. The physics is real (inertia-regulated runaway pin-pallet escapements are what kitchen timers use), and the claims rest on a dynamics sim with tolerance corners rather than hand-waving. Two things are missing: Fn-proportional friction in the large rim bearing, which I estimate is comparable to the contact moment arm, and a demonstrated layout for the hub under the umbrella. Neither changes the concept.

fixable_issues: Frame compliance at the arch roots changes the ordering, not just the scale, and the concept does not account for it. I re-ran the team's corobeam with an axial spring at the ends (judge-engineering/c1_frame.py). With the frame at 1000 N/mm, snap forces fall to 1.87/2.49/3.22 N and pull-back forces to -0.55/-0.64/-0.63 N, so cells 2 and 3 tie and the wake-up order is lost. At 500 N/mm the bz=9.8 cell is no longer bistable (Fmin +0.07 N). Deeper cells suffer more because arch axial stiffness scales with bz while frame stiffness does not. If the window frame is an open portal (stem slot through the chin bar, 4 mm side walls), I estimate about 600 N/mm. The frame needs to be a closed ring of at least ~4000 N/mm, for example a bridge over the stem at z > bz plus wider walls, checked by FE.

Creep: the asleep state holds 0.66% strain (about 20 MPa in PLA). Children will leave it squished, and a hot car makes it worse. Stress relaxation shifts the stress-free shape toward the asleep state and erodes the pull-back margin. Specify PETG, not just recommend it.
Fatigue at a 1.0% peak (about 30 MPa, around 55% of printed-PLA UTS) suggests 10^3-10^4 snaps, not 10^4-10^5. Needs a cycling coupon.

Single 0.45 mm Arachne lines: ±0.03 mm line width gives about ±25-30% force, and the result depends on slicer settings. Q = h/t = 3.3 sits close to the bistability limit of about 2.3, so a fat line (0.55 mm) squeezes the margin.
Under off-axis squeezes the V-interlock skirts carry moments, and sliding friction adds to the 0.55-0.8 N pull thresholds.
A fractured arch could leave a small-parts sliver. Add the bridge straps as standard.
best_ideas_to_keep: A truly monolithic body: every gap is a vertical through-slot, with no large Z-gap surfaces over moving parts. This is the most reliable print-in-place geometry there is.
Programming snap order by Z-depth (layer count), so it is immune to common-mode flow error. This is a good manufacturing-aware idea, provided the frame stiffness is high.
Hard stops in both directions keep overload out of the beams.
A validated corotational FE (convergence plus a Qiu cross-check) is already in the repo, and it is easy to extend with root springs.
scores.comment: Printability is excellent and the FE groundwork is real. My frame-compliance check shows the central robustness claim only holds if each belly window is a closed, stiff ring. Otherwise the deepest cell loses bistability or ties in pull-back order. That is fixable in CAD. PLA creep in the held state is the long-term weakness.

fixable_issues: Strain: 1.1% on every press through the plateau and 1.22% at the stop (about 33-37 MPa in PLA, 60-70% of printed UTS) on 10 single-line flexures. Fatigue life is likely 10^3-10^4 presses in PLA, which is short for a squishy. Make PETG mandatory or reduce strain with longer leaves.

Plateau sensitivity: frame compliance tilts the plateau (my check, judge-engineering/c2_frame.py: ±1% clamped, ±6% at 1000 N/mm, ±13% at 500 N/mm). It stays monostable, so the failure is graceful. Make the ring stiff.

Off-centre thumb loads tilt TOP into the 0.45 mm shear faces. Coulomb friction then creates hysteresis on the order of 0.3-0.6 N against a 3.3 N plateau. The 'zero stiffness' feel will be partly friction-dominated, and the FE does not model it.
The interleaved cross-shaped TOP inside the ring BOTTOM is intricate. Making every TOP/BOTTOM boundary a constant-gap shear line or a computed aperture needs careful automated checking.
The same slicer dependence as C1 for 0.45 mm single lines. Force scatter is 2.3-4.6 N across prints.
best_ideas_to_keep: Stress-free at rest and monostable: no creep set, unlike any bistable concept.
Monolithic, with vertical-slot-only gaps.
Pairing negative and positive stiffness, all at one line width, so printer error mostly scales force rather than changing the curve's shape.
Hard stops in both directions.
scores.comment: Print-in-place reliability matches C1. It is better than C1 on creep (stress-free at rest), worse on fatigue (higher strain on every cycle), and its headline feel depends on friction that has not been modelled. If the plateau tilts, it degrades into a soft monostable button, which is still a working toy.

fixable_issues: The loudness envelope is encoded in sub-millimetre geometry and does not survive FDM tolerance. My Monte Carlo of v = ω√((h−c)²−c²) used σ_c = 0.05 (common) and σ_h = 0.04 (per tooth). The quiet beats (h = 0.82, 0.85, 0.91) come out silent in 43%, 32% and 15% of prints, and the 95th percentile is 3x louder than nominal. The timing is robust; the cross-fade, which carries the illusion, is not. Scale c and h up through a lever ratio (strain allows about 2x), or add a calibration.

The free-fall assumption ignores nose radius. A printed nose tip has a radius of 0.2-0.3 mm or more. It rides over the crest corner until the drum has moved about one nose radius. At 1 rev/s the drum moves only about 0.3 mm per 2.5 ms quarter-period. So the first part of each drop is drum-paced and the tap speed depends on crank speed, which contradicts the claim. The quiet beats will vanish at slow cranking. The 1-DOF contact sim must include the real nose geometry.
Lever leaf creep while parked on a crest shifts c, and c is the most sensitive parameter.
Right-track teeth and noses need 45° under-chamfers up to 2.2 mm high, which leaves about 3 mm of contact height on a 5 mm track. That is sensitive to seam blobs.
The one-way ratchet will be forced backwards. The captive hub takes the load, but repeated forcing will mark the drop faces.
best_ideas_to_keep: Same robust topology as C9: the drum is printed on the bed, captured by a 45° umbrella/V-rim, and the levers are monolithic with the frame. Only 2 bodies, with XY gaps.
Low flexure strain (0.42%, essentially one-directional) plus a fail-safe captive hub behind each flexure.
Angular tooth timing from the log2 warp is geometrically exact and robust.
A WAV preview generated from the computed click train.
scores.comment: As a two-voice ratchet clicker it will print and work. The computed element that makes it special, the loudness cross-fade, sits right at FDM tolerance and is further degraded by nose-corner contact. Expect a convincing accelerando-and-reset more often than a seamless Risset illusion unless the geometry is scaled up.

fixable_issues: Two large-area print-over-gap interfaces: the Ø40 head plate over the hood, and the collar over the runner. The rib spec is ambiguous: '0.4 mm gap … on 0.3 mm skate ribs' reads as 0.1 mm at the ribs, which will tack or fuse. Use C5's scheme: 0.4 mm at the ribs and 1.0 mm in the field.

The collar has to bridge the void the runner sweeps beside the cradle (±10 mm travel plus tilt), and pillars cannot go into the swept zone. Verify the claimed spans of 10 mm or less with the actual swept envelope.

Curvature mismatch at the centre contact is small (runner ρ 11.8 vs cradle ρ 14.5, about 19T vs 23T at m1.25, a 4-tooth difference). In conventional internal-gear terms that means interference. I checked the proposed swept-complement generation in a circular approximation (judge-engineering/c4_internal.py) and the cradle teeth survive with normal fill (about 0.44 at pitch, 0.25 near tip), so it is workable. Still, verify contact ratio ≥1.2 on the real non-circular geometry.
There is no restoring force (gravity centring about 0.05 N), so tack after printing shows directly as stiffness. Pin-slot plus mesh clearances give about 1° of tilt slop.
best_ideas_to_keep: Only 2 bodies, no flexures. A fixed pin from the back plate keeps the mesh engaged, with separation (0.35) well under tooth depth (2.5), so it cannot skip.
Gesture-to-centrode synthesis checks out: I re-ran centrode3.py and arc lengths match at 48.9/48.9 mm. The computed 3 mm dip is what removes the cusp, an honest computational result.
Cradle teeth generated as the swept complement of the head teeth are conjugate by construction.
scores.comment: The mechanism is sound and simple, and the tooth generation holds up despite the tight curvature ratio. Its print-in-place risk is the classic large flat sandwich of moving plate between two fixed plates, which is less reliable than bed-printed or vertical-slot topologies.

fixable_issues: The stated layer stack has zero Z gap between the two cam layers and the opposite followers (cam B and arm B at z 2.4-5.4, cam A and arm A at 5.4-8.4).
