I computed it from cam2.py (judge-engineering/c3_overhang.py): cam A overhangs cam B by up to 1.32 mm over 10.8 mm², directly above nose B's swept band, and nose A passes over 38 mm² of cam B. Both need a 0.4 mm gap plus 45° chamfers or a cantilever overhang, which cuts cam contact height from 3 mm to about 2.2-2.6 mm. Nobody addressed this.

The front shell prints over the rotor and rocker tops. '0.4 mm Z gap with 0.3 mm skate ribs' means 0.1 mm at the ribs, which effectively fuses. Fix by using 0.4 at the ribs and 1.0 in the field, or by putting the dial and rocker on the bed.
Desmodromic play of 0.3 per contact, times the 3.8:1 lever, gives ±1.1 mm of head rattle. Each direction reversal is also a free-flight impact.

The rotor post is cantilevered and loaded by cam contact forces of about 5.5 N. Tilt within 0.4 mm clearances changes the effective cam phase, and the dial chamfer under the shell has to carry the moment.
A peak pressure angle of 30° is acceptable for thumb drive, but friction from the rocker's large sandwich area probably dominates. That friction is not modelled.
best_ideas_to_keep: Spring-free conjugate (desmodromic) cams: no creep, no fatigue. Nose positions on the Thales circle of PO give radial follower motion. I verified that the opposing noses produce opposite torques.
Cam synthesis from storyboard keyframes with cycloidal blends and a scipy-optimised pivot to reduce peak pressure angle. The numbers reproduce.
The rocker's hidden edges are arcs concentric with its pivot, so the gap stays constant (pinch-safe).
scores.comment: The kinematic design is good and checked, but the physical layer stack as written does not work: the twin-layer cams interpenetrate the opposite follower bands with no Z gap, and the front shell sits about 0.1 mm over the moving tops. Both are fixable, but at the cost of contact height and more print-over-gap area.

fixable_issues: The chosen print pose (head at peak, crank 80°) leaves the lower head pocket empty under the front wall. The pocket is about 36 mm wide (head Ø36) by about 20 mm (y -36 to -15.6). Pillars cannot go into the head's swept zone, so the 1.8 mm front wall must bridge about 36 mm over a 3-layer-deep void, far beyond the ≤10 mm rule. Print in the hidden pose instead, so the wall lands on the head's skid ribs.

Ø4 vertical pins B and C are loaded laterally across layer lines whenever the protruding head (20 mm above the wall) is pushed. Example: 20 N at a pin over about 5.8 mm of lever is about 18 MPa, roughly the strength between PLA layers. Upsize to Ø6 or add shear collars.
Five layers with four print-over-gap interfaces, all large: wheel Ø42 over the back plate, rocker, coupler and head, front wall. Every one must free up.
0.4 mm of radial play at B and C, over a 30 mm lever, gives about ±1 mm and ±1.5° of head wobble.
The skid-rib scheme (0.4 at ribs, 1.0 field, 6 mm pitch) is correct; it just has to be applied consistently.
best_ideas_to_keep: Revolute-only Grashof crank-rocker. I reproduced the minimum transmission angle of 58.9°, s+l 48.2 < p+q 57.3, and the head path (rise 20.7, drift ±4.6). It is smooth and backdrivable, with no slides or cams to bind.
The correct skid-rib Z-gap scheme.
The detent cantilever is checked: about 0.95 N and 0.46% strain.
Differential-evolution motion synthesis covering both position and orientation, with the output in a JSON file.
scores.comment: The kinematics are the most thoroughly verified of the linkage concepts, but the physical build is a deep stack of four moving plates. The chosen print pose creates a huge unsupported bridge, and the exposed head levers thin Z-oriented pins. Workable after fixes, but there are many interfaces that must all free up.

fixable_issues: Z capture of the wheel is one-sided. The front lip only overlaps the wheel teeth at the mesh, and the pocket is 44 mm pitch diameter against a 30 mm wheel, so the far side of the wheel is open behind the open window. The hub peg sits in a plain 1.6 mm-deep groove. Tilting the wheel about 7.6° about the lip lifts the peg clear, and the wheel can be pried out. Use a V-ridged peg in an undercut V-groove along the centre path.
The wheel's OD of 32.5 (hull width about 32.2) only just clears the 31.7 mm small-parts cylinder. The 22 mm rider is a small part.

The rider pendulum has almost no torque margin: about 0.09 N·mm maximum restoring torque (3 g, e = 3 mm), against pin friction of about 0.02 N·mm plus tack and rub from printing over a 0.4 mm gap. Any fuzz drags Hammy around upside down. Increase e and mass, or use a conical point pivot.

All motion is powered by a 10 g wheel under gravity (about 0.05-0.07 N of driving force after spill) through a print-in-place spur mesh. It works once broken in, but fresh-print tack will mask the dwell-and-whoosh until then.
A non-circular internal mesh with an equivalent tooth difference of about 11, plus pocket/hump curvature transitions, needs the 2D sweep check.
best_ideas_to_keep: Potential-landscape synthesis is physically sound. I independently reproduced the quasi-static spill at about 84° from the arc geometry: pocket arcs span ±84° before meeting the hump ridge.
The non-circular ring is generated by virtual hobbing, so it is conjugate by construction.
Few parts. The large wheel is the only rolling element.
scores.comment: The behaviour design is clever and the numbers hold up, but the build relies on gravity-scale forces fighting print-in-place friction (worst for the rider), and the stated capture scheme lets the wheel be levered out through the open window. Fixable, but less robust than rigid thumb-driven concepts.

fixable_issues: Four stacked print-over-gap interfaces: N2 (Ø46) over pedestal and wheel, planet over N2, cover over planet, dome over cover. One fused interface stops the whole drive.

The 1.6 mm cover over the ring interior (Ø24) is split into two D-shaped halves by the 5 mm slot. Each half is a cantilever with a free edge, printed over a mostly empty cavity of 4.6 mm or more. Expect sag onto the planet and carrier.

The peg base (planet top, z 13.6) is flush with the ring top (z 13.6). At the Tusi extremes the peg (r = 2) sits over the ring teeth band (r 11-13.25), so the gap is zero and it will rub or fuse. Lower the ring or neck the peg.

The 16T single-lobe driver's small lobe (r1 = 7.2, equivalent to 11.5T) is at the 25° undercut limit, and the effective pressure angle reaches 41-46°. That makes rough, lumpy torque and weak tooth tips in PLA.
The 12T m1.0 planet has about 1.4 mm teeth with 0.4 mm clearances, at the edge for FDM.
N2 is a Ø46 gear on a short Ø6 stub. It is Z-capped only by the ring annulus and can wobble under the oblique mesh loads.
best_ideas_to_keep: Using the Tusi straight line functionally, so a plain straight slot works, is clever. All rotation axes are along Z.
The thumb wheel is printed on the bed and captured by a V-ridge with no axle.
The pitch-curve inverse synthesis checks out: r1 7.2-13.0 and r2 17-22.8 follow from g = 1.3 + 1.867|cos|^4, with perimeters closing at 125.7 mm.
The keep-out volume is generated automatically from swept moving parts.
scores.comment: The geometry is right, but this is the deepest gear stack of the ten: three meshes, one of them non-circular with a near-undercut 1-lobe driver, built in five Z levels with a slotted cover bridging a cavity. It has the most ways to fuse or bind for its payoff.

fixable_issues: Seven bodies and six-plus joints in one print, in mirrored pairs. Every pin, pad pocket, rocker and paw-over-face sandwich must free up, and any single fusion locks that side. Reliability compounds badly.

The return spring is printed stress-free at the shy pose, so return force goes to about 0 just where the paws need to finish covering the eyes. With about 0.3 N/deg of pad stiffness against plausible joint and sandwich friction of 10-20 N·mm, there is a 2-3° dead band, so the paws park about 1.5-2.5 mm short. Preload needs a pre-bent flexure plus a snap-over stop.
The minimum transmission angle of 34.8° plus print-in-place pin friction will feel sticky near the end of the squeeze.

The forearm-paws (34 x 16) fit the small-parts cylinder lengthwise, so retention depends entirely on Ø4 mushroom-headed Z pins (in tension across layers) and an 8 mm collar bridge, under a prying load (fingers under a paw).

There are internal inconsistencies: the flexure leaves are specified 7 mm tall (Z) but the pad layer is 3.2 mm (2.4-5.6). The Q1/Q2 pins need arc slots through the face core, which the spec does not mention. The face must bridge over the rocker and pad swept pockets.
Butterfly-flexure virtual-centre drift is still unverified (the elastica is listed as a to-do).
best_ideas_to_keep: Three-pose (Burmester-type) motion generation, including paw orientation, with printable pin-spacing constraints. The trade-off between accuracy and printability is reported honestly.
Leaf taper computed for uniform strain (about 0.65%).
Hard stops on the pads keep overload out of the flexures and linkage.
scores.comment: It has the most moving bodies, the most joints, an unpreloaded print-in-place spring return, and child-safety retention of small-part-sized paws that relies on Z pins in tension. Each issue is fixable on its own, but together it is the least likely to come off a typical printer working and to stay working in a child's hands.

judged.hybrid_suggestion:
Port C3's storyboard cam synthesis into C9's print topology. Rotor and rocker would both print on the bed with XY-only gaps and be captured by C9's 45° umbrella and V-ridge rim. Replace the two stacked plate cams with a single-layer positive-drive groove (track) cam, with the rocker nose dropping into an open-top groove so only a narrow rocker arm crosses the rotor over a Z gap.

This removes C3's layer conflicts (cam A overhangs cam B by up to 1.3 mm over nose B's band, and nose A passes over 38 mm² of cam B with zero Z gap in the stated stack). It also removes the front shell printed about 0.1 mm over the moving tops. With one clearance instead of two, desmodromic slop roughly halves, and the honest 'computed from a storyboard, no springs' story survives with a rigid, creep-free, fatigue-free mechanism.

If a compliant concept is preferred instead, two changes are needed:
- Take C2's stress-free monostable architecture (no creep set).
- If C1 is used, give each belly window a closed frame of at least about 4000 N/mm and specify PETG. My FE re-run shows frame compliance near 1000 N/mm ties the C1 pull-back order, and near 500 N/mm it removes bistability from the bz=9.8 cell.

Check scripts are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Apps/023789a6-f9f1-563f-a565-9790ebbd0388/scratchpad/ideation/judge-engineering/ (c1_frame.py, c2_frame.py, c3_overhang.py, c4_internal.py).

fixable_issues: The contact sim (esc_dyn2.py) has viscous damping at the head pivot (c_a = 2e-8) but no Coulomb friction at the Ø14 V-ridge hub. Pin impacts of 5-36 N on a 7 mm hub radius at μ 0.35 could take roughly 15-20% of each kick. Add pivot Coulomb friction and re-run the tolerance corners before claiming the low-torque 'giggle' mode exists.

The concept itself puts R21 rim V-groove drag at 5-20 N·mm, against a 1-40 N·mm working band. At gentle turning the feel may be dominated by constant Coulomb drag rather than the √T 'honey' governor feel. Shrink the bearing radius, or put the bearing on a small hub, and keep the rim only for capture.

The visible giggle is only readable in the 6-15 Hz band. Realistic finger cranking at 1-2 rev/s gives about 2-10 N·mm, 8-25 Hz and 40-90 impacts/s, so much of normal play is a blur plus a buzz. Tune per-skin inertia (heavier head) to push the readable band to where kids actually turn it.
At hard push it makes 150-175 impacts/s, a loud rattle in a classroom. Add soft banking or limit the knob radius.
The model is a 2D rigid one with penalty contact (ζ 0.25). Real PLA restitution is unknown. The escapement-only coupon has to come first, and the brief's 'verified' claim depends on it.
best_ideas_to_keep: The child's thumb is the mainspring and the character's head is the foliot, so the expression IS the regulator. This is the most honest 'the mechanism makes the character do something' in the set.
A spring-free, inertia-only regulator avoids the creep and fatigue failure that kills printed springs.

A bidirectional, jam-free pin-pallet geometry found by configuration-space screening, then re-centred in its tolerance window and checked on 8 corners (pivot ±0.4, pin ±0.2). That is a computed element that actually matters.
Speed-limited 'turning through honey' with a purring vibration is a haptic I have not seen in any fidget.
Retuning per-skin inertia from the mesh, so every skin feels the same while each has its own 'voice'.
scores.comment: Novelty check: I searched for a hand-driven print-in-place escapement and found none. The only escapement fidgets are the wind-up Swiss Escapement Desktop Fidget (Printables 710195, steel nails, supports) and MakerWorld VergeFlow (382225, gravity-driven, bearings and fishing line). Knob 'clickers' (MakerWorld 3015240, 3053223) are pawl ratchets, not escapements. Runaway escapements are old (timers, fuzes), but using one as an inertia-only, bidirectional character regulator in a single print is new. I checked the scratchpad: esc_dyn2.py and fin_T.log reproduce the stated numbers, from 5-6 Hz at 1 N·mm up to 41-51 Hz and 163-175 impacts/s at 40 N·mm, in both directions, with no jams. Play value is the strongest in the set. The loop is continuous with no dead time and works both ways, and it gives three channels at once: touch (governor resistance plus vibration), sound (a purr rising to a buzz) and sight (head shiver and ear flicks). It also stops instantly, which suits a fidget. The main risk to the play value is unmodelled friction at both bearings, which could flatten the gentle-push mode the character depends on.

fixable_issues: It depends on rolling resistance. The team's own c2_dyn2.py shows that at c_rr 0.03 and 120°/s the wheel makes a second ~50 mm run at a frame angle of 168-176° (D=16, rh 10 or 16), which skips a pocket. Only at c_rr ≥ 0.05-0.08 does it settle. Real PLA gear-mesh losses are unknown, so a slider coupon for rolling resistance is essential.
The numbers don't agree: the concept says the run is ~28 mm, but the sim gives about 47 mm net run for D=16. Reconcile with the chosen rh=12 before anything is published.
The landing is 1.2 mJ from 10 g, which may feel like a tap rather than a 'THUNK'. Use a solid-infill or thicker wheel rim, or the D=18 option, for a more satisfying drop.
It only works when held vertical and turned, and a full turn needs two hands or a regrip. Advertise the 'steering wheel' or edge-rolling modes.
The rider can be dragged around if pin friction is too high (steady lean ≈ asin(μ r_pin / e) ≈ 12°). Use a conical pivot or a larger e.
best_ideas_to_keep: An intermittent indexer with no pins, pawls, springs or slots: dwell and release both come from the gravitational potential landscape of a computed non-circular internal ring gear (a saddle-node at a designed tilt).
The design targets are behavioural (spill angle 80-100°, drop of at least 10 mm, no runaway), which is exactly the 'this shape was computed to make X happen' story.
Virtual hobbing of the 24T wheel along the pitch curve makes the internal teeth conjugate by construction.
A pendulum rider that stays upright while the wheel spins under it gives a charming character beat (leans back on the 'wheee', bobs forward on landing).
Two play modes: slow indexing ('wait... whoosh... thunk', then 2-3 rocks) and fast-swirl loop-the-loop.
scores.comment: Novelty check: I found nothing comparable. Searches for print-in-place hamster-wheel or gravity-indexer fidgets returned only wheel clickers (MakerWorld 2616913 and similar), and patent searches only turned up industrial pocket-indexers. Non-circular gears in fidgets are always driven, decorative pairs, and gravity rollers are loose marbles. A captive geared roller on a ring computed from its potential landscape is genuinely new, and the computation is the whole point rather than decoration. Play value is high. The wait-whoosh-thunk-slosh rhythm is the same addictive loop as rainsticks and marble labyrinths, it varies with how fast you turn, and the upright hamster adds character. It ranks below C9 because it needs the toy held vertical with large wrist rotation, the payoff per event is gentle (10 g), and correct indexing depends on a friction value nobody has measured, and the team's own sim shows it skipping pockets when friction is low.

fixable_issues: The 'melt' lasts only 2.8 mm (0.6-3.4 mm) under a thumb. Human force discrimination is about 7-10%, and print-to-print scatter is a median ±9% half-band (p90 16.5%), so many prints will feel like a mild 'give' rather than a marshmallow. Lengthen the stroke with a lever or a second stage.
Shear-face and V-interlock friction under off-axis thumb presses adds hysteresis that blurs exactly the zero-stiffness feel being sold. Quantify it with the tilt model and widen the tuft.
It is silent mid-stroke and has no click. That is good for classrooms, but the auditory channel is weak for repeat fidgeting. The optional 'giggle-snap' preset (k −15%) should be a shipped variant.
The facial features are small (5×4 mm eyes, 4 mm mouth lobes), and the expression only reads with the black-floor colour swap.
best_ideas_to_keep: A quasi-zero-stiffness 'squishy' made from rigid PLA. A feel kids have never had from hard plastic.

Negative-stiffness arch and positive folded leaves co-optimised into a flat plateau. I re-ran squish_final.py: nominal F = 3.306-3.337 N over 0.6-3.3 mm, MC plateau 2.29-4.59 N, and 100% return. The computed element is real and is the product.
One extrusion line per flexure, so flow error mostly scales force rather than tilting the plateau.
Analog 'aperture topology': a single translation closes the eyes and opens the mouth, so half a press is a giggle.
scores.comment: Novelty check: QZS from positive and negative stiffness in parallel is textbook (Carrella et al. 2007; a 3D-printed flexure QZS stage from Warwick, wrap.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/128813). I found no toy or fidget that uses it, and the prior-art map lists only 3 constant-force printables, none for children. So it is new in this domain, and the honest computed story is strong. Play value is the concern under my lens. A 3.5 mm silent press with an end 'tok' is a calm fidget, but it may not hold attention for minutes the way snaps, purrs or rhythmic events do. The unusual feel also has to survive friction and printer scatter that are on the order of the plateau tolerance.

fixable_issues: The illusion is likely too fast at kid crank rates. The tempo doubles every revolution, so at 1-2 rev/s it doubles every 0.5-1 s. Risset rhythms usually need several seconds per doubling, and at this speed it will probably read as a repeating one-second 'bouncing-ball' figure. A crank-to-drum reduction (e.g. 1:4) fixes this but adds a print-in-place gear stage.

Torque ripple is 5× (peak 26 vs mean 5.4 N·mm) and is synchronised with the beats. Each tooth slows the hand exactly where the timing must be steady, which smears the schedule. Spread the ramps or add flywheel mass.

Only 3 layers, with tap dynamics from 1.5 down to 0.75 and silence in mechanical PLA taps whose timbre depends on resonance. That is a thin envelope for the illusion. Test with recorded real taps, not the synthetic 1.6/3.1 kHz click in the preview WAV.
It is one-way, and children will crank backwards into the ratchet stop. Make the sticks fold away when reversed, as two-way clickers do.
The paw motion is small (0-4.7 mm), so the visual character payoff is weak and the effect rests almost entirely on the sound.
best_ideas_to_keep: Encoding an auditory illusion in tooth geometry: the irregular tooth pattern IS the product. Spacing comes from a log2 time-warp and heights from inverting the stick's snap-overshoot law. That is a very concrete, testable 'computed to make X happen'.
A WAV preview generated before printing, which is a good verification habit.
Two voices split across Z-stacked tracks, so main beats alternate left-right on the bunny's paws.
Low-strain (0.42%), one-directional flexure levers with a captive fail-safe hub.
scores.comment: Novelty check: I found no mechanical Risset rhythm anywhere. Searches returned only audio software (Stowell 2011, online generators). The closest physical items are music boxes, Printables ThumbDrum 233091, and a student crank-drum-machine proposal (handandmachine.org). So the content is highly novel, but the mechanism is a classic cam-and-striker music box. I checked risset2.py: the envelope is a valid 3-layer Risset (k≡0 mod 4 beats stay at 1.5, k≡2 fades 1.5→0.84, odd beats 0.75→0), so the design is honest. Play value is the problem. The illusion needs a steady, slow crank, and children supply a fast, uneven one through a 5× torque ripple. Without the illusion, what remains is a one-way crank clicker with a repeating rhythm. That is still pleasant, but it is a fragile payoff with a small visual component.

fixable_issues: The only haptic events are four 'toks' from backlash crossing, so the feedback comes from slop rather than design. Add designed detents or a soft click at the POP and the hide so the dial has a tactile rhythm.
A 30° peak pressure angle on PLA-on-PLA sliding cams at about 5.5 N normal force will feel notchy and wear. Re-optimise to about 26° as proposed.
cam2.py reports 'concave? True' for both cams but no concave-radius versus 2 mm nose check. Verify that the follower fits every concave region.
Head jiggle of ±1.1 mm may read as loose, and the 4-beat story becomes predictable after a few turns. Consider two storyboards selectable by turning direction.
best_ideas_to_keep: Spring-free desmodromic twin cams on separate layers trap one rocker, avoiding the printed-spring creep that defeats push-push and bobble toys.

Cams synthesised from a keyframed storyboard (cycloidal blends, conjugate pair, scipy tuning of pivot and noses to bring peak pressure angle from 34.9° to 30.3°). This is real computation and is reproducible in cam2.py.
A 12 mm pop with a 16° curious lean is the most readable expression change for a young child.
A continuous rotary input plays a timed narrative (peek, duck, POP, hide) instead of a single repeated motion.
scores.comment: Novelty check: cam synthesis from a target motion is standard machine design, and Coros et al. (SIGGRAPH 2013) did it for character automata. Cam-driven peek-a-boo toys go back decades: Kohner's 'Action toy' US 4,164,827 uses a pair of cams to move hands over and away from the eyes. Click-Wink Bunny (1393629) is the print-in-place precedent. What is new is the print-in-place conjugate twin-cam and the multi-beat storyboard in a hand-held fidget, a moderate step. Play value is good on charm (the POP is great for kids) but middling as a fidget: there are no designed clicks, sliding-cam friction makes it notchy, and the loop is the same four beats every turn.

fixable_issues: The visual readout is weak: eyes go from 3.7 to 0.9 mm and the stack shrinks 11%. Children will feel three clicks, but the 'falling asleep in order' story barely shows without the black-floor colour swap. Amplify the eyelid stroke with a lever or use a larger lid.

The snap order is the computed feature, but the order itself isn't perceptible as such. What children feel is a force ladder (2, 3, 4 N). Make the ladder the advertised experience, e.g. 'each frog is harder to put to sleep'.
Absolute forces scatter about ±30% with line-width error. Ship the coupon and the 0.50 mm variant.
Resting strain while squished (0.66%) means creep if left asleep. Tell users to store it awake.
best_ideas_to_keep: Programming snap order by Z-depth (layer count) so common-mode extrusion errors cancel. This is a clever, manufacturing-aware computed element, and the Monte Carlo (99.3% / 100% order preserved) is real.
A strain-budgeted bistable arch (1.0% peak) from a converged corotational FE, far gentler than typical printed clickers.
Six snaps per cycle with every partial state stable: a strong tactile clicker loop with a 'count the sleepers' game.
The eyelid is the neighbour's chin, so the face is a mechanical readout of the chain's state.
scores.comment: Novelty check: clickers are the most saturated fidget category, and multi-bistable fidgets already exist (MakerWorld 1958021 'Expandable Bistable Spinner', built from bistable auxetic cells). Series chains of printed snap-through units with programmable multistage behaviour were published in 2026 (Adv. Eng. Mater., doi 10.1002/adem.202502854). What is new is the Z-depth ordering trick and the face readout. That is a real, robust computed element, but the result is still a 3-stage clicker in a stacked-frog shell. Play value is solid: tick-tick-tick and tock-tock-tock are satisfying, and the force ladder is a nice tactile progression. The expressive payoff is the weakest of the character concepts.

fatal_flaws: As a fidget loop it is inherently a bounded (±10 mm), pose-holding, near-silent 1-DOF rock with no restoring force and no designed click. Each gesture ends with nothing pushing back, and that can't be fixed without adding a spring or detent the concept was built to avoid.
fixable_issues: The claimed 'tik-tik-tik' texture is doubtful. Involute teeth rolling under a light thumb load do not click, and only a reversal flips the backlash. Add rolling detents, e.g. a deliberately shallow-flanked tooth every few pitches.

The perceptual payoff of the computed centrode is subtle. Children will see 'head tilts side to side', and the 3 mm 'perk-up', which distinguishes it from a hinge, may go unnoticed. Exaggerate the dip and lift, or add a second gesture.
There is about 1° of tilt play and possible wobble at the extremes. The contact ratio at low-curvature ends still needs verifying.
With no centring it won't 'bobble back'. Consider a computed gravity valley that is deeper than the 0.05 N one.
best_ideas_to_keep: Inverse synthesis from gesture to centrodes to conjugate teeth. The cleanest 'we described the motion, the computer found the only two curves that roll into it' story in the set.

scan.py shows the computer finding a cusp (minimum radius 2.6 mm with no dip) and resolving it with a 3 mm dip that becomes the 'perks up' expression. The computation creates expression rather than decorating it.
A coupled slide, lift and eased tilt that no fixed pivot can produce: a pivot below the head drops it, and a pivot above it swings the centre the wrong way.
A method that generalises to any 1-DOF gesture (shy duck, sleepy droop).
scores.comment: Novelty check: I found no print-in-place or toy joint synthesised from a gesture via centrodes. The closest work is Coros 2013 (linkages) and Xu 2020 (non-circular gears from shapes, not motions), so the computational element is genuinely new and meaningful. It is the most intellectually novel concept here. Under the play-value half of my lens it is the weakest. A posable head-tilt with marginal tactile or auditory feedback and bounded travel will hold a child for seconds, not minutes, and the computed refinement is visually subtle.

fatal_flaws: The mechanism class is the most traditional automaton element: a crank-rocker four-bar carrying a peeking head on its coupler. The novelty rests only on print-in-place, hand-held packaging and a standard differential-evolution path synthesis. Nothing in the mechanism itself is new.
fixable_issues: The pure four-bar's top dwell is only about 26%, so it reads as a continuous bob rather than a peek-and-hold. Only the 0.2 mm deeper detent compensates. A 6-bar or a dwell cam would give a real peek pause.
0.4 mm pin play over a ~30 mm lever gives about ±1 mm and ±1.5° head wobble, which reads as loose.
Rolling on a table relies on PLA rim friction and may slip.
There are four stacked bodies with large overlaps; any tack locks the whole thing.
best_ideas_to_keep: Head position and orientation optimised together: a near-vertical 20.7 mm rise (±4.6 mm drift) with a 30° curious tilt sweep. Verified in peek_report5.py.
Three play modes from one degree of freedom: thumb scroll, roll-along push toy (one peek per 132 mm), and backdrive by pushing the head down.
12 low-strain detent clicks with a deeper 'hold' click at the peak.
Revolute-only guidance frees up more reliably than print-in-place sliders.
scores.comment: Novelty check: four-bar peeking characters are classic karakuri and paper automata. UT Austin's 'Peek-A-Bear' uses a crank-driven four-bar for head and arms, and robives.com has paper four-bar characters. Coros 2013 synthesises exactly such coupler motions. TonyHanma has already published crank automata on Printables. The synthesis here is real and well constrained, but it is textbook motion generation. Play value is good: continuous scrolling with detent clicks, a big readable 20 mm rise, and the roll-along mode is a lovely extra for kids. It loses points because the motion is a continuous bob with no real dwell and because the mechanism is the least surprising in the set.

fatal_flaws: The user-visible behaviour, twisting an input to make a character's eyes slide side to side, already exists as a simple print-in-place model: MakerWorld 'Shifty Eyed Pumpkin' 642517 (twist the stem and the eyes slide). Everything novel here (Tusi straight line, timing-synthesised non-circular pair) is hidden inside and invisible to the child.
fixable_issues: The computed timing gain is modest. I re-ran c1c.py: the time spent holding near an extreme goes from 29% (circular) to 42%, and the middle-crossing from 49% to 35%. A sinusoidal Tusi already dwells at its ends, so the 'hold then dart' difference may not be noticeable. Push towards gmin 1.2 or p 6 and accept the convexity and deviation trade-offs, or use a deliberate Geneva-like dwell.
There are no designed clicks, only gear rumble. Add detents at the glance extremes to make the hold tactile.
The effective pressure angle of the non-circular pair is up to 41-46°, which gives a lumpy feel. The 12T m1.0 planet is fine-pitched for FDM.
It is a 20 mm thick body with four stacked over-gap interfaces, so the main print risk sits on the only moving feature.
best_ideas_to_keep: Using the Tusi straight line functionally: an exact straight path lets the face be one continuous cover with a straight slot.
A non-circular pitch-curve pair inverse-synthesised from a target gaze timeline (closure, convexity, integer teeth). This fills a listed gap.
The large 24 mm pupil glance is very readable and funny ('shifty side-eye').
Hobbing all gears with one virtual-rack code path.
scores.comment: Novelty check: Tusi and hypocycloid spinners exist (143028, 450158), and the expression has a direct print-in-place precedent in MakerWorld 642517, which does it with a stem and stops. The mechanism combination is new, and both gaps it targets are real. But a child sees only a pupil sliding left and right, which a far simpler mechanism already delivers, and the computed timing improvement is small (hold fraction 0.29 to 0.42). As a fidget it is a continuous scroll with soft rumble and a single repeated gesture: pleasant, but low on tactile events.

fatal_flaws: The core play concept, squeezing the toy to move its arms from covering the face to revealing it, is existing toy prior art: US patent application 2016/0101365 'Squeezable face-covering toy and its squeeze mechanism' (hinged panels plus spring, squeeze reveals the face). There is also Kohner's cam-driven peek-a-boo 'Action toy', US 4,164,827. Novelty reduces to 'print-in-place version with a synthesised paw path', and that can't be fixed without changing the concept.
fixable_issues: The PLA flexure return spring at about 0.65% strain limits life to roughly 10^4-10^5 squeezes. After that the fidget loses auto-return, its central feature. Ship PETG as the default.
The minimum transmission angle is 34.8°, so the end of the squeeze may feel sticky right at the BOO payoff.
The return force (4-6 N) against fresh print-in-place friction may leave the paws short of covering the eyes.
Seven bodies in one print, so any fused joint kills one side.
best_ideas_to_keep: Analog, graded expression (half squeeze peeks, full squeeze is BOO), with independent left and right loops so a one-sided squeeze winks.
Three-position motion generation (cover, peek, BOO) that also rotates the paws palms-out. A real computed element, though classic Burmester-type synthesis.
A flexure taper computed for uniform strain under the actual moment distribution.
Hard stops coincide with the BOO pose, giving a tactile 'tock' exactly at the payoff.
scores.comment: Play value is high: peek-a-boo is universally loved by young children, and a squeeze stress-ball with a show plus one-sided winks is a rich loop. Novelty is the weakest in the set. The play pattern exists as a commercial squeeze-toy patent and a 1970s cam toy, Peek-A-Bear-style karakuri cover the same gesture, and the synthesis method is textbook three-position motion generation. Under my lens, a good toy whose 'new AI-designed mechanism' claim would not survive scrutiny.

judged.hybrid_suggestion:
No hybrid clearly beats C9 on its own. It has the strongest combination of a genuinely new mechanism (a hand-driven, spring-free foliot escapement in which the character's head is the regulator) and a continuous, multi-sensory, two-way fidget loop. C8 is the clear runner-up standalone and is the lower-risk second build.

One low-risk graft is worth considering: C9 plus the 'computed rhythm' idea from C10. Replace C9's uniform 8-tooth star with an escape wheel whose tooth pitches and heights are computed (still screened by C9's configuration-space jam-free test and its 8 tolerance corners) to give a patterned giggle ('heh-heh-HEH') at gentle turning instead of a uniform buzz. Each skin then gets a recognisable laugh or purr signature, and C9 gains a second 'computed to make X happen' layer without depending on C10's fragile Risset illusion.

Before either is chosen, fix C9's play-critical gaps:
- Add Coulomb friction at the head pivot to the dynamics model.
- Shrink the R21 rim bearing so its drag stops masking the √T governor feel.
- Tune head inertia so the readable 6-15 Hz shiver falls at the 2-10 N·mm torques children actually apply.

fixable_issues: Head pushes get amplified into small internal arms. Kids will push the popped chick back in, and during the dwells (pressure angle near 0) the cam cannot be backdriven, so the force goes straight into the follower arms. Through the 3.8:1 lever a 10 N push gives about 38 N at the nose and about 38 MPa in a 4 x 3 mm arm; 20 N gives about 76 MPa, which breaks it. The break stays inside the sealed cavity, so this is a durability problem, not an escape hazard. Fix: widen the arms to at least 7 mm in-plane and add rocker-to-body hard stops at both swing extremes so pushes go into the frame.

The 8 x r3 dial scallops share a Z band with the front-shell hole, so a notched rim turns against a fixed edge with a 0.4 to 3.4 mm varying gap. That is an in-running skin nip. Fix: put scallops only on the 1 mm proud part of the dial and keep the in-hole band a plain circle.

Small-parts margin on the dial is thin. My caliper check puts the scalloped Ø34 dial at about 33.5 mm minimum width, only about 1.8 mm over the 31.7 mm cylinder. A chipped rim could close that gap; Ø36 or more is safer.
The large-area 0.4 mm Z gaps (front shell over rotor and rocker) may tack. Users forcing a stiff break-in is where parts get cracked. Ship the 0.5 mm variant and a coupon.
Engraved eyes are invisible in single-colour prints. Use 2 mm-deep pockets or raised dome eyes in areas the shell never covers.
Chamfer the head's lower edges where they slide under the shell edge, to avoid skin shear in the 0.4 mm gap.
best_ideas_to_keep: The desmodromic twin-cam traps the rocker both ways with no spring, so nothing creeps and no flexure can splinter.
Every body exceeds the small-parts cylinder: the rotor via the dial, and the rocker-head is over 50 mm long.
All cam nips sit in a sealed sandwich with 0.4 mm openings. The rocker's hidden edges are arcs concentric with its pivot, giving a constant 0.45 mm gap.
Storyboard keyframes drive the cam synthesis (peek, duck, POP, hide). It is a narrative that needs no instructions, and it plays backwards on reverse.
The dial chamfer under the front shell captures the rotor in Z even if the cantilevered post fails.
scores.comment: Best on my lens. There is no detach path: all three bodies are larger than the cylinder, there are no flexures, the mechanism is enclosed, and every moving-to-fixed edge in finger reach is either a Z-overlap or a constant-gap arc. The forces are thumb-limited. The peek-a-boo storyboard is the most legible play in the set: a 6-year-old turns the flower dial and immediately gets it. The skins (chick in egg, bunny in magician hat, ghost in pumpkin, kitten in sock) are classic and friendly. The real weakness is abuse of the head, the part kids will shove. The fixes are concrete (wider arms, swing-end stops) and stay inside the concept.

fixable_issues: The knurled Ø42 rim is exposed through a ~100° window with a 0.5 mm gap, which is an in-running nip. Roll-along play on a table or floor also picks up hair and fibre. Fix: round the window lips to r ≥ 2, shroud the in-running side, or expose only the out-running side.

The Ø4 B/C pins are Z-printed and span a layer, so the bending lever is about 5 mm. Near crank dead-points, a head push of 20 N gives about 16 MPa across layers, and 40 N about 32 MPa: a break risk. Use Ø6 pins, double-shear pins capped by the front wall, or shorter cantilevers.

The 1.8 mm front and back plates span about 60 mm with only perimeter walls. A hard squeeze or stomp could crack the front wall and expose the internal rocker (about 36 x 9 mm, small enough for the small-parts cylinder) and the 14 x 1.2 mm detent pawl. Add internal posts and use 2.4 mm plates.

The peeking head is a 4 mm plate cantilevered 19 mm above the wall. Prying it toward the viewer loads the 10 x 4 mm neck to about 28 MPa at 30 N x 25 mm. Thicken the neck in Z, or add a back lip behind the head.
Pin play of 0.4 mm gives ±1 mm / ±1.5° of head wobble, which reads as loose to kids.
best_ideas_to_keep: Coupler-synthesized motion gives a 20.7 mm near-straight rise with a 30° curious-tilt sweep. This is the largest and most readable character motion in the set.
The head ducks behind the front wall (Z-overlap), so there is no closing wedge at the wall top.
The Ø36 head is larger than the cylinder, and all small links are enclosed.
It has three play modes (thumb scroll, roll-along push toy, push-head backdrive), and a deeper detent holds the 'peek' pose.
All joints are revolute along Z, with no sliders to fuse.
scores.comment: Second-most charming and very intuitive: a critter rises, looks around and ducks. The push-along mode is a real kid toy pattern. Safety is decent but less closed than C3. It has an exposed knurled wheel nip (a hair-catch risk in roll mode), Z-printed Ø4 pins that see interlayer stress near their limit when kids push the head down at dead points, and thin 1.8 mm plates protecting a sub-cylinder rocker. All of these are fixable without changing the concept.

fixable_issues: The end stop is the Ø5 Z-printed pin hitting the slot end. Every push to the end of travel loads it in bending across layers (about 6-11 MPa at 20-40 N), every cycle, so it will fatigue. Move the end stops to the body cavity walls or the cradle run-out.

The raised face comes within 6 mm of the collar edge, which is inside the 5-12 mm finger band. It is a shallow (~3 mm) trough, so the risk is low, but chamfer the collar edge or hold the gap at ≥12 mm.
The head's lower edge slides over the hood with a 0.4 mm Z gap and should be chamfered against skin shear.
The 0.4 mm Z gaps over large areas (head over hood, collar over runner) may tack.
Charm ceiling: the head goes only where the thumb pushes it and then holds, with no surprise and no return. Add a gentle detent at the 'huh?' pose, or a slight gravity bias.
best_ideas_to_keep: Only two bodies, both far larger than the cylinder. The head is triple-captive (sandwich, pin-in-slot, mesh) with no flexures.
The pinch analysis is computed: the raised face stays clear of the collar edge, and every visible moving boundary is a Z-overlap.
The rolling gear joint is synthesized from a gesture. The computed 3 mm 'perk-up' dip comes out of the manufacturability constraint.
Kids can pose the head (curious, sad, sleepy) for pretend play.
scores.comment: Very safe architecture: two big parts, a sealed mesh, and the only driving force is the child's own push. The pinch audit is part of the plan. The weak point is the Z-printed pin, which doubles as the end stop and takes a hit every cycle. Charm is moderate. The puppy head-tilt is adorable and recognisable, but for a 6-10 year old it is 'a head that moves where I push it'. The clever coupled lift and tilt is subtle, and the face itself never changes.

fixable_issues: The drum turns one way only. Kids aged 6-10 will crank backwards, hit a hard ratchet stop, conclude it is broken, and force it. That drives the trailing nose end-on into its 1.2 mm leaf (Euler ~15 N) until the 0.6 mm hub clearance closes, which kinks the flexure. Fix: add a print-in-place freewheel between the knob and the drum so reverse just slips.
The left track and nose are printed on the bed (z 0-4.5), so the back face is open at the mechanism. Add a back plate with a Z gap.

Paw motion is a ≤4.7 mm snap at about 100 Hz (2.5 ms), mostly too fast to see. The 'endless accelerando' payoff is an auditory illusion with only about 20 dB of PLA dynamic range. It is abstract for kids and may not register.
If the drum stops with a stick resting on a crest, it creeps. Add short crests and parking dwells, as the concept already notes.
best_ideas_to_keep: Each flexure lever has a fail-safe V-ridged captive hub, so even a cracked leaf cannot release a part.
Leaf strain is low and one-directional (0.42%).
Two bodies only, both large. Teeth sit under the umbrella and exposed gaps are 0.45-0.6 mm shear gaps.
An audio WAV preview lets you hear the computed result before printing.
Strong beats alternate between the left and right paws.
scores.comment: Safety is solid: two large bodies, belt-and-braces captive levers, low stored energy, and forces limited by the finger on the crank. On charm, a drumming bunny is cute and cranking is intuitive. But the one-way crank will confuse and be abused, the visible paw action is a fast twitch, and the clever payoff is perceptual and not guaranteed to register with a child.

fixable_issues: The escapement is printed directly on the bed (z 0-5) with no back plate. The star wheel, pallet pins and under-arm are exposed on the back face, where the holding fingers rest. That creates in-running pin/tooth nips at up to 175 impacts/s, and any fragment can fall out. Fix: add a 2 mm back plate with a 0.4 mm Z gap, which also removes the first-layer fusing risk under the pins.

The Ø4.3 x 5 mm pallet pins are Z-printed. My estimate is about 12 MPa bending across layers at the 36 N peak impact, repeated at up to 10^4 impacts per minute, so interlayer fatigue is likely. A broken pin is a 4 x 5 mm small part. Fix: pins ≥6 mm with root fillets, shorter, or redesign the pallets as in-plane features.
The head (the foliot) is the obvious thing to grab. It is held by two ~100° shoulder arcs plus a V-ridge, so it needs a yank and twist test. The head itself is not a small part.
The ear-to-frame gap swings from about 3 to about 13 mm, inside the finger band, though forces are low (1-3 N).
At hard pushes the buzz is loud, and above about 20 Hz the head is a blur that reads as 'broken or shivering'. The visible 'giggle' only happens in a narrow torque band.
best_ideas_to_keep: The foliot escapement needs no springs: the child's thumb is the mainspring and the head is the regulator.
The governor feel (turning through honey) means nothing coasts and the head stops instantly on release.
Head inertia is tuned per skin so every character feels the same.
Tolerance-corner verification, checked in both directions.
The purr frequency is matched to a real cat's purr, and the bee skin buzzes in the bumblebee band.
scores.comment: Good small-parts architecture (three large bodies, no flexures), undermined by an open back face that exposes the escapement and by tiny Z-printed pallet pins under high-cycle impacts. Both are fixable. 'Turn the yarn ball and kitty purrs' is instantly understood and lovely, but the expression is a vibrating head rather than a changing face, and much of its range is a noisy blur.

fixable_issues: Six single-extrusion-line arches (0.45 x 46 mm) sit in belly windows (46 x 8.5 mm) that go right through the part, front and back, so fingers and pencils can reach them. One fracture leaves sharp 23 mm stubs; two fractures free a 23 x 0.45 x 5-10 mm splinter that is both a small part and a cutting hazard. Fix: cover the windows front and back with print-over-gap plates or ≥2 mm straps so fragments stay captive. Make PETG the default.

The eye apertures are closing in-plane gaps on the face (3.7 mm down to 0.5 mm at the stop). Once at the stop, skin trapped in the eye sees the full palm squeeze. Fix: close the lid behind a fixed Z-overlap lip so the closing happens under a cover, not at the surface.

Verify that the skirt lower edges against the lower-body shoulders are true constant-gap shear lines over the 8.4 mm stroke. Any horizontal shoulder face would be a 2.8 mm closing gap around the outline.

The visual readout is tiny: eyes go from 3.7 to 0.9 mm and the stack shortens 11%. In single colour, kids hear and feel the snaps but barely see the frogs fall asleep. Make the colour swap mandatory, or reveal a printed closed-eye arc.
Printing quality decides strength: one under-extruded one-line wall starts a crack. Make the force coupon a go/no-go gate.
At 78 mm tall with a high centre of gravity, it tips over when stood up.
best_ideas_to_keep: Monolithic single body: nothing is designed to separate.
Hard stops in both directions push overload into the 4 mm frames, and peak strain is about 1% (FE and Monte Carlo scripts exist).
Snap order is programmed by Z-depth, so it survives flow error.
Six snaps per cycle, and every intermediate state is stable, which makes a 'sleepiness counter' play pattern.
Frog, loaf-cat and dango skins share one core.
scores.comment: Squish the stack and the frogs fall asleep: kids get it without instructions, and the tick-tick-tick is very satisfying. On safety, the single-body design is strong, but the whole function rests on six one-line PLA beams in open windows, and those fail as splinters. The face change is also small. Covering the windows and moving the eye closure under a lip would lift it a lot.

fixable_issues: The pupil dome (Ø10 x 3 mm) sits on top of the cover and is held only by a Ø4 Z-printed peg 2.4 mm tall. A thumbnail pushing the pupil across the slot axis gives about 13 MPa interlayer stress at 20 N and about 25 MPa at 40 N. The dome then pops off as a 10 mm small part on the outside of the toy. Fix: add a flange wider than the slot under the cover so the dome stays captive even if the peg snaps, or recess the pupil into the slot with an undercut.
The thumb-wheel rim pokes out 5 mm through a 0.5 mm window, an in-running nip that also catches hair in roll-along play.
It has four stacked print-over-gap interfaces (N2, planet, cover, dome), the highest fusing risk in the set. A forced break-in of a fused stack is exactly when the peg snaps.
The planet+peg+dome assembly (~15 mm) is a small part. It is triple-captive, but the dome fix above is what makes that claim true.
The 20 mm thick body is chunky for small hands.
best_ideas_to_keep: The Tusi couple's exact straight line lets the face be one continuous cover with a narrow slot, so no teeth are exposed.
Big, readable pupil travel (24 mm across a 36 mm eye) with a computed hold-and-dart rhythm, a genuinely funny 'side-eye' personality.
The keep-out volume is the swept volume of every moving part, subtracted from each skin, so skins can't collide by construction.
Large wheel and carrier (Ø38 and ~46 mm).
scores.comment: The expression is very legible and comedic; kids love shifty eyes, and the robot-scanner and pirate-parrot skins are fun. But the one feature kids will poke, the pupil, is a 10 mm dome outside the cover held by a short peg printed across layers: a foreseeable break-off small part. That is fixable with a captive flange. The stacked gap-printing makes fusing and forced break-in likely.

fixable_issues: It has ten single-line 0.45 mm flexures (2 arches plus 8 leaves of 16 x 0.45 x 9.9 mm) in through-pockets. A leaf fracture gives a splinter that fits the small-parts cylinder. Cover the pockets and default to PETG.

The folded-leaf pockets sit between the tuft (the thumb button) and the ears. As the thumb presses, the stage gaps close from ≥2.3 mm to about 0.5 mm right under the edge of the thumb, nipping skin and catching hair at the main touch point. Move the leaves inboard under the face bar, or cover them.
There are three closing apertures on the face. The eyes close from 4.0 mm to about 0.5 mm, and the mouth lobes snap shut from 4.0 to 0.45 mm on release at about 3.3 N. Use Z-overlap lids.
The plateau force varies 2.3-4.6 N across prints, and 4.7% of prints get a soft snap, so the feel is not consistent from toy to toy. The tilt check for off-centre presses is not done yet.
The features are small (5 x 4 mm eyes, 4 mm mouth lobes on a 62 mm face), so contrast depends on a filament swap. The stroke is silent mid-press, which some kids find less rewarding than a click.
best_ideas_to_keep: Analog face morph: with a single translation, the eyes are the only closing voids and the mouth the only opening void, so half a press gives a giggle and a full press a laugh.
It is monostable and stress-free at rest, so it doesn't creep. Up-stops and down-stops protect the flexures.
The 'squishy made of hard plastic' haptic is a real wow moment.
Monolithic single body.
scores.comment: Very charming and instantly understood: press the tuft and the cat laughs. It also has the best expression-per-input ratio of the compliant pair. But it is the most fragile concept on my lens: ten one-line flexures, several in open pockets right next to the thumb, plus three closing apertures on the face. All of these are fixable, but only by giving up the pure vertical-slot print approach.

fixable_issues: The wheel's small-parts margin is almost zero. My caliper check of the 24T m1.25 gear (OD 32.5 mm) gives a minimum width of about 32.3 mm through the tooth tips, only about 0.6 mm over 31.7. FDM tip rounding or a couple of chipped teeth erase that. Fix: go to OD ≥36 mm (26-27T) and re-run the track synthesis.

The 22 mm rider fits the small-parts cylinder and sits in an open window that invites fingers. It is held by the wheel's front lip, a 1.5 mm overhang printed over a 0.4 mm gap, plus a Z-printed Ø4 pin with a conical cap. Thicken the lip and use a pin with a bulge that does not rely on interlayer strength.

The floor under the closed-loop 1.6 mm groove is only 0.8 mm thick. The floor inside the loop hangs on a 4-layer web, so a drop or squeeze can crack out a ~35 mm island and open the back. Use a raised rail pair or a 2 mm floor.
The wheel is held in Z only by 1.6 mm front lips with 1.5-2 mm overlap, and nobody has checked pry resistance.
Charm: it does nothing flat on a table and has to be held vertical and rotated. Hammy himself barely acts (stays upright, leans ≤20°) and his visible face is only 19 mm.
best_ideas_to_keep: An intermittent indexer driven only by a gravity potential landscape: no pawls, springs or detents.
The mesh nip is covered by the front lip, and the gravity-driven 10 g wheel pinches at only about 0.1 N.
An upright pendulum rider stays level while the wheel spins.
A hamster in a wheel is instantly recognisable to kids.
scores.comment: The story is lovable and the wait-whoosh-thunk rhythm is satisfying. On safety, though, the wheel's 'not a small part' claim rests on a 0.6 mm margin through gear tips. The only character is a sub-cylinder disc behind a thin printed lip in an open window, and the back plate has a 0.8 mm weak loop. Expressiveness is limited to leaning.

fatal_flaws: Two independent paws on a 66 mm face can never each exceed the 31.7 mm cylinder without colliding, so the concept's most-grabbed features are inherently small parts. They are exactly what children are invited to touch and pull. As specified, the forearm-paws ride on top of the face, held by two Z-printed Ø4 mushroom pins and an 8 mm print-over-gap collar bridge. My estimate for a 30 N pry at 25 mm on the 7 x 3.5 mm forearm is about 52 MPa, at PLA's limit. That breaks off a 14 x 16 mm mitten, the same failure as the UK OPSS dragon recall. The only escape is a re-architecture with paws in a middle layer under a windowed front plate, which changes the look substantially.
fixable_issues: Seven bodies in one print, each with joints that must free up; any fused joint locks that side.
Butterfly flexures at about 0.65% strain cap PLA life at roughly 10^4-10^5 squeezes. Failure is captive, but it ends the auto-return.
The paws slide over the face with a 0.4-1.0 mm gap and the flexure snaps them back, a skin-shear line on the face. It is low force but sits where children touch.
The transmission angle drops to 34.8°, so the end of the squeeze feels sticky.
The virtual-centre drift and the elastica check are still to-do, so the pad-arc 0.6 mm gap claim is unverified.
best_ideas_to_keep: The shy, then peek, then BOO choreography is the most emotionally resonant character idea in the set, and kids get it instantly.
Analog graded expression, with a one-sided wink from independent left and right sides.
Paws only move apart, so the minimum paw gap of 11.6 mm never closes, and hard stops sit at both ends.
Flexure leaves are tapered for uniform strain.
scores.comment: The highest charm score in the set and the lowest on safety. The thing that makes it delightful (paws on the face that uncover the eyes) is a pair of graspable small parts on thin forearms and pins, the textbook break-off choking scenario. Keep the choreography and rebuild it on a sealed mechanism (see hybrid).

table.name: Purr-Bobble Kitty: a hand-powered, spring-free foliot escapement
Hammy's Petal Wheel: gravity-indexed rolling track

spec.chosen_name: Purr-Bobble Kitty: a closed-back, thumb-powered foliot escapement in which the kitty's head is the regulator
spec.why_chosen:
I chose C9. It has the highest combined score (22.3), it is ranked first by both the engineering and the novelty/play judges, and no judge found a fatal flaw in it. It is also the only concept where the expression is the mechanism: the kitty's head is the foliot that governs the speed. It has no springs, no flexures and a computed, tolerance-checked geometry that cannot jam. I did not graft another mechanism onto it. Instead I fixed every issue the judges raised. I re-checked each fix numerically in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Apps/023789a6-f9f1-563f-a565-9790ebbd0388/scratchpad/ideation/synth/:

- **Open back (safety):** a 2 mm back plate now seals the escapement. The moving parts sit on skid ribs, using C5's scheme (0.4 mm gap at the ribs, 1.0 mm elsewhere). The first layer no longer has any moving gaps, so elephant foot cannot fuse the mechanism.
- **Pallet pins across layers (safety):** the pins are now in-plane tapered fingers on the head's own plate, so no pin is cantilevered across layers. A C-space check of the real finger, leg and hub outline showed that only the round pallet tips can ever touch the wheel (deficit 0).
- **Large R21 rim bearing friction (engineering and novelty):** two Ø8 fixed posts with V-ridge capture replace it. The 6-DOF dynamics, including 0.25–0.5 mm journal play, Coulomb journal friction, knob side load, gravity and hard banking, give bearing losses of about 23% (wheel) and about 10% (head).
- **Hub/umbrella topology conflict:** the hub now sits in the band layer below the umbrella cone, and a bridged frame roof covers the legs.
- **Tolerance window:** a static lock map plus dynamic corner runs placed the pin depth. Lock-free covers the full ±0.4 mm × ±0.2 mm tolerance box. All 60 hard-banking corner runs work in both directions, and friction up to μ 0.5/0.5 works.
- **Small-part margin:** the wheel is now Ø36.
- **Ear-to-frame finger gap:** removed, because the head floats only over the backdrop.
- **Pinch rules:** I applied C3's rules (concentric arcs or Z-overlap only) and C4's swept-envelope generation for every hidden clearance.

C3 scored highest on the safety lens. Its benefits are covered here by the closed sandwich, and C9 keeps the more novel mechanism and the richer feedback: touch, sound and sight.
spec.runner_up: C3 (Peek-a-Boo Pod), rebuilt in this closed-sandwich topology with the safety judge's "Shy Bear" storyboard: fixed paws on the front shell, and a cam-driven head that peeks, ducks, then goes BOO. Each body would be larger than the small-parts cylinder, and the cams would be desmodromic with no springs. It is the better choice when a quiet toy with a very readable peek-a-boo story matters more than mechanism novelty and haptic richness, for example in a classroom or for the youngest end of 6+. The cost is that its conjugate-cam synthesis is a known machine-design method, its only feedback is backlash "toks", and it adds a second stacked cam layer that the engineering judge flagged.
spec.spec_markdown:
# Purr-Bobble Kitty: build specification (v1.0, synthesis stage)

A single print in PLA with three captive bodies (frame, wheel, head). No supports and no hardware.

Every number below comes from the scripts in
`/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Apps/023789a6-f9f1-563f-a565-9790ebbd0388/scratchpad/ideation/synth/`:

- `layout.py`, `layout2.py`, `layout3.py`: 2-D layout and sweeps.
- `esc_layout*.py` and `check_cspace_final.py`: C-space checks.
- `esc_dyn3.py`, `run_*.py`, and the `*.log` files: dynamics.
- `static_map.py`: static lock map.
- `layout_top.png` and `layout_swing.png`: top views.

They build on the ideation scripts in `.../ideation/haptic/` (`esc_opt.py`, `esc_dyn2.py`, `esc_window.py`).

---

## 1. Concept and story

**What the child sees and feels.** A chubby kawaii kitty sits on a round cushion, hugging a big yarn ball in her lap. The child circles the knob on the ball with a fingertip, or rolls the ball's face with a thumb.

- The ball will not spin freely. It moves as if through honey, and you can feel a purr in your fingertip.
- The kitty's whole head shivers ±10° and her ears flick, as if she were giggling.
- Turning gently gives a slow, visible giggle-shiver: about 5–11 Hz, 50–90 soft clicks per second, like a real purr.
- Pushing harder raises the pitch through a purr to a buzz: about 37 Hz and 130 clicks/s at 40 N·mm.
- On release she stops at once. Nothing coasts.
- It works the same in both directions.
- With the toy held upright and the knob untouched, her head gently tilts to one side and rests there, like a curious tilt. That is because the head is a balanced inverted pendulum resting on a banking stop.

**How it works, in one line.** The yarn ball is the escape wheel of a 13th-century-style foliot escapement with no springs. The child's thumb is the mainspring, and the kitty's head is the foliot, so the expression is the regulator.

**The honest "AI-designed" story.** "The shape of the 8-tooth star wheel, the two pallet tips and the exact place where Kitty's head pivots were found by a computer search. The search rejected every geometry in which a hand-pushed wheel could ever lock her head or slip past it. It checked turning in both directions, posts printed 0.4 mm off, pallets 0.2 mm too fat or thin, bearing play and friction. Every hidden pocket and gap in the body was then computed as the swept shape of the motion."

**Shared core and three skins.** One parametric core is used by all three skins: escapement, posts, head band layer, wheel band and umbrella, body cavity, roof, paws and ribs. Each skin is its own complete single print.

1. **Purr Kitty** (default): cat head with ears, sitting on a round quilted cushion, with a yarn-ball wheel and toe-bean paws.
2. **Bumble**: bee head with two chunky antennae and a five-petal flower backdrop. The wheel is a pollen ball with a honeycomb relief, and a hard push lands in a bumblebee buzz band.
3. **Pip the Robot**: rounded-square robot head with an antenna ball and a visor, in a round porthole backdrop. The wheel has gear-rim relief and a power symbol, and the robot makes a beep-rattle.

---

## 2. Mechanism

### 2.1 Coordinate system and conventions

- Units are mm and degrees.
- O = (0, 0) is the wheel axis. +Y is "up" when the toy is held upright.
- Z is the print height. The bed is at z = 0, the toy's back lies on the bed, and the front faces +Z.
- P = (0, 24.710) is the head axis.
- φ is the wheel rotation about O and ψ is the head rotation about P. Both are counter-clockwise-positive when viewed from +Z.
- The head range is ψ ∈ [−12.42°, +12.42°]. The banking limits are hard stops.
- "Head frame" means the head geometry at ψ = 0. Posed geometry is Rot_P(ψ) applied to it.

### 2.2 Bodies, joints and degrees of freedom

| Body | Joint to frame | DOF | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| FRAME (F) | — | 0 | Back plate (backdrop/cushion), body fill, roof, two fixed posts, paws, ribs |
| WHEEL (W) | Revolute: Ø8.70 bore on the fixed Ø8.00 post at O; V-ridge captures Z | 1 (φ) | Star teeth in the band layer, Ø36 "umbrella" (yarn-ball face), Ø10 knob |
| HEAD (H) | Revolute: Ø8.70 blind bore on the fixed Ø8.00 post at P; V-ridge captures Z | 1 (ψ), banking ±12.42° | Band layer (hub, legs, pallet fingers), face (full height), front layer that overhangs the roof |

**Motion flow.**

1. The finger torque T on the knob turns W.
2. A star tooth flank meets one round pallet tip, kicks the head away and sends it swinging.
3. The other pallet dives into the next tooth gap and is caught by the next tooth's opposite flank. The swing reverses and the cycle repeats.

The result is one head oscillation per tooth, so f_head ≈ 8 × (wheel rev/s). The wheel and head are coupled only through this intermittent contact. The mechanism is a runaway pin-pallet escapement with no restoring spring. The wheel speed rises roughly with √T, which gives the governor or "honey" feel.

### 2.3 Escapement geometry (frozen core values)

Parameters, from the ideation search, re-centred and re-verified here:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| N | 8 |
| Rt (tip radius) | 14.2992 |
| Tooth height | 5.3968 |
| Rr (root radius) | 8.9024 |
| tip_frac | 0.0765 |
| root_frac | 0.1333 |
| Corner rounding | r_f = 0.70 |
| rp (pallet tip radius) | 2.1448 |
| drho (pallet depth) | 1.8686 |
| m (pallet span in pitches) | 2 |
| tilt | 0.8792 |
| ψ_b (banking) | 12.42° |

Derived values:

- pitch p = 45°
- γ = (m + ½)·p/2 = 56.25°
- ρ = (Rt + Rr)/2 + rp + drho = 15.6142 (pallet-centre radius)
- **D = ρ·tilt / cos γ = 24.710** (so P = (0, D))
- **Pallet centres (head frame) = (±ρ sin γ, ρ cos γ) = (±12.983, 8.675)**
- Pallet arm |pallet − P| = 20.632
- Pallet span = 112.5° (2.5 pitches)
- Pallet radial direction u = (±0.8315, 0.5556)

**Star2D (wheel frame).** For k = 0…7, with a0 = 45°·k, take the polar vertices in this order:

1. (Rr, a0 − 3.000°)
2. (Rr, a0 + 3.000°)
3. (Rt, a0 + 22.5° − 1.721°)
4. (Rt, a0 + 22.5° + 1.721°)

So root lands are centred on 0°, 45° and so on, and tip lands on 22.5°, 67.5° and so on. Then round the convex corners (offset −0.70 then +0.70, round joins) and the concave corners (offset +0.70 then −0.70).

**Pallet fingers (head frame).** Each finger is the union of:

- the disc(pallet_i, 2.1448), and
- a trapezoid running radially outward along u_i for 7.0 mm. Its half-width is 2.1448 at the pallet centre and 3.129 at its outer end (8° half-angle taper).

### 2.4 Computational design element: algorithm, equations, objective

**(a) Jam-free C-space screen (static, hard banking).**

The wheel's signed distance field is SDF_W on a 0.05 mm grid. The pallet clearance is

c(φ, ψ) = min_i [ SDF_W( Rot(−φ)·( P + Rot(ψ)·(p_i − P) ) ) − rp ]

The free set is c ≥ 0. A "lazy" head stays at its current ψ unless pushed. For each φ step of 0.25° over two pitches, in both directions, the head moves to the nearest free ψ in [−ψ_b, ψ_b].

A design is rejected if any of these hold:

- The free channel disappears (a jam).
- The contact pressure angle on a forced push exceeds 90° − atan μ − 8° = 62.7° at μ = 0.35.
- The best print-pose clearance is below 0.5 mm.

The ideation random search (1000+ samples) chose the parameters above to maximise swing under these constraints.

**(b) Contact dynamics, extended here to 6 DOF (`esc_dyn3.py`).**

- Wheel state: x, y, φ, with J_w = 4e-6 (finger included), m_w = 6 g.
- Head state: x, y, ψ, with I_h = 5.25e-6 and m = 15.8 g. The centre of mass is 11.3 mm above P, so gravity makes the head an inverted pendulum.
- Pallet contacts: penalty k = 5e4 N/m, ζ = 0.25, Coulomb μ.
- Journals: radial play c_r, penalty k_b = 2e5 N/m, friction torque μ_b·N·r_b with r_b = 4.0 mm.
- Knob: tangential force T/r_k at the knob, which also side-loads the wheel journal.
- Banking: hard stops at ±12.42° (k = 100 N·m/rad).
- Viscous losses: c_w = 2e-7 and c_a = 2e-8 N·m·s.
- Integration: explicit, dt = 1e-5 s.

**(c) Tolerance-window placement of the pallet depth (new in this stage).**

- **Static lock map** (`static_map.py`). At drho = 1.8686 there are no static jams anywhere in the box Δpivot ∈ [−0.4, +0.4] × Δrp ∈ [−0.2, +0.2]. The worst pressure angle in the box is 59°, below the 62.7° limit. Static locks start at drho ≤ 1.72 in the worst corner (Δrp = +0.2, Δpivot = −0.4).
- **Dynamic free-spin edge** (with play and hard banking). The first tooth slip appears at drho ≥ 2.17 in the worst corner (Δpivot = +0.4, Δrp = −0.2, c_r = 0.5).
- **Result.** drho = 1.8686 has about −0.15 mm margin to static lock and about +0.30 mm margin to slip, both at the worst tolerance corner. Journal play tends to relieve locks, because contact forces push the bodies apart.

**(d) Shadow test for the real head outline (`check_cspace_final.py`).**

The full band-layer outline of the head was checked against the real star at 91 × 51 poses (fingers, legs and hub, built as in §2.5). Where the pallets are free, the rest of the head is never closer to the wheel than the pallets: deficit = 0.000 mm.

- Best print pose: φ = 12.0°, ψ = +5.96°, giving a minimum pallet-to-tooth gap of **1.38 mm**.
- Symmetric alternative: φ = 0°, ψ = 0°, giving 0.69 mm.

**(e) Swept-envelope synthesis.** The body cavity, roof, face undercut slot, backdrop, stop pads and rib fields are all computed as unions of the moving outlines over ψ ∈ [−12.42°, +12.42°]:

- Sample at least 100 poses (step ≤ 0.25°).
- Add 0.05 mm to every swept offset for chord error.

**(f) Per-skin inertia tuning.** Compute I_h about P from each skin's head mesh at the specified infill. It must fall in [4.0, 8.0]e-6 kg·m². Trim with closed internal pockets (walls ≥ 2.0) or with ear/antenna size.

**Verified performance** (solid head, c_r 0.35, μ = μ_b = 0.35, hard banking, gravity upright, both directions; `final2.log`):

| T (N·mm) | Wheel (rev/s) | Head shiver (Hz) | Swing (° p-p) | Clicks/s | Peak contact (N) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.61–0.74 | 5.1 | 16–17 | ~50 | 2.4 |
| 2 | 1.05–1.14 | 7.7–9.0 | 18–20 | ~75 | 4.5 |
| 3 | 1.27–1.34 | 10.3–11.5 | 20–22 | 72–87 | 5.4 |
| 5 | 1.61–1.73 | 12.8–14.1 | 19 | 90–97 | 7.4 |
| 10 | 2.43–2.47 | 18–20.5 | 22–24 | 105–117 | 12.7 |
| 20 | 3.53–3.56 | 28 | 24–25 | ~120 | 17.8 |

Bearing losses are 22–27% at the wheel and 6–19% at the head. That compares with ≥ 50% for the ideation R21 rim bearing.

**Robustness** (`hardbank*.log`, `final2.log`, `jw.log`):

- **Tolerance corners:** 60/60 hard-banking corner runs work. The corners were Δpivot ±0.4, Δrp ±0.2, c_r 0.25/0.5, T = 1/3/20, both directions.
- **Friction:** every corner works at μ/μ_b = 0.5/0.5 and at 0.2/0.2. At μ = 0.6 (dry PETG-like), 3 of 16 runs stall, so the material must be PLA.
- **Head inertia:** works from 2.9e-6 to 1e-5.
- **Wheel inertia:** works from 8e-7 to 1.5e-5. The only failure is a harmless occasional tooth slip at J_w 8e-7 combined with the worst shallow corner.

**Why the cam-style "pressure angle ≤ 30–35°" rule does not apply.** This is an impulse escapement, not a continuously driven cam. The governing criterion is friction lock: the contact angle must stay below 90° − atan μ − margin. The computed worst case is 56–59°, against a 62.7° limit at μ 0.35 with 8° margin. The dynamics model friction explicitly and show no lock for μ ≤ 0.5.

**Dead points.** The knob drives the wheel directly with no linkage. The escapement's free channel stays open throughout the tolerance box in both directions.

### 2.5 Exact 2-D definitions (all skins)

Notation:

- ⊕ / ⊖: offset (round joins).
- Swept(X) = ∪ over ψ ∈ [−12.42°, 12.42°] of Rot_P(ψ)(X), in the world frame.
- SweptInv(X) = ∪ over ψ of Rot_P(−ψ)(X), in the head frame.
- open_t(X) = (X ⊖ t/2) ⊕ t/2. This removes slivers thinner than t.

**Head frame**

- Hub2D = disc(P, 7.0)
- Leg2D_i = stadium of width 7.0 from A_i = (±17.462, 11.667) (that is, 21.0·u_i) to B_i = (±11.0, 26.0). B_i must lie at least 3 mm inside Face2D.
- Face2D comes from the skin (§4.4).
- WheelEx2D = SweptInv(disc(O, 14.90))
- BallEx2D = SweptInv(disc(O, 19.00))
- **HeadBand2D** = [(Face2D ∪ Hub2D ∪ Leg2D_L ∪ Leg2D_R) − WheelEx2D] ∪ Finger2D_L ∪ Finger2D_R
- **FaceUp2D** = Face2D − BallEx2D. The minimum gap from the face to the ball rim over the full swing is 1.53–1.71 mm.

**World frame**

- Exposed2D = HeadBand2D − FaceUp2D. These are band parts not hidden under the head's own face.
- **Body2D** = round_r3( disc(O, 21.5) ∪ [Swept(Exposed2D) ⊕ 3.0] ∪ SkinBodyDecor2D ∪ PawFootprints2D ). The wall is at least 2.5 mm beyond every channel.
- Cavity2D = Swept(HeadBand2D) ⊕ 0.55
- **Fill2D** = open_1.6( Body2D − Cavity2D − disc(O, 14.80) ) ∪ StopPads2D
- **StopPads2D**: for s = ±1 and i = L, R:
  - Pad = [Rot_P(s·12.42°)(Leg2D_i) ⊕ 0.55] − Swept(HeadBand2D), intersected with disc(Rot_P(s·12.42°)(M_i), 3.0), where M_i = (A_i + B_i)/2 = (±14.23, 18.83).
  - This gives four pads. Each leg flank touches its pad exactly at ±12.42°.
- **Roof2D** = open_1.6( Body2D − disc(O, 17.10) − disc(P, 7.50) )
- RoofSweepInv = SweptInv(Roof2D ⊕ 0.55), in the head frame.
- **FaceMid2D** = FaceUp2D − RoofSweepInv
- **I3_2D** = FaceUp2D ∩ RoofSweepInv. This is where the face's front layer overhangs the roof, about 189 mm² for the kitty.
- **Backdrop2D** = round_r2( Body2D ∪ [Swept(FaceUp2D) ⊕ 2.0] ∪ SkinBackdrop2D )

### 3.4 Print orientation, layers, overhangs and bridges

**Orientation and slicing**

- One print, face up, with the back plate on the bed. Do not scale.
- 0.2 mm layers, 0.4 nozzle, no supports, no brim (the back plate is a large flat base).
- **The first layer has no moving gaps at all**, so elephant foot cannot fuse the mechanism. Use 0.1 elephant-foot compensation for looks only.
- Every working clearance is either a vertical wall with an XY gap, or a Z gap of one of these designed types:
  1. **Floating over skid ribs.** The head and wheel undersides (z 3.0) sit over back-plate ribs (z 2.0–2.6) at 0.40, with 1.00 elsewhere. The face's front layer in I3 sits over roof-top ribs (10.4–11.0) at 0.40.
  2. **Bridges with 1.0 mm air below.** The roof bridges the leg channels (span ≤ 13.0).
  3. **Bridges with small spans.** The umbrella plate bridges the tooth gaps (≤ 10.3, 0.6 over the pallets). The bore roofs bridge Ø8.7 (0.4 over the post tops).
  4. **45° self-supporting surfaces.** The umbrella cone, V-ridge and V-groove flanks, and paw lips.

**Rib layout**

- Back plate: arcs about P at r = 6.0 + 4.5·j (j = 0…8), clipped to Swept(HeadBand2D) − disc(O, 14.8). Rings about O at r 7.0, 11.0 and 13.8, clipped to disc(O, 14.3). Keep everything at least 0.3 mm clear of post root fillets.
- Roof top: arcs about P at r = 9.0 + 4.0·j (j = 0…7), clipped to Roof2D ∩ Swept(I3_2D ⊕ 0.5).
- The visible back-plate arcs read as cushion quilting, and the visible roof arcs read as a collar ruff.

**Overhang rule.** Any downward-facing area steeper than 45° from vertical must be one of:

- the bed,
- a listed bridge, or
- a listed rib-supported float.

Nothing else is allowed.

**Print pose.** Wheel at φ = +12.0° (Star2D rotated CCW; knob at 12.0°). Head at ψ = +5.96°. The kitty prints with a 6° curious head-tilt.

**Export**

- One 3MF: one object with three parts (frame, wheel, head) so per-part infill can be set. Also export one STL with three shells.
- Per-body STLs.
- STEP is optional.

## 4. Parametric model structure

### 4.1 Tool choice

- **Python + manifold3d** for everything solid. Use `CrossSection` (Clipper2: robust integer 2-D booleans and offsets) for all 2-D work and sweeps. Use `extrude` per Z band, `revolve` for the posts, bores, umbrella and keep-out, and `Manifold` booleans to assemble. This approach is fast and robust.
- **shapely/numpy** only for analysis: SDF grid, distances, C-space. shapely unions of many rotated copies threw topology exceptions in testing, so do the production sweeps in `CrossSection`.
- **build123d** is optional: B-rep fillets on skin outlines and STEP export.
- **OpenSCAD 2021.01** only to `import()` STLs for headless PNG renders. CGAL is too slow for the sweeps.
- **trimesh** for proximity, ray-cast thickness, mass properties and 3MF export.

### 4.2 Modules

1. `params.py`: one JSON or dict holding all named parameters:
   - escapement: `N, Rt, tooth_h, tip_frac, root_frac, r_f, rp, drho, m, tilt, psi_b`
   - layout: `post_d, bore_d, ridge_h, ridge_z, hub_r, leg_w, leg_A_r, leg_B, finger_L, finger_taper, R_u, R_hole_roof, R_hub_cut, body_r, wall, gap_xy, gap_rib, gap_field, sweep_allowance, ball_ex_r, wheel_ex_r, backdrop_margin, r_k, knob_d, knob_h, paw spans, rib pitches`
   - Z levels: `z_bp, z_band0, z_band1, z_roof0, z_roof1, z_front0, z_front1, z_feat`
   - print pose: `phi_print, psi_print`
   - skin name
2. `escapement.py`: `star2d()`, `pallet_centres()` (equations in §2.3), `fingers2d()`.
3. `sweep.py`: `swept(cs, pivot, psi_b, n≥100, allowance)`, `swept_inv()`. Implement with CrossSection rotate + batch union.
4. `core2d.py`: HeadBand2D, FaceUp2D, Exposed2D, Body2D, Cavity2D, Fill2D, StopPads2D, Roof2D, FaceMid2D, I3_2D, Backdrop2D, rib fields.
5. `solids.py`: extrusions per §2.6/§2.7; posts and V-ridges (revolve a triangle profile); bores and V-grooves; umbrella and keep-out (revolve); knob; paws (lip built as a stack of 0.2 mm slices or a hull of two offset sections); stepped top fillets; bottom chamfers.
6. `skins/kitty.py`, `skins/bee.py`, `skins/robot.py`: each skin implements the interface in §4.3.
7. `assemble.py`: pose bodies to the print pose, assert pairwise disjointness, export.
8. `verify/`: scripts for §5. Reuse `esc_layout2.py`, `static_map.py`, `esc_dyn3.py` and `run_hardbank.py`, fed from the CAD outlines and trimesh mass properties.

### 4.3 Skin interface (contract)

A skin supplies the following. The core derives everything else automatically.

- `face2d(C_h)`: polygon. It must contain disc(P, 7.5) and both leg ends B_i with ≥ 3 mm margin. No feature narrower than 6.0 mm, and outer corners r ≥ 2.
- `face_features()`: a list of (2-D shape, mode, depth). Raised features are 0.6 (z 15.4→16.0). Debossed features are 0.3–0.5. All stay ≥ 3 mm inside FaceUp2D's edge.
- `backdrop2d()`: extra outline unioned into Backdrop2D. The final outline must stay ≤ 64 W × 85 H.
- `body_decor2d()`: raised 1.6 reliefs (feet, tail and so on) on the roof. Each must lie inside Body2D and ≥ 2 mm outside Swept(FaceUp2D).
- `paw_style()`: plan outline inside the core paw spans, with top debossing.
- `wheel_relief2d()`: groove pattern for r ≤ 16.5, excluding a Ø14 zone around the knob.
- **Inertia check:** I_h about P from trimesh (solid PLA, 1.24 g/cm³) must be in [4.0, 8.0]e-6 kg·m², and the centre of mass 8–14 mm above P. If not, add closed pockets in FaceMid2D (walls ≥ 2.0) or resize the ears.

## 6. Child safety and print/finishing instructions

### Safety design

- **Three bodies, all larger than the small-parts cylinder:** wheel Ø36.0, head 41 mm minimum width, frame about 53 × 83 mm.
- **Nothing designed to detach.** Each moving body has two independent geometric captures (§3.3).
- **No springs or flexures.** Nothing can fatigue, creep or splinter.
- **Escapement sealed.** The nip is enclosed by the back plate behind, the umbrella in front, and the roof and fill around it. The only openings are 0.4–1.0 mm Z gaps and shear slits.
- **Exposed moving boundaries.** Each is a concentric constant gap, a Z overlap, or a slit under 2 mm:
  - umbrella rim to frame: 0.6 concentric / 0.9 overlap
  - face front layer edges sliding over the roof: 0.4–1.0 Z gap
  - face chin to ball rim: 1.5–1.7
  - knob to paw lip: 1.0 constant
  - head over backdrop: Z gap only, so the ears have no in-plane neighbours at all
- **Low energy.** The only power source is the child's finger. The head carries ≤ 6 mJ even at the fastest buzz, and the ear tip moves ≤ 1.5 m/s.
- **Robust shapes.** All edges r ≥ 1.0 (exterior ≥ 1.5). Ears, antennae and paws are at least 8 mm wide at the root and 12 mm thick in Z. The knob is Ø10 with a root fillet.
- **Noise.** At a hard push the buzz is loud, about 130 clicks/s.
- **Label:** "Ages 6+. Home 3D-printed toy, not certified to EN 71 / ASTM F963. An adult should inspect for cracks before each play session. Do not give to children who mouth toys."

### Material

- Use **PLA or PLA+ only**. The mechanism needs pallet friction μ ≤ 0.5.
- Do not use dry PETG: at μ ≈ 0.6 it can stall at worst-case tolerances.
- Avoid silk PLA (weak and higher shrink).

### Slicer settings

- 0.2 mm layers.
- 3 perimeters. Frame infill 20% gyroid. **Head and wheel at 100% infill** (part modifiers); this gives the computed inertia.
- 5 top / 5 bottom layers.
- Arachne is fine.
- Seam: rear/aligned. Paint the seam onto the outer back-plate and body outline, never on post or bore walls.
- Z-hop 0.4.
- Bridges: fan 100%, speed about 25 mm/s, "thick bridges" off.
- Max fan for overhangs.
- No supports, no brim.
- Expect about 2.5–3 h on an MK4 / A1 / P1S, and about 37 g.

### Freeing (break-in)

1. Let the bed cool below 30 °C before removing the print. Removing it hot can tack the floats.
2. Hold the body and rock the head left and right 10 times with gentle thumb pressure. You should feel crisp releases as the rib contacts let go.
3. Turn the knob slowly: 5 turns each way, then 30 s fast each way.
4. If the wheel will not move, look for strings in the slits around the ball and between the chin and the ball. Clear them with a pick, then retry.
5. Never use pliers.
6. No lubricant is needed in PLA.
7. Finally, pull the head and the ball firmly (about 20 N). Neither should move more than about 1 mm.

**Optional colour.** A filament swap at z 15.6 and back at z 16.2 prints the raised eyes, nose and mouth in black. The knob will get a decorative dark band. Never use stickers or glued eyes: they are small parts.

| Rib-supported floats tack (head and wheel over the back plate, about 1,590 mm² total; face front over roof ribs, about 190 mm²) | Stiff or frozen after printing | Cool fully, then break in. If still stuck, use the "loose" variant (rib gap 0.45, journals 0.40, swept gaps 0.60). Rib pitch can drop to 4.0 |
